lessons.title: What System Design Is and How to Approach It
lessons.content:
Picture a tea stall at the corner of your street. One person boils water, pours tea, takes the money and chats with customers. For ten customers an hour, that is perfect. Now picture a wedding with 5,000 guests. The same one person cannot do it. You need many cooks, many serving tables, a store room, people carrying food, a plan for when the gas runs out, and someone watching that every table got its food. Nobody plans a big wedding by cooking faster; they plan how the work is split, where things are kept and what happens when something goes wrong. System design is that wedding plan, but for software.

What system design is: System design is the work of deciding the parts of a large software system and how they connect, so that it does what users need, stays fast, does not lose data and keeps working when parts break. The parts are things like web servers, databases, caches, queues, load balancers and storage for files. The output is usually a diagram of boxes and arrows plus written reasons: why this database, why a cache here, what happens when this machine dies. Writing code that works for one user is the easy part. Making the same feature work for ten million users at once, without losing anyone's money, is the hard part.

Why it matters: Every app you use daily, like Facebook, YouTube, a bKash-style wallet or a Daraz-style shop, is used by millions of people at the same time. If a design is weak, the app becomes slow on Eid night, a payment is charged twice, or photos disappear. Fixing a bad design after millions of users arrive is very expensive, like rebuilding the foundation of a house while people live in it. That is why companies ask system design questions in senior engineering interviews, and why engineers who can design well are trusted with the most important work.

The five goals: Scalability means the system can handle more users by adding more machines, without a rewrite. Availability means it answers when people use it; it is measured as a percentage of time it is up, like 99.9 percent. Reliability means it gives correct results and does not lose data, even when parts fail. Performance means it is fast, usually measured as how long a request takes (latency) and how many requests it handles per second (throughput). Maintainability means engineers can understand, change and fix it easily years later. Good designs balance all five; pushing one to the extreme usually hurts another.

Three courses that sound alike: System Analysis & Design (deep-cse-4-6) asks "what should we build?": it talks to users, draws use cases and data flow diagrams, and decides features. System Design starts after that and asks "how will it survive a huge crowd?": how many servers, which database, where the cache sits. Distributed Systems (deep-cse-6-3) is the theory underneath: clocks, replication, consensus, CAP. In this course we use those ideas as ready-made tools. When we need replication or Raft, we recap in a few lines and point to the lesson there instead of teaching it again.

High-level and low-level design: High-level design (HLD) is the city map: which big parts exist and how data flows between them, for example "phone app talks to a load balancer, which sends requests to stateless API servers, which read from a cache and a database". Low-level design (LLD) zooms into one building: the classes, database tables, API fields and algorithms inside one service. This course is mostly about high-level design, with enough low-level detail (tables, APIs, IDs) to show the design really works.

What makes it hard, part 1, scale: One computer has limits. A good server might handle a few thousand simple requests per second and store a few terabytes. If your app needs 100,000 requests per second, one machine is simply not enough, so the work must be spread across many machines. The moment you have many machines, you must decide who stores which data and how they stay in agreement.

What makes it hard, part 2, failure: With one machine, failure is rare. With 1,000 machines, something is always broken. If each machine fails on average once in 1,000 days, then a fleet of 1,000 machines sees roughly one failure per day. Disks die, networks split, a whole data center can lose power. A good design assumes failure is normal and keeps working anyway.

What makes it hard, part 3, trade-offs: Almost every choice gives something and takes something. A cache makes reads fast but can show old data. Copying data to three machines makes it safer but writes become slower and cost more. Splitting an app into many small services lets teams work independently but makes debugging harder. There is rarely one correct answer. A good designer says "I chose X because our users care most about Y, and the cost is Z, which is acceptable here."

The step framework: Whether you are designing at work or in an interview, the same steps keep you from getting lost. Step 1, clarify requirements: what must the system do, and how well. Step 2, estimate: how many users, requests per second, how much storage. Step 3, define the API: the requests the client can make. Step 4, design the data model: what we store and how we look it up. Step 5, draw the high-level design: the main boxes and arrows. Step 6, deep dive into the hardest parts. Step 7, find bottlenecks and failure points, and discuss trade-offs. Lessons 02 to 17 teach the tools for each step; lessons 18 to 25 use all the steps on real case studies.

Step 1 and 2 in a tiny example: Suppose someone says "design a system for school exam results". First you ask: who uses it, how many students, do they only read results or also update them? Say 2 million students check results, mostly within the first hour after publishing. That is 2,000,000 / 3,600, about 556 requests per second on average in that hour, and the first few minutes will be much higher, maybe 5 times, so about 2,800 per second. Data is small (one row per student) and almost never changes after publishing. Already you can see the design: this is read heavy, so caching is the hero.

Step 3 and 4 in the same example: The API might be just one request: GET /results/{roll} returns the marks. The data model is one table: roll number, name, subject marks, GPA. Lookup is always by roll number, so the roll number is the key. Simple choices like these, made early, guide everything after.

Step 5, 6 and 7 in the same example: The high-level design: students' phones go to a CDN or cache first; misses go through a load balancer to a few API servers; servers read from a database with read replicas. Deep dive: since results never change after publishing, we can preload every result into the cache before 2 pm, so the database barely sees traffic. Bottleneck check: what if the cache machine dies? Use two cache copies. What if someone floods the site? Add rate limiting (lesson 14). In ten minutes we went from a vague idea to a plan that would actually survive result day.

Boxes-and-arrows vocabulary: You will meet these parts in every lesson, so here is a quick map. Client: the phone app or browser. DNS: turns a name into an IP address. Load balancer: spreads requests across servers. Web or API server: runs your code; ideally stateless, so any server can handle any request. Cache: fast memory store for popular data. Database: the long-term source of truth. Object storage: cheap storage for big files like photos and videos. CDN: copies of files on servers near users. Message queue: a waiting line for work that can be done later. Workers: programs that take jobs from the queue. Monitoring: dashboards and alerts that show the health of everything.

Functional thinking vs non-functional thinking: A beginner draws boxes for features: a login box, a payment box, a search box. A designer also asks quality questions for each arrow: how many requests per second travel this arrow, how long can the user wait, what if the box at the other end is down? Those numbers and failure questions are what turn a drawing into a design.

Real-life example 1, a bKash-style wallet on Eid night: Normal evenings might see a steady flow of transfers, but on Eid eve millions of people send salami at the same time. A designer for such a wallet would first list requirements (transfers must never be lost or doubled; balance must be correct), estimate the peak, then choose: a strongly consistent database for balances, replicas for safety, a queue for SMS confirmations so a slow SMS gateway never blocks a payment, and rate limits to stop bots. This is illustrative, not a claim about any company's real internals, but it shows how requirements lead to choices.

Real-life example 2, a cricket score app during a Bangladesh vs India match: Millions of fans refresh the score every few seconds, but the score changes only once per ball, roughly every 30 to 40 seconds. Requirements: very read heavy, a few seconds of delay is fine, never go down during the last over. Design: put the latest score in a cache and on a CDN with a short time to live of a few seconds, and push updates to open apps instead of having each phone ask again and again (lesson 05). The single writer, the scorer, updates one record; millions of readers never touch the database.

How this course is organised: Lessons 02 and 03 cover requirements and estimation. Lesson 04 walks the journey from one server to millions. Lessons 05 to 09 cover networking, APIs, load balancing, caching and CDNs. Lessons 10 to 13 cover databases, data modeling, scaling databases and queues. Lessons 14 to 17 cover rate limiting, reliability, observability with deployment and security, and microservices. Lessons 18 to 24 are classic case studies: URL shortener, chat, news feed, notifications, autocomplete, video streaming and ride-hailing. Lesson 25 is a flash-sale capstone plus an interview playbook.

Common mistakes: The biggest mistake is jumping straight to boxes without asking questions. You might design a giant system for something only a thousand people will use. The second is ignoring numbers: "add a cache" means nothing until you know how much data and how many reads. The third is over-engineering: microservices, sharding and five databases for a small app is a bad design too, because every extra part costs money and can break. The fourth is forgetting failure: always ask "what happens if this box dies?" The fifth is presenting one answer as perfect instead of naming its trade-offs.

What exams and interviews ask: Define system design and its goals (scalability, availability, reliability, performance, maintainability). Explain high-level vs low-level design. List the steps of a design approach. Compare vertical and horizontal scaling. And the classic open question: "Design X", where X is a URL shortener, a chat app or a news feed. Interviewers mostly judge how you think: do you clarify, estimate, choose with reasons and spot weak points.

Recap: System design plans the parts of a big software system and how they connect so it stays correct, fast and alive under huge load and constant failure. It differs from System Analysis & Design (what to build) and builds on Distributed Systems (the theory). It is hard because of scale, failure and trade-offs. A steady seven-step framework, requirements, estimation, API, data model, high-level design, deep dives, bottlenecks, keeps you on track. In the next lesson we start with step one: writing requirements that are clear enough to design from.
key_points: System design decides the parts of a big software system and how they connect so it stays correct, fast and available under huge load.
System Analysis & Design asks what to build; System Design asks how it survives the crowd; Distributed Systems gives the theory underneath.
High-level design is the city map of services and data flow; low-level design is the inside of one service: classes, tables, APIs.
Scale, failure and trade-offs are what make it hard; with 1,000 machines something is always broken.
Use the seven steps: requirements, estimation, API, data model, high-level design, deep dives, bottlenecks and trade-offs.
Common parts: client, DNS, load balancer, stateless servers, cache, database, object storage, CDN, queue, workers, monitoring.
There is rarely one right answer; a good design names its choices, the reasons and the costs.
lessons.tip: Before drawing any box, say out loud: who uses it, how many, what must never go wrong. Those three answers shape every later choice.
lessons.task: Take an app you use daily (for example a cricket score app). On paper write three functional requirements, two non-functional ones, then draw five boxes (client, load balancer, servers, cache, database) and write one line on what each does in that app.

quiz.q: Which question is System Design (not System Analysis & Design) mainly about?
options: How many servers, which database and what happens when a machine dies?
What colour should the buttons be?
Who should be on the project team?
quiz.explain: System Analysis & Design decides what to build; System Design decides how it is built to survive huge load and failures.

quiz.q: A fleet has 1,000 machines and each fails on average once every 1,000 days. About how often does some machine fail?
options: Never, if the code is correct
quiz.explain: 1,000 machines each failing once per 1,000 days gives about 1,000 / 1,000 = 1 failure per day, so failure must be treated as normal.

quiz.q: What is the right first step when asked to design a system?
quiz.explain: Without knowing what the system must do and how well, every later choice is a guess.

quiz.q: 2 million students check exam results within one hour. What is the average request rate in that hour?
quiz.explain: 2,000,000 / 3,600 seconds is about 556 requests per second on average, and the first minutes will be several times higher.

quiz.q: Which statement about trade-offs in system design is correct?
options: A perfect design has no trade-offs
A cache makes reads faster but can return old data
More replicas always make writes faster
quiz.explain: Almost every choice gives something and costs something; a cache trades freshness for speed.

lessons.title: Requirements: Deciding What the System Must Do and How Well
lessons.content:
Imagine your uncle asks a builder, "Build me a house." A careless builder starts pouring cement right away. A good builder first asks: how many people will live there, how many floors, do you need a garage, what is the budget, does the area flood in the monsoon? The same land could become a one-room tin shed or a six-storey building, and both would be "a house". Software is the same. "Build a chat app" could mean a classroom chat for 40 students or WhatsApp for two billion people. Requirements are the questions and answers that tell you which one you are building.

What requirements are: A requirement is a clear statement of something the system must do or a quality it must have. In system design we split them into two kinds. Functional requirements describe behaviour: what users can do. Non-functional requirements describe qualities: how fast, how reliable, how big, how safe. Both are needed. A design that has every feature but takes ten seconds to load fails, and so does a design that is lightning fast but cannot send money.

Why this step comes first: Every later choice depends on requirements. Whether you need a cache depends on how read heavy the system is. Whether you need strong consistency depends on whether stale data hurts anyone. How many servers you need depends on how many users and requests. If you skip this step, you are guessing, and in interviews skipping it is the most common reason candidates fail even with good technical knowledge.

Functional requirements: Write them as short user actions, usually "a user can ...". For a Daraz-style shop: a user can search products, view a product page, add items to a cart, place an order, pay, and track the order. A seller can add products and update stock. Keep the list short and focused on the core. In an interview you agree on three to five core features and say clearly what is out of scope, for example "reviews and recommendations are out of scope for now". Scope control matters because you cannot design everything in 45 minutes, or in one sprint.

Non-functional requirements: These are the qualities. The most common are: scale (how many users and requests), latency (how fast each request must be), availability (how much of the time it must be up), durability (how sure we are data is never lost), consistency (whether everyone must see the latest data immediately), security and privacy, and cost. Each one should become a number or a clear rule where possible. "Fast" is not a requirement; "product page loads within 200 ms for 99 percent of requests" is.

Scoping questions to ask: Good designers carry a small set of questions. Who are the users and how many: daily active users (DAU) and peak? What are the main actions, and how often does each happen? Is it read heavy or write heavy? How big is each item (a text message is about 100 bytes, a photo is hundreds of kilobytes)? How long must data be kept? Which data must never be wrong, and which can be a bit stale? Is it global or mainly one country? Are there legal rules, like keeping financial data inside Bangladesh? What must happen when things fail?

Read/write ratio: This one number shapes a design more than almost anything else. Worked example for our shop: say 5 million users visit per day and each views about 20 pages. That is 100 million page views per day, about 1,157 per second on average. Orders might be 200,000 per day, about 2.3 per second. The ratio of reads to writes is about 500 to 1. So the shop is heavily read heavy: caching product pages and using a CDN for images will matter a lot, while the order path is small in volume but must be correct.

Latency and why averages lie: Latency is the time from sending a request to getting the answer, measured in milliseconds (ms). Do not judge it by the average. Worked example with 10 response times in ms: 80, 90, 95, 100, 110, 120, 130, 150, 400, 900. The average is 2,175 / 10 = 217.5 ms, which describes almost nobody: eight requests were faster than 160 ms and two were much slower. Percentiles are better. The p50 (median) is the value half the requests are at or below; using the nearest-rank method on our sorted list, that is the 5th value, 110 ms. The p90 is the 9th value, 400 ms. The p99 here is the 10th value, 900 ms. The p99 tells you how the unlucky 1 percent feel, and at millions of requests that 1 percent is tens of thousands of real people.

Why tail latency matters even more at scale: If loading one page calls 10 backend services, and each service has a 1 percent chance of being slow, the chance that at least one is slow is 1 minus 0.99 to the power 10, about 9.6 percent. So a "rare" slowness becomes common for the whole page. That is why requirements usually set p99 or p95 targets, not averages.

Availability and the nines: Availability is the fraction of time the system is working. It is often written as "nines". 99 percent sounds great, but it allows 87.6 hours of downtime per year, more than three and a half days. 99.9 percent (three nines) allows 8.76 hours per year, or about 43 minutes per month. 99.99 percent (four nines) allows about 52.6 minutes per year. 99.999 percent (five nines) allows about 5.3 minutes per year. Every extra nine is ten times stricter and usually much more expensive, because it needs more redundancy, automatic failover and careful deployments. So choose the nines the business truly needs: a payment system may need four nines, an internal report tool may be fine with two.

Durability: Durability means data, once accepted, is not lost. It is different from availability. A system can be down for an hour (not available) but still have every byte safe (durable). For a wallet, durability of the ledger is the top requirement; losing a transaction is far worse than a short outage. Durability comes from writing data to disk and keeping copies on several machines and in more than one place. Object storage services in the S3 style advertise designs aimed at eleven nines of durability, which shows how seriously stored files are protected.

Consistency needs per feature: Not every feature needs the same consistency. Recall from Distributed Systems (deep-cse-6-3-16 and 6-3-17) that strong consistency costs latency and sometimes availability during a network partition. So decide per feature. Balance and order payment: strong consistency, the user must never see wrong money. Product stock on a listing page: can be a few seconds stale, but the final checkout must check the real stock. Like counts, view counts, "people also bought": eventual consistency is fine. Writing this down early stops you from paying the high price of strong consistency everywhere.

SLA and SLO, a recap: A service level objective (SLO) is an internal target, like "99.9 percent of requests succeed and p99 latency is under 300 ms over 30 days". A service level agreement (SLA) is a promise to customers, usually with money back if broken, and is set looser than the SLO so the team has a safety margin. The measured value is the service level indicator (SLI). The idea of an error budget, how much failure the SLO still allows, was worked in deep-cse-6-3-25. In design work, the SLO is where your latency and availability requirements end up.

Constraints: Constraints are limits you must work within, not features. Budget: a startup cannot run 500 servers. Team: three engineers cannot run twenty microservices well. Time: launch in two months. Compliance: financial or health data may have to stay inside the country, and some rules require keeping records for years. Existing systems: maybe you must use the company's current database. Constraints often decide between two designs that look equally good on paper.

A worked requirement list for a Daraz-style shop: Functional: search products; view product page; cart; place order; pay; track order; sellers manage products and stock. Out of scope for now: reviews, chat with seller, recommendations. Scale: 5 million DAU, 100 million page views per day, peak during a sale about 10 times normal. Latency: product page p99 under 300 ms; search p99 under 500 ms. Availability: browsing 99.9 percent; checkout and payment 99.99 percent. Durability: no confirmed order is ever lost. Consistency: payment and order records strong; stock shown on pages may be stale by a few seconds but checkout must be exact; ratings eventual. Constraints: payment records kept for years, small team, limited budget. With this one page, a reader already knows that caching, a CDN, a strong database for orders and protection against sale spikes are central.

From requirement to design hint: Each requirement quietly suggests a building block. Very read heavy points to caches and CDNs (lessons 08 and 09). Sudden spikes point to queues and rate limits (lessons 13 and 14). Strict money rules point to a relational database with transactions (lesson 10). Huge write streams point to partitioning (lesson 12). Four nines points to redundancy in every layer and automatic failover (lesson 15). Reading your requirement list this way gives you a first sketch before you draw a single box.

Real-life example 1, a university admission result site: Requirements: show results by roll number, about 300,000 applicants, nearly all in the first hour, read only, results must be exactly correct and identical for everyone. Non-functional: survive the first-minute spike, p99 under one second is acceptable. These requirements point to a simple design: precompute and cache every result, put a static page behind a CDN, and keep the database almost idle. Many slow result sites in the past were not short of hardware; they skipped this kind of thinking.

Real-life example 2, a ride-hailing app like Pathao: Functional: rider requests a ride, nearby drivers are offered it, a driver accepts, both see live location, payment at the end. Non-functional: matching within a few seconds, location updates every few seconds from every active driver, two drivers must never get the same ride (strong consistency on the assignment), but the dots on the map can be a second or two old (eventual is fine). Writing these down tells you the hard parts before you draw anything: a huge stream of location writes and a small, strict assignment step. We will design this in lesson 24.

Common mistakes: Writing vague words like "fast", "scalable", "secure" with no numbers. Listing twenty features and designing none deeply. Forgetting non-functional requirements entirely and drawing only feature boxes. Treating all data as needing the same consistency. Choosing five nines without asking whether the business needs it, or whether the budget allows it. Forgetting the peak: designing for the daily average when the real danger is Eid night or a flash sale.

What exams and interviews ask: Define and give examples of functional and non-functional requirements. Convert availability percentages into downtime. Explain why percentiles are better than averages, and compute a median or p90 from a short list. Explain durability vs availability. In design interviews, the first five minutes are judged on whether you ask good scoping questions and write a short, agreed list.

Recap: Requirements turn a vague idea into something you can design. Functional requirements list what users can do; non-functional requirements set numbers for scale, latency, availability, durability, consistency, security and cost. Use percentiles like p99, not averages. Every extra nine of availability is ten times stricter. Decide consistency per feature. Respect constraints like budget, team size and law. Next lesson we turn those requirements into numbers with back-of-the-envelope estimation.
key_points: Functional requirements say what users can do; non-functional requirements say how fast, reliable, big, safe and cheap.
Turn every quality into a number: 'p99 under 300 ms' instead of 'fast'.
The read/write ratio (for example 500 to 1 for a shop) strongly shapes the design.
Averages hide slow requests; use percentiles. In 80..900 ms samples the average is 217.5 ms but p50 is 110 ms and p99 is 900 ms.
99.9 percent allows 8.76 hours of downtime a year; 99.99 percent allows about 52.6 minutes; each nine is ten times stricter.
Durability (never lose data) differs from availability (being up right now).
Decide consistency per feature: money strong, like counts eventual.
Constraints such as budget, team size and data-location laws often decide between designs.
lessons.tip: Keep a fixed list of ten scoping questions on a card (users, peak, actions, read/write, item size, retention, consistency, region, law, failure) and ask them every time.
lessons.task: Pick an app like Chaldal or a cricket score app. Write 4 functional requirements, 1 out-of-scope item, and 5 non-functional requirements, each with a number (users, p99 latency, availability nines, retention, consistency).

quiz.q: Which of these is a non-functional requirement?
options: A user can add an item to the cart
Product pages load within 300 ms for 99 percent of requests
A user can track an order
quiz.explain: It describes a quality (latency) with a number, not a user action.

quiz.q: Response times are 80, 90, 95, 100, 110, 120, 130, 150, 400, 900 ms. What is the median (p50) by nearest rank?
quiz.explain: Sorted, the 5th of 10 values is 110 ms; 217.5 ms is the average, pulled up by the two slow requests.

quiz.q: About how much downtime per year does 99.9 percent availability allow?
quiz.explain: 0.1 percent of 8,760 hours is 8.76 hours per year.

quiz.q: A system is down for one hour but loses no data. What can you say?
options: Its availability dropped but durability held
Its durability dropped but availability held
Both durability and availability are perfect
quiz.explain: Availability is about being up; durability is about never losing accepted data.

quiz.q: Which feature most clearly needs strong consistency?
options: Number of views on a video
quiz.explain: Showing wrong money is harmful; the others can be a little stale without hurting anyone.

lessons.title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation: Quick Numbers That Shape a Design
lessons.content:
Before a wedding, the family does quick math on a scrap of paper: 5,000 guests, about 250 grams of rice each, so roughly 1,250 kg of rice; each table seats 10, so 500 table-sittings; if people eat in three waves, about 170 tables are needed. Nobody needs the exact number of grains. They need numbers good enough to book the right hall and the right number of cooks. In system design this paper-scrap math is called back-of-the-envelope estimation: rough calculations, done in a few minutes, that tell you how big each part of the system must be.

What it is: Estimation turns requirements (lesson 02) into numbers: requests per second, storage per year, network bandwidth, number of servers and size of the cache. The goal is the right order of magnitude, meaning the right number of zeros. Whether you need 580 or 600 requests per second does not change the design. Whether you need 600 or 60,000 changes everything: one server versus a whole fleet.

Why it matters: Numbers stop you from two opposite mistakes. Without them you might build a huge distributed system for a load one laptop could handle, wasting money and adding things that can break. Or you might build something tiny that falls over on launch day. Estimation also reveals the real bottleneck early: sometimes it is storage, sometimes network bandwidth, sometimes the number of writes per second, and each one leads to a different design.

Units and powers of two: Data sizes go up in steps of about a thousand. 2 to the power 10 is 1,024, close to a thousand, and is a kilobyte (KB). 2 to the power 20 is about a million, a megabyte (MB). 2 to the power 30 is about a billion, a gigabyte (GB). 2 to the power 40 is about a trillion, a terabyte (TB). 2 to the power 50 is a petabyte (PB). For estimates, treat each step as exactly 1,000; the small error does not matter. Useful sizes to remember: a character of English text is 1 byte (a Bangla character in UTF-8 is usually 3 bytes); a short text message with its details is about 100 bytes to 1 KB; a compressed phone photo is a few hundred KB to a few MB; one minute of HD video is tens of MB.

Bits versus bytes: Network speeds are measured in bits per second (Mbps, Gbps), while storage is in bytes. One byte is 8 bits. So 1 GB per second of data needs 8 Gbps of network. Mixing these up gives answers 8 times wrong, one of the most common slips.

Latency numbers every designer should know: You do not need exact values, only rough sizes, because they differ by thousands of times. Reading from main memory (RAM) takes about 100 nanoseconds. A random read from an SSD takes about 100 microseconds, roughly a thousand times slower than memory. A seek on a spinning hard disk takes about 10 milliseconds, about a hundred times slower than an SSD. A round trip between two machines in the same data center is about half a millisecond. A round trip from Dhaka to a server in Singapore is around 50 ms, and to Europe or the USA it is a few hundred ms, limited by the speed of light in fibre. Lesson to take away: memory is far faster than disk, and a network trip across the world is far slower than anything inside one data center. That is why caches live in memory and why we put servers or CDN copies near users.

From users to requests per second: Start from daily active users (DAU) and how many requests each makes. Worked: 10 million DAU, each making 5 requests per day, gives 50 million requests per day. A day has 86,400 seconds, so the average is 50,000,000 / 86,400, about 579 requests per second, which we call QPS (queries per second). A quick mental trick is to round a day to 100,000 seconds: 50 million divided by 100,000 is 500, close enough.

Peak factor: Traffic is not flat. People use apps more in the evening, and much more during events. Designers multiply the average by a peak factor, often 2 to 3 for a normal daily peak, and maybe 10 or more for special events like Eid night, a flash sale or a big cricket match. With 579 average QPS and a peak factor of 3, plan for about 1,700 QPS. The system must survive the peak, not the average.

Separate reads from writes: Estimate reads and writes separately, because they scale differently. Reads can be served by caches and replicas; writes must reach the main copy of the data. A system with 17,000 reads per second and 70 writes per second needs a very different design from one with 17,000 writes per second.

Storage: Storage per day equals new items per day times size per item. Then multiply by days kept, and by the number of copies. Do not forget replication: if every file is stored 3 times for safety, real storage is 3 times bigger. Also leave room for growth, because next year usually has more users than this year.

Servers from QPS: If one server can handle a known number of requests per second, the server count is peak QPS divided by that number, plus spare capacity. The per-server number depends heavily on what each request does; a simple cached read might allow thousands per second per server, while a heavy request might allow only tens. In estimates we state an assumption, like "1,000 QPS per server", and move on.

Cache memory with the 80/20 rule: In many systems a small part of the data gets most of the traffic: roughly 20 percent of items get 80 percent of reads. So instead of caching everything, cache the hot 20 percent. Cache size equals number of items in the hot set times item size.

A full worked example, a photo-sharing app: Assumptions: 10 million DAU; 2 million photos uploaded per day; average photo size 500 KB; each user views 50 photos per day; photo metadata (owner, time, caption, location) about 1 KB; photos kept forever; 3 copies of each photo; peak factor 3.

Worked, uploads: 2,000,000 / 86,400 is about 23 uploads per second on average, about 70 at peak. Uploads are clearly not the hard part.

Worked, storage: 2,000,000 photos times 500 KB is 1,000,000,000 KB, which is 1 TB per day. A year is 365 TB. With 3 copies, about 1,095 TB, roughly 1.1 PB per year. That is far too much for one machine, so photos go to object storage built for petabytes (lesson 10), not into the database. Metadata: 2 million times 365 times 1 KB is about 730 GB per year, which a well-run database can hold.

Worked, reads: 10,000,000 users times 50 views is 500 million views per day, about 5,787 per second on average and about 17,400 per second at peak. Reads outnumber uploads by about 250 to 1. This is a read-heavy system.

Worked, bandwidth: If each view downloads a 500 KB photo, average outgoing data is 5,787 times 500 KB, about 2.9 GB per second, which is about 23 Gbps. Incoming upload data is 23 times 500 KB, about 11.6 MB per second, roughly 93 Mbps. Outgoing traffic is the giant, so a CDN (lesson 09) must serve the photos, and smaller thumbnails should be used in feeds.

Worked, servers and cache: If one API server handles 1,000 metadata requests per second, the peak of about 17,400 needs about 18 servers; with 30 percent headroom, plan about 23. For the cache, suppose most views go to photos from the last 30 days: 30 times 2 million is 60 million photos, times 1 KB of metadata is 60 GB. The hot 20 percent is about 12 GB, which fits comfortably in the memory of a single cache server, with a second one as a copy. In five short calculations we learned: object storage for photos, a CDN for delivery, a modest server fleet, and a small metadata cache.

Handy shortcuts: One request per second all day is about 86,400, roughly 100,000 requests per day. So 1 million requests per day is about 12 per second, and 1 billion per day is about 12,000 per second. 1 KB per second all day is about 86 MB per day. Memorising these few anchors lets you convert in your head and catch silly answers quickly, like a "chat app" that somehow needs a petabyte per day.

Sanity check: when is one machine enough? After the numbers, ask honestly whether a single good server, with a copy for safety, would cope. A modern server has tens of CPU cores, hundreds of GB of memory and several TB of SSD. If your peak is 200 QPS and your data is 50 GB, the honest design is one database server with a replica, and that is a strength, not a weakness. Estimation exists as much to stop over-engineering as to prevent overload.

Real-life example 1, an SMS OTP service in Bangladesh: Suppose a bank sends a one-time password for each login, and 3 million logins happen per day. That is about 35 SMS per second on average, maybe 350 per second at a 10 times peak on salary day. Each SMS row stored for audit is about 200 bytes, so 3 million times 200 bytes is 600 MB per day, about 219 GB per year. The math says storage is small, but the SMS provider's sending limit and cost per message are the real constraints. Estimation pointed straight at the true bottleneck.

Real-life example 2, live cricket scores: A match app has 5 million people watching, and each phone asks for the score every 10 seconds. That is 500,000 requests per second, a huge number, for data that changes about once every 30 to 40 seconds. The estimate shouts that polling is wasteful: pushing updates over open connections (lesson 05), or serving the score from a CDN with a few seconds of caching, removes almost all of that load.

Common mistakes: Confusing bits and bytes (8 times wrong). Forgetting replication when estimating storage (3 times wrong). Designing for the average instead of the peak. Spending ten minutes on exact arithmetic instead of rounding. Forgetting units in the answer; "400" means nothing, "400 GB per day" means a lot. Assuming every request costs the same. And not writing assumptions down, so nobody can check or change them later.

What exams and interviews ask: Convert DAU and actions per user into QPS. Estimate storage for a year with replication. Estimate bandwidth and convert between bytes and bits. Recall rough latency sizes (memory vs SSD vs disk vs network). Explain why the peak matters. Interviewers mostly watch whether you state assumptions clearly, round sensibly and draw a design conclusion from each number.

Recap: Back-of-the-envelope estimation gives the right order of magnitude in minutes. Remember thousand-steps from KB to PB, 8 bits per byte, and the rough latency ladder from memory to disk to network. Compute QPS from DAU, apply a peak factor, split reads and writes, compute storage with replicas, bandwidth, server count and cache size with the 80/20 rule. Every number should end in a design decision. Next lesson we watch one small server grow, step by step, into a system for millions.
key_points: Estimation aims for the right order of magnitude, the number of zeros, not exact values.
KB, MB, GB, TB, PB each step about 1,000; 1 byte = 8 bits, so 1 GB/s is about 8 Gbps.
Latency ladder: memory about 100 ns, SSD read about 100 microseconds, disk seek about 10 ms, Dhaka-Singapore round trip about 50 ms.
QPS = DAU x requests per user / 86,400; 10 M x 5 / 86,400 is about 579.
Multiply by a peak factor (2-3 daily, 10+ for events) and estimate reads and writes separately.
Storage = items per day x size x days kept x copies; forgetting replicas is a common 3x error.
Servers = peak QPS / per-server QPS plus headroom; cache the hot 20 percent of data.
Each number should lead to a design decision, such as object storage, a CDN or a cache.
lessons.tip: Write every assumption in a small box at the top of the page before calculating. It keeps the math honest and lets someone else change one number and redo it in seconds.
lessons.task: Estimate for a food-delivery app: 2 million DAU, each opens 8 restaurant pages a day, 300,000 orders a day, 2 KB per order record kept for 5 years with 3 copies. Compute average and peak (x3) read QPS, order write QPS, and total order storage. Check with a calculator.

quiz.q: 10 million daily users each make 5 requests a day. What is the average QPS, roughly?
quiz.explain: 50,000,000 / 86,400 is about 579 requests per second.

quiz.q: 2 million photos of 500 KB each are uploaded per day and stored with 3 copies. About how much storage is needed per year?
quiz.explain: 1 TB per day x 365 = 365 TB, times 3 copies is about 1,095 TB, roughly 1.1 PB.

quiz.q: Outgoing data is about 2.9 GB per second. What network speed is that?
quiz.explain: Multiply bytes by 8: 2.9 x 8 is about 23 gigabits per second.

quiz.q: Which is the slowest?
options: Round trip inside one data center
Round trip from Dhaka to a server in the USA
quiz.explain: Crossing the world takes hundreds of milliseconds, far slower than memory, SSD or a local network hop.

quiz.q: Why do designers multiply average QPS by a peak factor?
options: Because the system must survive the busiest moments, not the average
Because averages are always too high
To reduce the number of servers
quiz.explain: Traffic spikes in evenings and events like Eid or a flash sale; designing only for the average fails exactly when it matters.

lessons.title: From One Server to Millions: The Scaling Journey
lessons.content:
Think of a small biryani shop in Old Dhaka. On day one, the owner cooks, serves, takes money and washes plates. As word spreads, he hires a cashier so he can focus on cooking. Then a second cook. Then he keeps the rice and meat in a separate store room. Soon he opens more counters, puts a person at the door to send customers to the shortest queue, keeps ready-made plates for the most popular order, and opens a branch in Uttara. Each step solved one problem and created a new one: more cooks need the same recipe, more branches need the same prices. Software systems grow exactly like this, one bottleneck at a time.

What this lesson is: We follow one imaginary app, a recipe-sharing site called "RannaGhor", from its first user to millions. At each step we ask three questions: what problem forced this step, what the step does, and what new problem it brings. This journey introduces almost every building block of the course in the order you would actually need them. Later lessons go deep into each block; here we see how they fit together.

Step 1, a single server: Everything runs on one machine: the web server, the application code and the database. A user types rannaghor.com, DNS returns the server's IP address, the browser sends HTTP requests, and the server answers. This is simple, cheap and perfectly fine for the first few thousand users. Problems: if this one machine dies, everything is down, and the web code and the database fight for the same CPU, memory and disk.

Step 2, separate the database: Move the database to its own machine. Now the web tier and data tier can be sized independently: the web server needs CPU for code, the database needs memory and fast disk. You can also restart the web server for a code update without touching the data. New problem: still one web server and one database, each a single point of failure (SPOF), meaning one broken part takes the whole system down.

Step 3, vertical vs horizontal scaling: As users grow, the server gets busy. Vertical scaling (scale up) means buying a bigger machine: more CPU cores, more memory. It is simple and needs no code changes, which is why it is a smart first move. But it has limits: there is a biggest machine you can buy, big machines cost much more per unit of power, and it is still one machine, so still a SPOF. Horizontal scaling (scale out) means adding more ordinary machines side by side. It has no hard ceiling and gives redundancy, but the software must be designed so that many machines can share the work. For the web tier, that leads to the next step.

Step 4, make the web tier stateless: If server A remembers that user Rina is logged in, and her next request goes to server B, server B does not know her. That memory of a user between requests is called state, here session state. The fix is to make web servers stateless: no user-specific data is kept only in a server's own memory. Session data moves to a shared store (a cache like Redis or the database), or into a signed token the client sends with each request (lessons on sessions and tokens in deep-cse-5-3-20). Now any server can handle any request, and you can add or remove servers freely. This one idea is what makes horizontal scaling of the web tier easy.

Step 5, add a load balancer: With several stateless web servers, users need a single address. A load balancer sits in front, receives all requests at one public IP and forwards each to a healthy server, for example in turn (round robin). If server 2 dies, health checks notice and it stops receiving traffic; users barely notice. Servers can now sit on a private network, reachable only through the load balancer, which also improves security. Worked: if one web server handles 1,000 requests per second and peak is 3,500, four servers behind a load balancer cover it, and a fifth gives room to lose one. New problem: the load balancer itself must not be a SPOF, so it is run as a pair (lesson 07).

Step 6, database replication: Now the database is the bottleneck and the biggest SPOF. Recall from deep-cse-6-3-14 that with leader-follower (primary-replica) replication, one primary takes all writes and copies its changes to replicas. Reads can go to replicas. Worked: if one database handles 5,000 reads per second and the app needs 18,000, a primary plus three replicas give four copies to read from, about 20,000 reads per second. If the primary fails, a replica can be promoted. New problems: replicas lag slightly behind, so a user might not see their own fresh write if the read hits a replica (lesson 12 shows fixes), and writes still go to just one machine.

Step 7, add a cache: Many requests ask for the same things: the top 100 recipes, a popular recipe's page. Reading them from the database every time wastes work. A cache keeps recent answers in memory. The app checks the cache first; on a hit it answers in about a millisecond, on a miss it reads the database and stores the result for next time with a time to live (TTL). Worked: with 18,000 reads per second and a 90 percent hit ratio, only 1,800 reads per second reach the database, ten times less. New problems: cached data can be stale, and the cache needs memory and its own failure plan (lesson 08).

Step 8, add a CDN for static files: Images, videos, CSS and JavaScript files are the same for everyone. A content delivery network (CDN) copies them to servers spread around the world, close to users. A user in Sylhet fetches recipe photos from a nearby edge server instead of from the origin. This removes most bandwidth from your own servers and cuts page load time. New problem: when a file changes, old copies may linger, so you version file names or invalidate copies (lesson 09).

Step 9, a message queue and workers: Some work is slow and does not need to finish before replying, such as resizing an uploaded photo into four sizes, sending a welcome email or updating search indexes. Instead of making the user wait, the web server drops a job onto a message queue and replies immediately; separate worker machines take jobs from the queue and do them. If uploads spike, the queue grows and workers catch up; you can add more workers independently. Recall the details of brokers and delivery guarantees from deep-cse-6-3-06. New problem: work is now asynchronous, so jobs may run twice or fail and must be retried safely (lesson 13).

Step 10, multiple data centers: One data center can lose power, network or cooling. For high availability and for users far apart, run the system in two or more data centers, for example one in Dhaka and one in Singapore. GeoDNS or a global load balancer sends each user to a nearby healthy site. If one site fails, traffic moves to the other. New and hard problems: data must be replicated between sites far apart, which raises the consistency choices of CAP and PACELC (deep-cse-6-3-17), and deployments and failover must be tested regularly (lesson 15).

Step 11, sharding the database: Eventually writes or total data outgrow even a big primary. Sharding splits data across many databases, for example by user id, so each holds only a slice (deep-cse-6-3-22). Worked: 400 GB of data and 8,000 writes per second over 4 shards is about 100 GB and 2,000 writes per second each. New problems: queries across users become harder, a celebrity user can create a hot shard, and adding shards means moving data (lesson 12).

Step 12, logging, metrics and automation: With dozens of machines you can no longer log in to each one to check. You need central logs, metrics like requests per second, error rate and p99 latency, alerts that wake someone when they break, and automation for deploying code and adding servers. Without these, the big system is a dark room (lesson 16).

What the final picture looks like: Put together, a request now travels like this: DNS points the user to the nearest data center; static files come from the CDN; dynamic requests hit a load balancer, then one of many stateless web servers; the server checks the cache, and on a miss reads a replica or writes to the right shard's primary; slow side jobs go to a queue for workers; and every step reports logs and metrics.

The pattern behind all steps: Every step follows the same loop: measure, find the current bottleneck, apply the simplest fix that removes it, and accept the new trade-off it brings. You do not add a CDN, shards and three data centers on day one. You add them when numbers say you need them. The order above is typical, but a video app might need a CDN at step 2, and a wallet might need multiple data centers before it needs sharding.

Real-life example 1, a news portal on election night: A Bangladeshi news site normally serves a modest crowd, but on election result night traffic may jump many times over. Following the journey: articles are mostly the same for everyone, so a CDN and a cache absorb most reads; the stateless web tier behind a load balancer can grow by adding servers ahead of the night; the database barely notices because almost every read is a cache hit. Live result counts can be refreshed into the cache every few seconds by a worker, instead of each visitor querying the database.

Real-life example 2, a growing e-commerce startup: A Dhaka startup might start on one rented server. Months later, slow pages lead them to move the database to its own server and add a cache. A big sale campaign leads them to add a load balancer and three web servers, with sessions in a shared cache. Email and SMS order confirmations go into a queue after a slow SMS gateway once blocked checkouts. Only years later, if ever, do they shard. Each change was a response to a measured pain, not a guess.

Common mistakes: Jumping to microservices and sharding on day one. Keeping sessions in web server memory and then wondering why users get logged out when a load balancer is added. Forgetting that the load balancer and the database primary are themselves single points of failure. Adding a cache without a plan for stale data. Thinking vertical scaling is "wrong": it is often the cheapest correct first step. And scaling without measuring, so you fix a part that was never the bottleneck.

What exams and interviews ask: Compare vertical and horizontal scaling with pros and cons. Explain what a stateless web tier is and where session data goes. Draw the evolution from one server to a multi-data-center system. Explain what a single point of failure is and how to remove one. Show how replicas and caches reduce database load with simple numbers.

Recap: Systems grow one bottleneck at a time. Separate the database, scale up first, then scale out with stateless web servers behind a load balancer. Replicate the database for reads and safety, cache hot data, push static files to a CDN, move slow work to queues and workers, spread across data centers for availability, shard when one primary is no longer enough, and watch everything with logs and metrics. Each step fixes one problem and brings a new trade-off. Next lesson we zoom into the network itself: what really happens between the phone and the first server.
key_points: Systems grow one bottleneck at a time: measure, fix the current bottleneck, accept the new trade-off.
Separating web and database tiers lets each be sized and changed independently.
Vertical scaling is simple but capped and still a single point of failure; horizontal scaling has no hard ceiling but needs stateless design.
Stateless web servers keep session data in a shared store or a signed token, so any server can handle any request.
A load balancer gives one address, spreads traffic and skips dead servers; it must itself be redundant.
Read replicas multiply read capacity; a 90 percent cache hit ratio cuts database reads tenfold.
CDNs serve static files near users; queues move slow work to workers; multiple data centers survive site failures.
Sharding splits data when one primary cannot take all writes, at the cost of harder queries and rebalancing.
lessons.tip: For each box you add, write two lines next to it: the problem it solves and the new problem it creates. If you cannot write the first line, you do not need the box yet.
lessons.task: Draw the RannaGhor journey as 6 small pictures on one page: single server, separate database, load balancer with 3 web servers, add replicas, add cache and CDN, add queue and workers. Under each, write the bottleneck that forced it.

quiz.q: Why must web servers be stateless before adding many of them behind a load balancer?
options: So that any server can handle any request, since the next request may go to a different server
Because load balancers cannot talk to stateful servers
quiz.explain: If session state lived in one server's memory, a request routed to another server would not know the user.

quiz.q: What is the main limitation of vertical scaling?
options: There is a biggest machine and it remains a single point of failure
It always costs less than horizontal scaling
quiz.explain: Scaling up is simple but has a ceiling and leaves one machine whose failure stops everything.

quiz.q: The app needs 18,000 reads per second and the cache hit ratio is 90 percent. How many reads per second reach the database?
quiz.explain: Only misses go to the database: 10 percent of 18,000 is 1,800.

quiz.q: Which job is best moved to a message queue and workers?
options: Checking the user's password at login
Returning the recipe page the user asked for
Choosing which server gets the request
Resizing an uploaded photo into four sizes
quiz.explain: Resizing is slow and the user does not need to wait for it before getting a reply.

quiz.q: What new problem do read replicas introduce?
options: Replication lag can show a user stale data after their own write
The load balancer must be removed
quiz.explain: Replicas copy changes after a short delay, so a read hitting a replica may miss the latest write.

lessons.title: Networking Building Blocks for Designers: Round Trips, Protocols and Real-Time Connections
lessons.content:
Imagine sending your little brother to the corner shop for one egg at a time. Each trip takes five minutes there and back. If mother needs six eggs, that is thirty minutes, even though picking up an egg takes one second. The slow part is the walking, not the egg. Networks are just like this. The time to process a request on a server is often a few milliseconds, but each trip across the network can take 50 milliseconds or more. A designer who counts the trips can make an app feel instant; one who ignores them builds an app that feels slow no matter how fast the servers are.

What this lesson is: Computer Networks (deep-cse-4-3) taught how DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP work inside. Here we look at them through a designer's eyes: how many round trips each costs, how to avoid paying them again and again, which HTTP version to expect, and how to choose between polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events and WebSockets when an app needs live updates. We also meet proxies and reverse proxies, which appear in almost every architecture diagram.

Round trip time: A round trip time (RTT) is the time for a message to go from client to server and for the reply to come back. It depends mostly on distance and the speed of light in fibre, so no amount of money makes it zero. Within one data center an RTT is about half a millisecond. From Dhaka to a server in Singapore it is around 50 ms. To Europe or the USA it can be 150 to 300 ms. A mobile network adds its own delay on top, especially on weaker connections.

What happens when you open a URL, recapped: Step 1, DNS: the phone asks a DNS resolver for the IP address of the name. If the answer is cached on the phone or at the resolver, this is quick; otherwise the resolver may ask several servers (deep-cse-4-3-08). Step 2, TCP handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, costing one RTT before any data can flow. Step 3, TLS handshake: client and server agree on keys; TLS 1.3 needs one RTT, older TLS 1.2 needed two. Step 4, the HTTP request and response: one more RTT, plus the server's processing time. Step 5, the browser parses the page and may request more files.

Worked: the cost of a fresh connection: With a 50 ms RTT to Singapore, a brand-new HTTPS request with TLS 1.3 costs TCP (50 ms) plus TLS (50 ms) plus the request itself (50 ms), about 150 ms before counting DNS or server time. If the app makes 10 API calls one after another and opens a new connection each time, that is 10 times 150, about 1,500 ms, a full one and a half seconds. If it reuses one open connection, only the first call pays 150 ms and the other nine pay 50 ms each: 150 plus 450, about 600 ms. Same servers, same data, two and a half times faster, just by not repeating handshakes.

Keep-alive and connection pools: HTTP keep-alive (persistent connections) means a TCP connection stays open after a response so the next request can use it. Browsers and mobile HTTP libraries do this by default. On the server side, services talking to databases or other services use connection pools: a set of already-open connections that requests borrow and return. Opening a database connection can take several milliseconds and memory on both sides; a pool of, say, 20 connections per server avoids paying that cost on every request and also protects the database from being flooded with thousands of connections.

Fewer round trips by design: Other tricks reduce trips. Batch requests: one call that returns a user's profile, balance and last five transactions instead of three calls. Put servers or edge caches closer to users (CDNs, lesson 09). Avoid chains where call B can only start after call A finishes when they could run in parallel. Every time you see arrows going back and forth across an ocean in a diagram, ask whether some of them can be removed.

HTTP/1.1: The classic version sends requests as text over TCP. On one connection, a request must normally wait for the previous response, so browsers open several connections per site (commonly about six) to fetch files in parallel. Headers are repeated in full with every request, which wastes bytes when there are many small requests.

HTTP/2: HTTP/2 keeps the same meaning (methods, status codes, headers) but sends frames in binary and multiplexes many requests as separate streams over a single TCP connection, so a slow response does not block others at the HTTP level. It also compresses headers. The remaining weakness: it still runs on TCP, so if one TCP packet is lost, every stream on that connection waits for the retransmission. This is called head-of-line blocking at the transport layer.

HTTP/3: HTTP/3 runs on QUIC, a transport built on UDP that provides reliable, encrypted streams itself. Because each stream is handled separately, a lost packet delays only its own stream. QUIC combines the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes, so a new connection usually needs one RTT instead of two, and resumed connections can send data immediately. It also survives a phone switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data more gracefully. For designers the practical point is: modern clients and CDNs speak HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, so many small requests are much cheaper than they used to be, but round trips still cost.

Real-time updates, the problem: HTTP is request-response: the client asks, the server answers. But chat messages, ride locations and live scores originate at the server. How does the server tell the client something new happened? There are four common answers.

Short polling: The client asks every few seconds: "anything new?" It is simple and works everywhere. The cost is waste: most answers are "no". Worked: 1 million users polling every 2 seconds create 500,000 requests per second. If each request and response carry about 800 bytes of headers, that is 400 MB per second, about 3.2 Gbps, mostly to say "nothing new". Updates are also delayed by up to the polling interval.

Long polling: The client asks, and the server holds the request open until there is news or a timeout, say 30 seconds, then replies. The client immediately asks again. Updates arrive almost instantly and empty replies become rare. The costs: each waiting client holds an open connection on the server, and handling timeouts and reconnections adds complexity.

Server-Sent Events (SSE): The client opens one HTTP connection, and the server keeps it open and streams text events down it whenever something happens. It is one-way, server to client, which fits live scores, notifications and stock tickers well. It works over normal HTTP, and browsers reconnect automatically. If the client also needs to send, it uses ordinary requests.

WebSockets: A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request that is upgraded into a long-lived, two-way connection. Either side can send small messages at any time with very little overhead per message. This fits chat, multiplayer games and live collaboration. Worked: 1 million connected users who each receive about 20 messages an hour generate about 5,556 messages per second, far less than 500,000 polls per second. The cost moves elsewhere: the servers must hold 1 million open connections. If each costs around 10 KB of memory, that is about 10 GB, spread across several connection servers, and the system must know which server holds which user's connection. We will design exactly that in the chat case study (lesson 19).

Choosing a real-time method: If updates are rare and a delay of 30 seconds is fine, short polling is the simplest and good enough. If updates flow mostly server to client, SSE is simple and efficient. If both sides talk often and quickly, use WebSockets. Mobile apps that are closed cannot hold connections, so they rely on push notification services from the phone platform (lesson 21).

Proxies and reverse proxies: A forward proxy sits in front of clients and talks to the internet on their behalf, like an office proxy that filters websites. A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and receives requests on their behalf. Reverse proxies (Nginx-style) are everywhere in system design: they terminate TLS so backend servers do not each handle encryption, compress responses, cache common answers, route paths like /api to one service and /images to another, and hide the internal servers. A load balancer (lesson 07) is a reverse proxy whose main job is spreading load; an API gateway (lesson 06 and 17) is a reverse proxy with extra features for APIs.

When UDP is used: TCP guarantees order and delivery by retransmitting, which adds delay when packets are lost. For live voice and video calls and fast online games, a late packet is useless; it is better to skip it and play the next one. So these use UDP, adding only the reliability they need. DNS queries are usually over UDP too, because they are tiny and a retry is cheap. And as we saw, QUIC builds its own reliable streams on UDP.

Real-life example 1, a mobile banking app on a slow network: A user in a rural area on a weak mobile connection might have an RTT of 200 ms or more. If the home screen makes eight separate API calls in a chain, each with a new connection, it can take several seconds. A good design uses one persistent connection over HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, a single "home screen" API that returns balance, recent transactions and offers together, and a server region close to Bangladesh. The servers did not get faster; the trips got fewer.

Real-life example 2, a live cricket score app: The score changes once per ball. Option one: every phone polls every 5 seconds, millions of requests per second hitting the servers. Option two: phones that have the app open keep an SSE or WebSocket connection and receive a tiny message only when a ball is bowled, and phones with the app closed get a push notification only for wickets and boundaries. The second design uses a small fraction of the requests and feels more live.

Common mistakes: Ignoring round trips and blaming the servers for slowness. Opening a new connection per request between services. Choosing WebSockets for something that changes once an hour. Forgetting that long-lived connections pin a user to a particular server, which affects load balancing and deployments. Mixing up forward and reverse proxies. Assuming HTTP/2 removes all head-of-line blocking; on TCP it does not.

What exams and interviews ask: Describe the steps when a URL is opened and the round trips each costs. Compare short polling, long polling, SSE and WebSockets with use cases. Explain keep-alive and connection pooling. Compare HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. Explain what a reverse proxy does. Calculate the time saved by reusing connections for a given RTT.

Recap: Round trips, not server speed, often dominate latency. A fresh HTTPS connection costs about three RTTs with TLS 1.3, so reuse connections with keep-alive and pools, batch calls and move servers closer. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams on one TCP connection; HTTP/3 on QUIC also avoids TCP's head-of-line blocking and shortens handshakes. For live updates choose short polling, long polling, SSE or WebSockets based on how often and in which direction data flows. Reverse proxies terminate TLS, cache and route. Next lesson we design the requests themselves: clean, safe APIs.
key_points: Round trips dominate latency: Dhaka-Singapore is about 50 ms per RTT, no matter how fast the servers are.
A new HTTPS connection costs about 3 RTTs with TLS 1.3 (TCP, TLS, request), plus DNS if not cached.
Reusing connections (keep-alive, pools) cut 10 sequential calls from about 1,500 ms to about 600 ms in our example.
HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams on one TCP connection; HTTP/3 runs on QUIC over UDP and avoids TCP head-of-line blocking.
Short polling is simple but wasteful; long polling holds requests; SSE streams one way; WebSockets are two-way.
Long-lived connections save requests but cost server memory and need tracking of which server holds which user.
Reverse proxies terminate TLS, compress, cache, route and hide backend servers.
UDP suits live calls and games where late packets are useless; DNS and QUIC also use UDP.
lessons.tip: When you look at any architecture diagram, count the arrows that cross a long distance for one user action. Reducing that count is often the cheapest speed-up available.
lessons.task: Open your browser's developer tools (Network tab) on any news site. Note the protocol column (h2 or h3), how many requests the page makes, and the timing of one request. Then write how many round trips you think it needed.

quiz.q: With a 50 ms RTT and TLS 1.3, about how long does a brand-new HTTPS request take before server time and DNS?
quiz.explain: TCP handshake, TLS 1.3 handshake and the request itself each take one RTT: 3 x 50 = 150 ms.

quiz.q: What does HTTP/3 fix that HTTP/2 over TCP cannot?
options: It removes the need for encryption
It stops a lost packet on one stream from blocking all streams
It makes requests text instead of binary
It removes the need for DNS
quiz.explain: HTTP/3 runs on QUIC, which handles each stream separately, so a lost packet delays only its own stream.

quiz.q: A score changes once per ball and only the server sends updates. Which method fits best for users with the app open?
options: Opening a new TCP connection per update
quiz.explain: SSE is a simple one-way stream from server to client, ideal for live scores.

quiz.q: What is a main job of a reverse proxy?
options: Filtering websites for employees on behalf of clients
Terminating TLS and routing requests to backend servers
quiz.explain: A reverse proxy stands in front of servers: TLS termination, caching, compression and routing.

quiz.q: 1 million users poll every 2 seconds. How many requests per second is that?
quiz.explain: 1,000,000 / 2 = 500,000 requests per second, most of them answering 'nothing new'.

lessons.title: API Design: Resources, Status Codes, Pagination, Versioning and Idempotency
lessons.content:
Think of a restaurant menu. You don't walk into the kitchen and tell the cook which pan to use. You read the menu, say "one plate of kacchi, extra potato", and the kitchen handles the rest. The menu is a promise: these are the things you can ask for, this is how you ask, and this is what comes back. An API (Application Programming Interface) is exactly that menu, but for programs. Your phone app asks a server for things through the API, and the server promises to answer in a known shape. In system design, the API is usually the first concrete thing you write down after the requirements, because it fixes what the whole system must be able to do.

Why API design matters so much: Once a mobile app ships to millions of phones, its API calls are frozen inside those phones. Many people never update their apps. If you rename a field or change what a call means, old apps break. So a bad API decision lives for years. A good API is easy to understand, hard to misuse, safe to call twice, quick to page through big lists, and able to grow without breaking old clients. In an interview, writing 5 to 8 clear API calls early shows the interviewer you understand what the system actually does before you draw boxes.

Where this fits: Web Engineering (deep-cse-5-3-18) already taught REST basics: URLs, HTTP methods and status codes from a developer's view. Distributed Systems (deep-cse-6-3-05) taught RPC, retries and idempotency keys. Here we use those pieces as a designer: which calls to expose, how big lists are returned, how to keep retries safe, how versions evolve, and when REST, GraphQL or gRPC is the better fit.

REST recap, resources and verbs: REST thinks in resources, which are nouns, each with a URL. /users/42 is one user, /users/42/rides is that user's rides. The HTTP method says what to do. GET reads and must not change anything. POST creates something new, like POST /rides to request a ride. PUT replaces a whole resource. PATCH changes part of it, like PATCH /users/42 with a new phone number. DELETE removes it. A common beginner mistake is putting verbs in URLs, like /getUser or /cancelRide. Better: POST /rides/77/cancel is acceptable for an action that is not simple CRUD, but plain resources with methods should be your default.

Status codes that matter: The server tells the client what happened with a three-digit code. 200 OK means success, 201 Created means a new thing was made, and 204 No Content means success with nothing to return. 400 Bad Request means the client sent something malformed, 401 Unauthorized means "who are you? log in first", 403 Forbidden means "I know you, but you are not allowed", 404 Not Found means no such resource, 409 Conflict means the request clashes with the current state, like booking a seat already taken, and 429 Too Many Requests means slow down (lesson 14). 500 means the server itself broke, and 503 means it is overloaded or down for now. Why care? Because clients decide whether to retry from these codes: retrying a 503 later makes sense, retrying a 400 never does.

Request and response shape: Most APIs send JSON. Keep field names consistent (all snake_case or all camelCase), always include ids, send times in one standard format such as ISO 8601 in UTC (2026-11-06T09:30:00Z), and send money as integer poisha or cents, never as floating point, because 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 in floating point. Return errors in one fixed shape, for example {"error": {"code": "INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE", "message": "..."}}, so every client can handle them the same way.

Design from actions, not tables: Start from what a user does on a screen, not from your database tables. A checkout screen needs one call that returns cart items, prices, delivery fee and available payment methods together; making the app call five table-shaped endpoints means five round trips over a slow mobile network. The database can change later; the API should match the product.

Pagination, why lists need pages: A request like GET /orders for a busy seller might match 2 million rows. Sending all of them would take seconds, waste mobile data and crash small phones. So lists come in pages, say 20 items at a time. There are two main styles, and the choice matters at scale.

Offset pagination: The client says GET /orders?limit=20&offset=40, meaning skip 40, give the next 20. It is simple and lets you jump to page 50. But the database must still walk past every skipped row. Worked: page 10,000 with 20 per page means offset = 20 x 9,999 = 199,980 rows read and thrown away just to return 20. The deeper you go, the slower it gets. Worse, if a new order arrives while you are reading, everything shifts by one, so you see one item twice or miss one.

Cursor pagination: Instead of "skip N", the client says "give me 20 items after this one". The server returns a next_cursor, usually an encoded id or timestamp of the last item. The next request is GET /orders?limit=20&cursor=abc. On the database side this becomes WHERE id < 98765 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20, and with an index on id that is fast whether you are on page 2 or page 10,000. New items arriving at the top don't shift your position. The cost: you can't jump straight to page 50, only next and previous. Feeds, chats and order histories almost always use cursors. Lesson 20 uses this for the news feed.

Filtering and sorting: Let clients narrow lists with query parameters, like GET /orders?status=shipped&from=2026-10-01&sort=-created_at. Only allow filters and sorts that have matching database indexes (lesson 11), otherwise one innocent-looking request becomes a full table scan on 50 million rows.

Versioning: Sooner or later you must change an API in a way that breaks old clients. The common trick is to put a version in the URL, like /v1/rides and /v2/rides, or in a header. Old apps keep calling v1 while new apps use v2, and you retire v1 only when almost nobody uses it. Even better is to avoid breaking changes: adding a new optional field is safe, while removing or renaming a field, or changing its meaning, is breaking. Rule of thumb: be strict in what you send, and tolerant of unknown fields in what you receive.

Idempotency keys for POST: GET, PUT and DELETE are naturally idempotent: doing them twice leaves the same result. POST is not: two POST /payments calls could charge twice. Mobile networks in a moving bus drop replies all the time, so the app retries. The fix, recapped from deep-cse-6-3-05: the client generates a unique key, like a UUID, and sends it in a header such as Idempotency-Key: 7f3a.... The server stores key and result. If the same key arrives again, it returns the saved result instead of charging again. Keys are kept for a while, say 24 hours, then deleted.

Authentication in the API: Most APIs expect a token with each request, typically Authorization: Bearer <token>. The client gets the token by logging in. The server checks it on every call to know who is asking, then checks permissions, for example that user 42 can only see user 42's rides. Never put secrets or tokens in the URL, because URLs end up in logs. Lesson 16 covers security in more depth, and Web Engineering (deep-cse-5-3-20/21) covered sessions and tokens.

Rate-limit headers: Good APIs tell clients their limits. Headers such as X-RateLimit-Limit: 100, X-RateLimit-Remaining: 37 and, on a 429 response, Retry-After: 30 let well-behaved apps slow down on their own. Lesson 14 explains the algorithms behind them.

REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC: REST is the default for public and mobile APIs: simple, cache friendly, understood everywhere. Its weakness is over-fetching (getting fields you don't need) and under-fetching (needing three calls to build one screen). GraphQL lets the client send one query describing exactly the fields it wants, like user name, last 3 rides and each driver's rating, in one round trip. That's great for complex screens and many client types, but caching is harder and a careless query can be very expensive, so servers must limit query depth. gRPC sends compact binary messages over HTTP/2, defined in .proto files, and generates client code. It is fast and strictly typed, ideal for service-to-service calls inside a data center, but browsers can't call it directly without a proxy. Typical choice: REST or GraphQL at the edge for apps, gRPC between internal services.

Worked API for a ride-hailing app, step by step: First, list what users do: request a ride, see the fare estimate, track the driver, cancel, pay, rate. Now the calls. POST /v1/fare-estimates with pickup and drop coordinates returns {estimate_id, fare_poisha: 18500, expires_at}. POST /v1/rides with estimate_id and an Idempotency-Key header returns 201 and {ride_id: "r_901", status: "searching"}. GET /v1/rides/r_901 returns status and driver info. For live driver location, polling every second wastes calls, so the app opens a WebSocket (lesson 05) and receives location pushes. POST /v1/rides/r_901/cancel returns 200, or 409 Conflict if the trip already finished. POST /v1/rides/r_901/rating with {stars: 5}. GET /v1/users/me/rides?limit=20&cursor=... for history. On the driver side: PATCH /v1/drivers/me/status {online: true} and location updates every few seconds. Notice that money is in integer poisha, the ride request is protected against double booking, and history uses a cursor.

Real-life example 1, a wallet's send-money call: In a bKash-style wallet, the send-money screen calls POST /v1/transfers with {to: "01711xxxxxx", amount_poisha: 50000} and a fresh idempotency key generated when the user presses Confirm. If the network drops after the server moved the money, the app retries with the same key and the server answers "already done, here is the receipt" instead of sending another 500 taka. The response 402 or 409 style error with code INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE lets the app show a clear message in Bangla without guessing.

Real-life example 2, a shop's product list: A Daraz-style app shows search results 20 products at a time while you scroll. If it used offset paging, the shop would slow down for people who scroll very far, and items would jump around during a sale when prices and stock change. With a cursor, each next page continues exactly from the last product you saw. Product pages themselves are GET calls, so they can be cached by a CDN (lesson 09), while add-to-cart is a POST that must never be cached.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Using GET for actions that change data, so a crawler or a prefetching browser accidentally deletes things. Returning 200 OK with an error message inside, which confuses retries and monitoring. Using floating point for money. Using offset pagination for infinite feeds.
