Making breaking changes without a version. Forgetting idempotency for payment or booking POSTs. Designing APIs around database tables instead of user actions. Exams and interviews ask you to write the main API calls for a given system, compare offset and cursor pagination, explain idempotency, choose between REST, GraphQL and gRPC, or say which status code fits a situation.

Recap: An API is the menu of your system, and it lives inside users' phones for years, so design it carefully. Use resources with clear HTTP methods and meaningful status codes. Keep JSON shapes consistent, money in integers, times in UTC. Page big lists with cursors. Version when you must break, and prefer additive changes. Protect POSTs that move money or book things with idempotency keys. Pick REST for general public APIs, GraphQL for flexible client-driven screens, and gRPC for fast internal calls. Next, lesson 07 looks at the box that sits in front of your API servers: the load balancer.
key_points: An API is the system's menu: it fixes what clients can ask and what they get back, and old app versions keep calling it for years.
Use resource URLs with HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) and meaningful status codes like 201, 404, 409, 429 and 503.
Send money as integers (poisha), times in UTC, and errors in one fixed shape.
Offset pagination gets slower deeper in the list (page 10,000 skips 199,980 rows); cursor pagination stays fast and stable.
Version breaking changes (/v1, /v2); adding optional fields is safe, renaming or removing is not.
Idempotency keys make retried POSTs like payments safe.
REST for public and mobile APIs, GraphQL for flexible screen-shaped queries, gRPC for fast typed internal calls.
lessons.tip: When you design any API, first write the user's actions in plain words, then turn each one into a call. If a call moves money or books something, ask yourself: what happens if it is sent twice?
lessons.task: Pick a food-delivery app. On paper, write 6 API calls for it (method, URL, main request fields, main response fields and one error code each). Mark which ones need an idempotency key and which list needs cursor pagination.

quiz.q: A user scrolls to page 10,000 of a list with 20 items per page using offset pagination. Roughly how many rows does the database skip?
quiz.explain: Offset = 20 x 9,999 = 199,980 rows are walked over and thrown away, which is why deep offset pages are slow.

quiz.q: Which status code best fits trying to cancel a ride that has already finished?
quiz.explain: The request clashes with the current state of the resource, which is what 409 Conflict means.

quiz.q: Why should payment APIs accept an idempotency key?
options: So a retried request after a lost reply does not charge twice
quiz.explain: The server remembers the key and its result, so a retry with the same key returns the old result instead of repeating the charge.

quiz.q: Which change to a live API is NOT breaking for old clients?
options: Changing a field's unit from taka to poisha
quiz.explain: Old clients simply ignore unknown new fields. Renaming, removing or changing meaning breaks them.

quiz.q: Two internal services in the same data center need fast, strictly typed calls. Which is usually the best fit?
quiz.explain: gRPC uses compact binary messages over HTTP/2 with generated typed code, ideal for service-to-service calls.

lessons.title: Load Balancing: Spreading Requests, Health Checks and Avoiding a Single Point of Failure
lessons.content:
Picture the counters at Kamalapur railway station on the day before Eid. If everyone queued at counter 1 while counters 2 to 6 sat empty, the line would stretch out onto the road. So a guard stands at the entrance and waves each person to a free counter: "you to 3, you to 5". Nobody in the queue needs to know how many counters exist; they just follow the guard. A load balancer is that guard for servers. It sits in front of a group of identical servers, receives every request, and passes each one to a server that can handle it.

Why we need it: Lesson 04 showed that horizontal scaling, adding more ordinary servers, is how big systems grow. But clients only know one address, like api.example.com. Something must spread the requests over the servers, notice when a server dies, and stop sending it work. That is the load balancer's job. It gives three gifts at once: scale (more servers share the load), availability (a dead server is skipped, so users don't notice) and flexibility (you can add, remove or update servers behind it while clients keep using the same address).

How many servers? A quick worked sizing: suppose estimation (lesson 03) says the peak is 12,000 requests per second and one application server comfortably handles 2,000. You need 12,000 / 2,000 = 6 servers. But if one dies, the other 5 must take 12,000, which is 2,400 each, over their comfortable limit. So designers add spare capacity, called N+1: 7 servers, so losing one still leaves enough. Big systems spread servers across two or three data center zones, so they plan to lose a whole zone, not just one machine.

Layer 4 vs layer 7: Remember the network layers from deep-cse-4-3. A layer 4 load balancer looks only at transport-level information: IP addresses and TCP or UDP ports. It picks a server when a connection opens and then just forwards bytes, without reading them. That makes it very fast and able to carry any protocol, even non-HTTP traffic like a game server's UDP. A layer 7 load balancer understands the application protocol, usually HTTP. It reads the URL, headers and cookies, so it can make smart choices: send /api/payments to the payment servers and /images to the image servers, or send users with a beta-tester header to the new version. The price is more CPU work per request. Many systems use both: a layer 4 balancer at the very front spreading traffic over a group of layer 7 proxies, which then route by URL.

Round robin: The simplest algorithm: go around the servers in turn. With servers A, B, C, requests 1 to 9 go A, B, C, A, B, C, A, B, C, so each gets exactly 3. It needs no information about the servers. It works well when servers are identical and requests cost about the same. It works badly when some requests are heavy, like generating a PDF report, because one unlucky server can receive several heavy ones in a row.

Weighted round robin: If server A is a big machine and server B is half its size, give A weight 3 and B weight 1. Out of every 4 requests, A gets 3 and B gets 1, so 8 requests become 6 for A and 2 for B. Weights are also handy for slow rollouts: give a new version weight 1 and the old one weight 9, and the new version sees about 10 percent of traffic.

Least connections: The balancer keeps count of open connections to each server and sends the next request to the one with the fewest. Example: A has 10 active connections, B has 4, C has 7, so the next request goes to B. This adapts automatically when some requests take long, such as file uploads or WebSocket chats that stay open for minutes, because a server busy with long connections stops receiving new ones. A cousin, least response time, also weighs how fast each server has been answering recently.

IP hash and consistent hashing: Sometimes you want the same client to land on the same server every time, for example because that server has the user's data warm in its local cache. IP hash computes hash(client IP) mod N. Client 103.4.x.x might always map to server 2. The trouble, as deep-cse-6-3-22 worked out, is that when N changes from 3 to 4, most clients get remapped. Consistent hashing fixes that: only about 1/N of clients move when a server is added. Load balancers in front of caches and chat servers often use it.

Random and power of two choices: Picking a random server is surprisingly fine at large scale. A clever upgrade is "power of two random choices": pick two servers at random and send the request to the less loaded of the two. This needs almost no shared state but avoids most hot spots, and it is used in several modern proxies.

Health checks: A balancer must know which servers are alive. Active health checks: every few seconds it calls something like GET /health on each server; if a server fails, say, 3 checks in a row, it is taken out of rotation, and after a few successful checks it is put back. Worked: checking every 5 seconds with a threshold of 3 means a dead server can still receive traffic for up to about 15 seconds. Faster checks find failures sooner but cost more traffic and can wrongly remove a server that is just briefly slow. Passive health checks watch real traffic: if a server keeps returning errors or timing out, mark it bad. A good /health endpoint checks the server's own critical parts, but should not fail just because some optional downstream service is slow, otherwise one slow dependency can make the balancer remove every server at once.

Sticky sessions: If a server keeps a user's login session or cart in its own memory, the user must keep returning to that same server. Balancers can do this with a cookie that says "you belong to server B", called a sticky session. It works, but it has costs. Load becomes uneven, because one server may collect many heavy users. When server B dies, all its users lose their sessions and get logged out. And you can't easily remove B for an update. The better design, from lesson 04, is a stateless web tier: keep session data in a shared store like Redis or in a signed token, so any server can serve any request. Then the balancer is free to choose.

TLS termination: HTTPS encryption (deep-cse-6-2) costs CPU for the handshake. A common pattern is to finish TLS at the load balancer: the client's encrypted connection ends there, the balancer decrypts, reads the HTTP request to route it, and talks to backend servers over the private network, either in plain HTTP or with a fresh internal TLS connection when the network is not fully trusted. This keeps certificates in one place and lets the balancer do layer 7 routing. Inside banks and wallets, re-encrypting to the backends is the safer default.

Other jobs a balancer often does: Connection reuse (keeping a few long-lived connections to backends instead of one per client), compression, adding a request id header for tracing (lesson 16), basic rate limiting (lesson 14) and slow-start, which gives a freshly added server only a small share of traffic for its first minute while its caches warm up.

The balancer as a single point of failure: If all traffic goes through one balancer, its death takes the whole site down. The classic fix is a pair: active-passive. Both machines share a floating (virtual) IP address. The active one owns it and handles traffic; the passive one watches with heartbeats. If the active dies, the passive claims the floating IP within seconds and carries on. Active-active pairs, where both handle traffic, give more capacity. Cloud load balancers hide this from you by running many balancer machines behind one name, but the idea is the same.

DNS load balancing: The first and cheapest balancer is DNS itself (deep-cse-4-3-08). A domain can return several IP addresses, and resolvers hand them out in different orders. It costs nothing, but it is crude: DNS answers are cached for the TTL, so a dead server's IP can keep being used for minutes, and DNS has no idea how busy each server is. That's why DNS is usually used to choose between data centers or between groups of load balancers, not between individual servers.

Global server load balancing: When you have data centers in several regions, you want users to reach the nearest healthy one. GeoDNS answers the same name with different IPs depending on where the request comes from: a user in Sylhet gets the Singapore address, a user in London gets the Frankfurt one. If a region fails health checks, its address stops being given out. Anycast is another trick: the same IP address is announced from many locations through BGP routing (deep-cse-4-3), and the internet itself carries each user to the nearest one. CDNs and public DNS resolvers use anycast heavily.

Real-life example 1, a wallet on salary day: At the start of the month, a bKash-style wallet sees a surge as salaries arrive and people pay bills. A layer 4 balancer pair with a floating IP takes the traffic, spreading it over a fleet of layer 7 proxies. Those route /transfer to the transfer service and /statement to the statement service, each with its own pool of stateless servers using least connections. Health checks every few seconds remove a server whose database connection pool is broken. Because sessions are tokens, not server memory, no one is logged out when a server is replaced.

Real-life example 2, live cricket score: During a Bangladesh vs India match, a sports news site's traffic jumps tenfold within minutes. Most requests are the same score page, so the CDN (lesson 09) absorbs them, but the live comment and update streams use WebSockets that stay open for an hour. Round robin would pile long connections unevenly; least connections keeps them balanced. When engineers add 20 new servers mid-match, slow-start gives each a gentle ramp so their caches warm up without timeouts.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Forgetting that the load balancer itself needs redundancy. Using sticky sessions as a crutch instead of making servers stateless. Health checks that are too shallow (always return 200 even when the database is unreachable) or too deep (fail when any optional service hiccups, removing every server). Assuming DNS balancing reacts instantly despite TTL caching. Using hash mod N for cache servers and causing a reshuffle on every scale-up. Exams ask you to compare layer 4 and layer 7, trace round robin, weighted or least-connections choices on a small example, explain sticky sessions and why stateless is better, and show how to remove the balancer's single point of failure.

Recap: A load balancer is the station guard that spreads requests across identical servers, giving scale, availability and room to change servers freely. Layer 4 is fast and protocol-blind; layer 7 reads HTTP and routes smartly. Round robin is simple, weighted handles different sizes, least connections handles long requests, and hashing keeps a client on one server. Health checks decide who is in rotation, with a speed-versus-false-alarm trade-off. Avoid sticky sessions by keeping state out of servers, terminate TLS in one place, and remember the balancer itself must be redundant. Across regions, GeoDNS and anycast steer users to the nearest healthy site. Next, lesson 08 covers the fastest trick for taking load off servers: caching.
key_points: A load balancer spreads requests over identical servers, skipping dead ones, so the system scales and stays available behind one address.
Size with spare capacity: 12,000 QPS at 2,000 per server needs 6 servers, so run at least 7 (N+1).
Layer 4 forwards connections by IP and port, fast and protocol-blind; layer 7 reads HTTP and can route by URL, header or cookie.
Round robin for equal servers and requests, weighted for unequal servers, least connections for long-lived requests, consistent hashing to keep clients on the same server.
Health checks trade detection speed against false alarms; every 5 s with 3 failures means up to about 15 s of traffic to a dead server.
Sticky sessions cause uneven load and lost sessions; prefer a stateless tier with shared session storage or tokens.
The balancer itself needs redundancy (active-passive with a floating IP); DNS, GeoDNS and anycast balance between regions.
lessons.tip: Whenever you draw a load balancer in a design, immediately ask two follow-up questions out loud: how does it know a server is dead, and what happens if the balancer itself dies?
lessons.task: Simulate on paper: 3 servers A, B, C with current connections 5, 2 and 4. Ten new long requests arrive one by one and none finish. Assign them using round robin, then again using least connections, and compare the final connection counts.

quiz.q: Peak load is 12,000 requests per second and one server handles 2,000 comfortably. With N+1 spare capacity, how many servers should you run?
quiz.explain: 12,000 / 2,000 = 6 servers are needed, plus one spare so losing a server doesn't overload the rest: 7.

quiz.q: Which load balancer can send /api/payments and /images to different server pools?
quiz.explain: Only a layer 7 balancer reads the HTTP request, including the URL path, so it can route by path.

quiz.q: Servers A, B and C have 10, 4 and 7 open connections. Under least connections, where does the next request go?
quiz.explain: Least connections picks the server with the fewest open connections, which is B with 4.

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of sticky sessions?
options: Load becomes uneven and users lose sessions when their server dies
quiz.explain: Users are pinned to one server, so heavy users can overload it and its death logs all of them out. Stateless servers avoid this.

quiz.q: Why is DNS load balancing considered crude for choosing individual servers?
options: DNS cannot return more than one IP
Cached answers keep pointing to a dead server until the TTL expires, and DNS doesn't see server load
quiz.explain: Resolvers cache answers for the TTL and DNS has no load information, so it reacts slowly and blindly.

lessons.title: Caching in Depth: Patterns, Hit Ratio, Eviction, Invalidation and Stampedes
lessons.content:
Think of a tea stall near a school gate. The owner keeps a big kettle of hot tea ready on the stove, because every student wants tea at 10 a.m. If he boiled fresh water and leaves for each cup, the queue would never move. The kettle is a cache: a small store of ready-made answers kept close by, so popular requests are served instantly instead of being made from scratch. In computing, a cache keeps copies of data in a faster place, usually memory, so the system doesn't have to go back to the slow source, usually the database, every time.

Why caching is the designer's favourite trick: Reading from memory takes around 100 nanoseconds. A database query over the network usually takes milliseconds, because the request travels to another machine, the database may read disk, and it must plan and run the query. That's a gap of thousands to tens of thousands of times. Most apps also have a very uneven access pattern: a small set of things, like today's top products, the home page, or a celebrity's profile, gets most of the reads. Caching that small hot set gives three gifts: faster responses, much less load on the database, and lower cost, because one cache server can replace several database replicas.

Where this fits: Distributed Systems (deep-cse-6-3-25) already introduced cache-aside, write-through and write-back, plus invalidation and TTL. Computer Networks (deep-cse-4-3-06) covered HTTP caching and proxies. Here we work as designers: where to put caches, which pattern for which data, how much memory to buy, what hit ratio buys you, and how caches fail in production.

Where caches live: Caching happens at many layers, and a single request may pass several. The browser or app caches images and API responses it was told it may keep. A CDN (lesson 09) caches static files and sometimes whole pages near users. A reverse proxy in front of your servers can cache full HTTP responses. The application keeps a shared cache such as Redis or Memcached for database results and computed objects; it can also keep a tiny in-process cache inside each server's own memory, which is fastest but not shared. Finally the database itself keeps a buffer pool of recently used pages in RAM (deep-cse-4-2-16). The closer to the user the cache is, the more work it saves, but the harder it is to keep fresh.

Cache-aside (lazy loading), the default: The application talks to both cache and database. To read: look in the cache; on a hit, return it; on a miss, read the database, store the result in the cache with a TTL, then return it. To write: update the database, then delete the cache entry so the next read loads fresh data. Only data that someone actually asks for gets cached, and if the cache dies the app still works, just slower. The downside: every first read is a miss, and there's a short window where stale data can sneak in.

Read-through and write-through: In read-through, the cache library itself loads from the database on a miss, so application code only talks to the cache. In write-through, every write goes to the cache and the database together, so the cache is always fresh, but writes get a bit slower and you may cache data nobody reads.

Write-behind and write-around: Write-behind (write-back) writes to the cache only and flushes to the database later in batches. Writes become very fast, which helps things like view counters, but if the cache node dies before flushing, those writes are lost, so never use it for money. Write-around writes straight to the database and skips the cache, which suits data that is written often but read rarely, like audit logs.

What the hit ratio buys you, worked: Suppose a cache answers in 1 ms and the database in 10 ms. With a 90 percent hit ratio, the average is 0.9 x 1 + 0.1 x (1 + 10) = 2.0 ms, because a miss pays for the cache check and the database. That's five times faster than always going to the database. The bigger gain is load: at 10,000 reads per second, a 90 percent hit ratio sends 1,000 per second to the database, and 99 percent sends only 100. Going from 90 to 99 percent looks small but cuts database reads tenfold. That's why engineers chase hit ratio carefully.

Eviction, what to throw out: Cache memory is limited, so when it is full something must go. LRU (least recently used) throws out the item untouched for the longest. Worked with room for 3 items and accesses A, B, C, A, D, B, A, C: A, B, C fill the cache. A is a hit and becomes most recent. D is a miss, so the least recent, B, is evicted. B comes back as a miss and evicts C. A is a hit. C is a miss and evicts D. Final cache: B, A, C, with 2 hits out of 8. LFU (least frequently used) evicts the item with the fewest uses, which protects long-term favourites but is slow to forget yesterday's star. FIFO evicts the oldest inserted item regardless of use. Real caches like Redis offer approximate LRU or LFU policies because exact tracking costs memory.

TTL, expiry by time: Every entry can carry a time to live, such as 60 seconds. After that it is treated as missing and reloaded. TTL is a safety net: even if you forget to invalidate something, it can be wrong for at most the TTL. Choose TTL by how stale the data may safely be: a product description can live for an hour, a stock count for a few seconds, and a wallet balance usually shouldn't be served from a long-lived cache at all.

Sizing the cache: Use the 80/20 idea from lesson 03: a small share of items gets most of the traffic. Worked: a shop has 1 million products, each product page's cached data is about 5 KB. Caching the hottest 20 percent means 200,000 x 5 KB = 1 GB, which fits easily in one cache server's memory. Add headroom for overhead and growth, and replicate the cache so one node's death doesn't send all traffic to the database at once. For bigger data, shard the cache across many nodes with consistent hashing (deep-cse-6-3-22), so adding a node only moves a small slice of keys.

Invalidation, the hard part: There's a famous joke that the two hardest things in computing are cache invalidation and naming things. The danger is a race. Example with cache-aside: reader R misses and reads price 500 from the database. Before R writes it into the cache, writer W updates the price to 450 and deletes the cache key. Then R stores 500. Now the cache holds the old price until TTL expires. Fixes include short TTLs, deleting the key again a little later (delayed double delete), version numbers stored with the value, or updating the cache from the database's change stream. For most data, a short TTL plus delete-on-write is good enough; for data that must never be stale, read the database.

Cache stampede (thundering herd): A popular key expires, and in the same second 5,000 requests all miss and all hit the database for the same row. The database collapses, the requests time out, and nothing gets cached, so the next wave does the same. Fixes: a lock, so only the first request reloads while the others wait briefly or get the old value; early refresh, where an entry is refreshed in the background shortly before it expires; and jittered TTLs, like 300 seconds plus a random 0 to 30, so thousands of keys loaded together don't all expire in the same instant. After a full cache restart, warm it up gradually before sending full traffic.

Hot keys: Sometimes a single key is so popular, like the score of a final match, that even one cache node can't serve it. Spread it: keep several copies under keys like score:1, score:2 ... score:10 and have each reader pick one at random, or keep a tiny in-process cache on every application server for a second or two. A one-second-old cricket score is perfectly fine.

Redis vs Memcached as examples: Both are in-memory key-value stores used as caches. Memcached is simple and multi-threaded, storing plain strings, great as a pure cache. Redis adds data structures such as lists, sets, sorted sets and counters, optional persistence to disk and replication, so it's also used for leaderboards, rate limiters (lesson 14), sessions and queues. Either way, treat a cache as something that can lose its contents; the real copy lives in the database.

What not to cache: Data that changes on every request, data that is rarely read twice, highly personal data in a shared cache layer that might be served to the wrong user (mistakes in cache keys have leaked private pages in real incidents), and anything where a stale answer causes real harm, like the final balance check before a money transfer. Also be careful caching negative results like "not found": it saves database work for repeated lookups of missing items, but needs a short TTL so newly created items appear quickly.

Real-life example 1, a shop's product page: In a Daraz-style shop during a sale, product details are read millions of times and changed rarely. The service uses cache-aside: key product:123 holds name, images and description for 10 minutes, with a little random jitter. The price and stock, which change often, sit under a separate key with a 5-second TTL, so the page is fast but the price is never far behind. When the seller edits the description, the service updates the database and deletes product:123. At checkout, the stock is checked against the database itself, never the cache.

Real-life example 2, a news site on result day: When HSC results come out, an education news site's "how to check results" article gets enormous traffic within minutes. The article is cached in the CDN and in Redis, so the database sees only a trickle. Comment counts are written with write-behind counters in Redis and flushed to the database every few seconds, since losing a few counts in a crash is acceptable. Before publishing, engineers pre-load (warm) the cache so the first wave doesn't cause a stampede.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Caching everything without measuring the hit ratio. Forgetting TTLs, so wrong data lives forever. Updating the cache before the database, or not handling the invalidation race. Letting all keys expire at the same instant. Treating the cache as the source of truth and losing data when it restarts. Exams ask you to compare cache-aside, write-through and write-behind, trace LRU on a short access list, compute average latency from a hit ratio, explain cache stampede and its fixes, or decide what to cache in a given design.

Recap: A cache is the ready kettle: a fast, small copy of popular data close to where it is needed. It lives at many layers, from browser to database buffer. Cache-aside is the usual default; write-through favours freshness, write-behind favours write speed at the risk of loss. Hit ratio drives both latency and database load, and 90 to 99 percent means ten times fewer database reads. Evict with LRU or LFU, expire with TTL, size with the 80/20 rule, and guard against stampedes and hot keys. Never cache what must be exactly right at the moment of decision. Next, lesson 09 takes caching all the way to the user with CDNs.
key_points: A cache keeps copies of popular data in fast memory so most reads skip the slow database.
Caches exist at many layers: browser or app, CDN, reverse proxy, application cache (Redis, Memcached), in-process memory and the database buffer pool.
Cache-aside is the default; write-through keeps the cache fresh; write-behind is fast but can lose writes; write-around skips the cache for rarely read data.
With 1 ms cache, 10 ms database and 90% hits, average latency is about 2 ms; going from 90% to 99% hits cuts database reads tenfold.
LRU evicts the least recently used item, LFU the least frequently used; TTL limits how long stale data can live.
Cache stampedes are prevented with locks, early refresh, jittered TTLs and warming; hot keys are spread over copies or local caches.
Never treat the cache as the source of truth or use it for decisions that must be exactly right, like a final balance check.
lessons.tip: For every piece of data in a design, ask two questions before caching it: how often is it read compared with written, and how stale can it be before someone gets hurt? Those two answers pick the pattern and the TTL.
lessons.task: Run LRU by hand with room for 3 items on the access list P, Q, R, P, S, Q, P, R, S. Write the cache contents after each step, count hits, and then repeat with room for 4 items to see how the hit count changes.

quiz.q: Cache takes 1 ms, database 10 ms, and 90% of reads hit the cache. If a miss pays for both, what is the average read time?
At 10,000 reads per second, how many reach the database when the hit ratio rises from 90% to 99%?
quiz.explain: Misses are what reach the database: 10% of 10,000 is 1,000 and 1% is 100, a tenfold cut.

quiz.q: Which write pattern is fastest for writes but can lose data if the cache node crashes before flushing?
quiz.explain: Write-behind writes only to the cache and flushes later, so unflushed writes vanish with the node.

quiz.q: A hugely popular key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once. What is this called and what helps?
options: Cache stampede; locking, early refresh and jittered TTLs
Replication lag; read from the primary
quiz.explain: This is a cache stampede. Letting one request reload, refreshing early and spreading expiry times prevent it.

quiz.q: With LRU and room for 3 items, after accesses A, B, C, A, D, which item was evicted when D arrived?
quiz.explain: After A is reused, B is the least recently used, so B is evicted for D.

lessons.title: CDNs and Serving Static Content: Edges, Cache Headers, Versioned Files and Savings
lessons.content:
Think about how a soft drink company gets bottles to a tiny shop in a village in Kurigram. It doesn't send a truck from the factory every time someone wants one bottle. It keeps stock in regional warehouses and local distributors, so each shop is refilled from somewhere close. The factory only ships to the warehouses now and then. A CDN (Content Delivery Network) does the same for internet content. Your servers are the factory, called the origin. The CDN runs many edge servers in cities around the world, and those keep copies of your files close to users, so most requests never travel all the way to the origin.

Why it matters: Distance costs time. Light in fibre is fast but not instant, and every request needs several round trips: a TCP handshake, a TLS handshake and then the HTTP request itself (lesson 05). Worked: if the origin is far away with a 200 ms round trip, three round trips cost about 600 ms before the first byte even starts arriving. From a nearby edge with a 20 ms round trip, the same three trips cost about 60 ms. On top of speed, a CDN takes huge load off your servers and absorbs traffic spikes and many attacks, because thousands of edge machines share the work.

Where this fits: Computer Networks (deep-cse-4-3-06 and 09) explained web caching, CDNs and video streaming from the network side, and lesson 08 covered caching inside your system. This lesson is the designer's view: what to put on a CDN, how to control what it caches and for how long, how to update files safely, and how to estimate the savings.

Static vs dynamic content: Static content is the same for everyone and changes rarely: images, CSS and JavaScript files, fonts, app downloads, product photos and video segments. It's perfect for a CDN. Dynamic content is built per request or per user: your cart, your balance, a search result. It usually comes from your servers, though a CDN can still help it travel faster, as we'll see. In a typical shopping page, most of the bytes are images and scripts, so moving static content to the CDN removes the majority of the traffic from your origin.

Edge servers and points of presence: A CDN has points of presence (PoPs), which are data centers in many cities, each with many edge servers. When a user asks for cdn.example.com/img/shoe.jpg, the CDN routes the request to a nearby PoP, using DNS that answers with a close edge address, or anycast where the same IP is announced from every PoP (lesson 07). If that edge has the file, it answers immediately: a cache hit. If not, it fetches the file from the origin, keeps a copy, and answers: a miss. The next user in that city gets the copy.

Pull CDN: The common model. You don't upload anything in advance. The edge pulls a file from the origin the first time someone asks for it and caches it for as long as the headers allow. It's easy to set up and only popular files take up space. The cost is that the first visitor in each region gets a slower miss, and an unpopular file may expire and be pulled again later.

Push CDN: You upload files to the CDN yourself, ahead of time, and it distributes them. This suits large files that you know will be wanted, like a new app version or a big game patch, and sites whose content changes rarely. You are responsible for uploading new versions and deleting old ones, and you pay to store everything, even files no one requests.

Cache-Control and TTL: How long an edge (and the browser) may keep a file is controlled by HTTP headers from the origin. Cache-Control: max-age=3600 means "fresh for one hour". Cache-Control: no-store means "never cache this", which you must use for private responses like balances. Cache-Control: private means a browser may cache it but shared caches like a CDN may not. s-maxage sets a separate lifetime just for shared caches. After max-age runs out, the edge can revalidate with a conditional request using ETag or Last-Modified (deep-cse-4-3-06): the origin replies 304 Not Modified, which is tiny, instead of sending the whole file again.

Cache keys: The CDN decides whether two requests are "the same file" using a cache key, by default the URL including the host and path. Query strings matter: if a marketing link adds ?utm_source=facebook, every different tag could create a separate cached copy and lower your hit ratio. Good setups ignore tracking parameters in the key. Headers matter too: the Vary header tells the CDN that, for example, the gzip and brotli compressed versions are different objects. Getting the key wrong in the other direction is dangerous: if a personalised page is cached under a key that ignores the user, one user's page can be shown to another.

Invalidation vs versioned file names: Suppose you fix a bug in app.js and the CDN has cached the old one for a day. You can ask the CDN to purge (invalidate) that path, which works but takes time to reach every PoP and is often rate-limited. The cleaner trick is versioned file names, also called cache busting. Build tools put a hash of the file content in the name: app.3f2a9c.js. Change the content and the name changes to app.81b7d0.js. Now the old file can be cached for a year (max-age=31536000, which is 365 days in seconds, plus immutable) because it will never change, and the HTML page simply points to the new name. The HTML itself gets a short TTL or no-cache so users pick up the new references quickly. This pattern gives both perfect caching and instant updates.

Origin shield: With hundreds of PoPs, a newly published file can cause hundreds of misses hitting your origin at once, one from each PoP. An origin shield is a middle layer: one chosen regional cache that all edges ask first. Now the origin sees one request per file, and the shield serves the rest. It is a tiered cache, just like a regional warehouse sitting between local shops and the factory.

Savings, worked: A shop's home page loads about 2 MB of images and scripts. One million page views a day means about 1,000,000 x 2 MB = 2 TB of data. With a 95 percent CDN hit ratio, the origin serves only 5 percent, which is 100 GB a day, and the edges serve the other 1.9 TB from close to users. Your origin needs far fewer servers and much less outbound bandwidth, and users get faster pages. The CDN charges for its delivery, so the real design question is cost versus speed and origin load, and for busy sites the CDN usually wins on both.

Cost thinking: CDNs usually charge per gigabyte delivered and per request, with lower prices for higher volumes and different prices in different regions. Your origin's cloud provider also charges for data leaving its network. So designers compare: bytes served by the CDN times its price, against bytes the origin would send times the origin's price plus the extra servers needed. Shrinking the bytes helps both sides: compress text files, serve modern image formats, resize images to the size the phone actually shows, and lazy-load images below the fold (deep-cse-5-3-23).

When the CDN itself fails: A CDN is a dependency like any other. Large sites sometimes use two CDN providers and switch DNS between them if one has an outage, and they keep the origin able to serve directly in an emergency, at least for the most important pages. Keep this in mind when an interviewer asks, "what if the CDN goes down?"

Dynamic content acceleration: Even for uncacheable requests like a login or a payment, a CDN can help. The user's TLS handshake finishes at the nearby edge (short round trips), and the edge forwards the request to the origin over long-lived, already warmed-up connections on well-chosen network paths. Some CDNs can also run small pieces of code at the edge, for example to redirect, check a token, or pick a language, before a request ever reaches your servers.

Security at the edge: Because all traffic passes through the CDN, it is a natural place for protection. Its huge spread-out capacity soaks up many DDoS floods (lesson 16), a web application firewall can block common attack patterns, and the origin can be configured to accept traffic only from the CDN, hiding its real address. For private files, like a paid course video or a bank statement PDF, use signed URLs: links containing an expiry time and a signature, so the edge serves the file only to holders of a valid, unexpired link.

Video and big files: Video is the largest user of CDNs. Videos are cut into small segments of a few seconds each in several qualities, and the player fetches segments over plain HTTP, which CDNs cache like any other file. Popular videos stay hot at the edges while rare ones are fetched from the origin. Lesson 23 designs a whole video platform on this idea.

Real-life example 1, Bangladesh users and nearby edges: A Bangladeshi news site hosts its servers in one data center. Without a CDN, readers in Rajshahi, Sylhet and in the Middle East all pull every photo from that one place, and on election-result night the servers choke. With a CDN, photos and scripts come from PoPs close to each reader, often inside or near Bangladesh if the CDN has a presence there, while the origin serves only the article HTML and the live updates. Expatriate readers in Dubai get the photos from an edge in the Gulf region instead of from Dhaka.

Real-life example 2, a mobile game update: A popular game releases a 300 MB update. If ten lakh players download it on release day directly from the company's servers, that's an impossible spike. Instead the update is pushed to the CDN in advance under a versioned path like /patch/v2.4.1/, the app downloads it from the nearest edge, and the company's own servers only answer the tiny "is there a new version?" check.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Caching private, per-user responses because of a missing no-store or a bad cache key. Long TTLs on files with fixed names, so users get stale scripts for days; the fix is versioned names. Forgetting tracking parameters in cache keys and wrecking the hit ratio. Leaving the origin open to the internet so attackers can bypass the CDN. Thinking a CDN fixes slow dynamic APIs by itself. Exams ask you to explain what a CDN is and why it reduces latency, compare pull and push CDNs, explain cache invalidation versus versioned file names, describe Cache-Control headers, or estimate origin traffic from a hit ratio.

Recap: A CDN is a network of warehouses for your content: edge servers in many cities keep copies close to users, cutting round-trip time and origin load. Static files are ideal; dynamic requests can still benefit from edge TLS and warm connections. Pull CDNs fetch on first request; push CDNs are loaded ahead of time. You control caching with Cache-Control, ETags and well-chosen cache keys. Use content-hashed file names for long caching with instant updates, an origin shield to protect the origin, and signed URLs for private files. Next, lesson 10 moves from files to data: choosing the right database.
key_points: A CDN keeps copies of content on edge servers in many cities so users fetch from nearby instead of the far-away origin.
Nearby edges cut round-trip costs: three round trips at 200 ms is about 600 ms, at 20 ms about 60 ms.
Static content (images, scripts, video segments) suits CDNs; private per-user data must use no-store or private.
Pull CDNs fetch from the origin on the first miss; push CDNs are uploaded in advance.
Cache-Control, ETag and cache keys decide what is cached and for how long; bad keys can lower hit ratio or leak private pages.
Content-hashed file names (app.3f2a9c.js) allow year-long caching with instant updates; the HTML stays short-lived.
With a 95% hit ratio, 2 TB of daily traffic leaves only about 100 GB for the origin; an origin shield further protects it.
lessons.tip: When you add a CDN to a design, sort every response into three buckets: cache for a long time (versioned static files), cache briefly (public pages), and never cache (anything personal). Most CDN bugs come from putting something in the wrong bucket.
lessons.task: Open any news website on a computer, press F12 to open developer tools, go to the Network tab and reload. Click three files (an image, a script, the page itself) and note their Cache-Control headers and file names. Which ones look versioned, and which have short or no caching?

quiz.q: Why does fetching from a nearby edge server make a page start loading much sooner?
options: Each of the several round trips (TCP, TLS, HTTP) is much shorter
quiz.explain: Setting up and making a request needs several round trips, and each one costs far less when the server is close.

quiz.q: Which Cache-Control value should a response showing a user's wallet balance carry?
quiz.explain: Private, sensitive responses must never be stored by shared caches or browsers, which is what no-store says.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of names like app.3f2a9c.js?
options: The file can be cached for a very long time, and a change produces a new name so users get the update immediately
It forces the CDN to push files
quiz.explain: The content hash changes whenever the content changes, so old names never need invalidation and new names are fetched fresh.

quiz.q: 2 TB of daily traffic goes through a CDN with a 95% hit ratio. About how much reaches the origin?
quiz.explain: Only misses reach the origin: 5% of 2 TB = 0.1 TB = 100 GB.

quiz.q: What problem does an origin shield solve?
options: It stops users from using HTTP
It prevents hundreds of PoPs from all missing to the origin at the same time
quiz.explain: Edges ask one regional shield cache first, so the origin sees roughly one request per file instead of one per PoP.

lessons.title: Choosing a Database: Relational, NoSQL Families, Search, Time-Series and Object Storage
lessons.content:
Think about how a family stores things at home. Money and land papers go in a locked almirah with a careful list. Rice goes in a big drum where you just scoop from the top. Clothes go on hangers, photos go in albums, and the phone numbers of relatives go in a little notebook sorted by name. Nobody stores rice in the almirah or land papers in the rice drum, because each kind of thing is used differently. Choosing a database is the same decision for software: different data is written and read in different ways, so it belongs in different kinds of storage.

Why the choice matters: The database is the hardest part of a system to change later. Servers can be swapped in an afternoon, but moving billions of rows from one database to another can take months and risks losing data. A good choice makes the main queries fast and simple and keeps important data safe. A bad choice shows up as slow pages, complicated application code doing the database's job, or lost and inconsistent data. In interviews, "which database and why" is one of the most common questions, and the "why" matters more than the name.

Where this fits: Database Management Systems (deep-cse-4-2) taught the relational model, SQL, transactions and a first look at NoSQL (lesson 24). Distributed Systems (deep-cse-6-3-17) covered CAP, PACELC and BASE vs ACID. Here we use all that to choose. Lesson 11 then goes inside: data modeling, indexes and storage engines; lesson 12 covers scaling the database. Deep internals of big data systems wait for deep-cse-7-2.

Start with data shape and access patterns: Before naming any product, answer four questions. What does the data look like: neat records with fixed fields, nested documents, relationships like a social graph, a stream of timestamped readings, or big files? How will it be read: by one key, by ranges, by complex filters and joins, by full-text search? What is the read/write ratio and the volume (lesson 03)? And how correct must it be: is a slightly stale or lost update acceptable, or would it mean someone loses money? The database follows from these answers, not from what is fashionable.

Relational databases and their strengths: Relational databases such as PostgreSQL and MySQL store data in tables with a fixed schema, rows and columns, and you query them with SQL. Their big strengths are ACID transactions (all-or-nothing changes, deep-cse-4-2-20), joins that combine tables in one query, constraints that refuse bad data (a foreign key, a NOT NULL, a CHECK that balance is not negative), and decades of tooling. They also handle ad hoc questions well: a manager can ask a new question tomorrow and SQL can answer it. Their limits appear at very large scale: one primary handles all writes, and spreading a relational database across many machines takes extra work (lesson 12). For most new products, a relational database is the safe default until you have a clear reason otherwise.

Key-value stores: The simplest model: a giant dictionary from key to value. Get("session:9f2c") returns a blob; Put stores one. The store doesn't look inside the value. Because there are no joins or complex queries, key-value stores are extremely fast and easy to spread over many machines with hashing. Redis keeps them in memory; DynamoDB-style stores keep them durably on disk across nodes. Fits: sessions, caches, shopping carts, feature flags, rate-limit counters, and any lookup by a known key.

Document stores: A document store keeps each record as a self-contained document, usually JSON-like, which can have nested fields and lists, and different documents can have different fields. MongoDB-style stores are the common example. A product in a catalog is a good fit: a phone has screen size and battery, a shirt has size and fabric, and each product is read as one whole document. You can index fields inside documents and query by them. The trade-off: joins between documents are weak or missing, so data that is shared by many documents is often copied into each, and keeping copies in sync becomes your job.

Wide-column stores: Cassandra and HBase-style stores organise data by a partition key and, inside each partition, rows sorted by a clustering key. Think of a giant sorted map: for conversation 42, all messages sorted by time. They are built for enormous write volumes spread across many machines with no single primary, and for reading a slice of one partition quickly, like "the latest 50 messages of conversation 42". You must design tables around your queries in advance, because you can't run flexible joins or filters on non-key columns cheaply. Fits: chat messages, activity logs, sensor data, time-ordered feeds.

Graph databases: When the relationships are the main thing, a graph database stores nodes (people, places) and edges (follows, friend-of, located-in) directly. Questions like "friends of friends who live in Khulna" or "the shortest connection between two people" walk edges instead of doing many expensive joins. Neo4j-style databases are the usual example. Fits: social connections, recommendation, fraud rings where many accounts share the same device or phone number. Most systems don't need one; a relational table of edges handles simple cases.

Search indexes: Users type "red sneakers size 42" and expect good results despite spelling mistakes and word order. A normal database index can't rank text by relevance. Search engines like Elasticsearch-style systems build an inverted index (a map from each word to the documents containing it) and score matches. They are usually a secondary copy: the main database stays the source of truth, and changes are streamed into the search index, which may lag by a second or so. Information Retrieval (deep-cse-7-9) explains the ranking maths.

Time-series stores: Data like server CPU every 10 seconds, electricity meter readings, or GPS points is a stream of (time, value) records that are appended, rarely updated, and queried by time range with averages and maximums. Time-series databases compress such data heavily, roll old data up into hourly or daily summaries, and delete raw data after a retention period. Monitoring systems (lesson 16) are built on them.

Object (blob) storage for files: Photos, videos, PDFs and backups do not belong in database rows. A 2 MB photo stored as a database blob bloats backups, slows replication and wastes expensive database storage. Instead, store the file in object storage (S3-style), which keeps huge numbers of files cheaply and durably, and put only the file's key or URL plus metadata (owner, size, upload time) in the database. Worked: 1 million photo uploads a day at 2 MB each is 2 TB of new data daily, easy for object storage, painful for a relational database. Serve these files through a CDN (lesson 09).

ACID vs BASE recap: ACID databases promise that a committed transaction is complete, consistent, isolated from others and durable. Many distributed NoSQL stores follow BASE: basically available, soft state, eventually consistent, choosing availability and low latency during problems (deep-cse-6-3-17). It isn't a war of good and bad. Modern relational systems can scale out, and several NoSQL stores now offer transactions or strong consistency options. The useful question is per feature: does this data need all-or-nothing updates and always-correct reads, or can it tolerate brief staleness for speed and scale?

Polyglot persistence: Big systems rarely use one database. A shop might use a relational database for orders and payments, a document store for the product catalog, a search index for product search, Redis for carts and sessions, a wide-column store for user activity events, object storage for images, and a time-series store for monitoring. Each part uses the right tool. The cost is operational: every extra database needs backups, monitoring, upgrades and people who understand it, and data must be kept in sync between them, usually through events (lesson 13). So add a new kind of database only when it clearly earns its keep.

A decision checklist: First, do you need multi-row transactions and strong correctness, as with money, orders or inventory? Lean relational. Second, is every access by a single key? Key-value. Third, are records self-contained, varied in shape and read whole? Document. Fourth, are writes enormous and reads mostly slices by one key in time order? Wide-column. Fifth, are queries about multi-hop relationships? Graph. Sixth, is it free-text search? A search index alongside the main store. Seventh, is it big files? Object storage plus metadata in a database. Finally, prefer what your team already runs well; a familiar database operated carefully beats a fashionable one operated badly.

Worked choice 1, a wallet ledger: A bKash-style wallet must never lose or double-count money. A transfer debits one account and credits another, and both must happen or neither. That's a textbook case for a relational database with ACID transactions and constraints, often as an append-only ledger table of entries plus a balance per account. Volume check: 50 million transactions a day is about 580 per second on average, with peaks several times higher, which a well-tuned relational setup with partitioning by account can handle. Transaction history for the app's statement screen can be copied into a read-optimised store, and notifications go through a queue.

Worked choice 2, a chat app: Suppose 5 million users each send 40 messages a day: 200 million messages, about 2,300 writes per second on average. Messages are written once, rarely edited, and read as "latest messages of this conversation". At 200 bytes each that's about 40 GB of new data per day before replication. A wide-column store partitioned by conversation id and sorted by message id fits perfectly: writes spread across many nodes, and each chat screen reads one partition slice. User profiles and contacts can stay in a relational database, and photos go to object storage. Lesson 19 completes this design.

Worked choice 3, a product catalog: A shop with a million products of very different types, read far more than written, with search and filters. A document store holds each product as one document with its own attributes, a search index powers "search and filter", and a cache in front serves the hottest pages (lesson 08). Stock count and orders stay in the relational database because overselling must be prevented with transactions (lesson 25).

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Choosing NoSQL because "it scales" when the data is a few gigabytes and needs transactions. Storing images and videos inside database rows. Picking a wide-column store and then needing flexible queries it can't do. Using five databases in a small product and drowning in operations. Forgetting that a search index or cache is a copy that can lag. Exams and interviews ask you to compare SQL and NoSQL, name the NoSQL families with a use case each, justify a database for a given feature, explain where files should be stored, or define ACID and BASE.

Recap: Choose storage the way a family stores rice, money and photos: by how each kind of data is used. Begin with the data's shape, access patterns, volume and correctness needs. Relational databases give transactions, joins and constraints and are the safe default. Key-value stores are fastest for lookups by key, document stores fit self-contained varied records, wide-column stores absorb huge write streams read by partition, and graph databases walk relationships. Add search indexes for text, time-series stores for metrics and object storage for files. Many systems combine several, but each extra database has a real operating cost. Next, lesson 11 opens the database to see how data models, indexes and storage engines make queries fast or slow.
key_points: Choose a database from the data's shape, access patterns, volume and correctness needs, not from fashion.
Relational databases give ACID transactions, joins and constraints and are the safe default for money, orders and inventory.
Key-value stores suit lookups by one key; document stores suit self-contained records with varied fields read as a whole.
Wide-column stores absorb huge write volumes and read slices of one partition, like a conversation's latest messages.
Graph databases suit multi-hop relationship queries; search indexes handle free text and are usually a lagging copy.
Big files go to object storage with only their key and metadata in the database; 1 million 2 MB photos a day is 2 TB daily.
Polyglot persistence uses several stores, but each extra database adds backups, monitoring and sync work.
lessons.tip: Never answer "which database?" with a product name alone. Say the access pattern first ("we read the latest 50 messages of one conversation, and write 2,300 per second"), then the family that fits, then a product example.
lessons.task: Take an app you use, such as a ride-hailing or food app. List five kinds of data it stores (for example payments, profile photos, chat with the driver, search for restaurants, live location). For each, write its main read and write pattern and choose a database family, with one sentence of reason.

quiz.q: A wallet transfer must debit one account and credit another, both or neither. Which choice fits best?
options: A wide-column store with eventual consistency
A relational database with ACID transactions
quiz.explain: All-or-nothing updates with constraints are exactly what ACID transactions in a relational database provide.

quiz.q: Where should 2 MB user photos usually be stored?
options: In object storage, with only the key and metadata in the database
As blobs in the main relational table
quiz.explain: Object storage is cheap and durable for big files; keeping them in database rows bloats backups and replication.

quiz.q: A chat app writes about 2,300 messages per second and reads the latest messages of one conversation. Which family fits best?
options: Wide-column store partitioned by conversation and sorted by message id
quiz.explain: Wide-column stores spread huge writes across nodes and read one partition's sorted slice quickly.

quiz.q: Which query is a graph database especially good at?
options: Find a session by its id
Friends of friends who live in Khulna
quiz.explain: Multi-hop relationship questions walk edges directly instead of doing many joins.

quiz.q: What is the main cost of polyglot persistence?
options: Every extra database needs operations work and data must be kept in sync between them
quiz.explain: Each store needs backups, monitoring and expertise, and copies across stores must be synchronised, often through events.

lessons.title: Data Modeling, Indexes and Storage Engines: Shaping Data for Fast Queries
lessons.content:
Imagine a school library with 50,000 books thrown in one huge pile. To find "Thakurmar Jhuli" you would have to lift books one by one until you hit it. Now imagine the same library with shelves sorted by subject and a card catalogue that says "Folk tales, shelf 12, row 3". Same books, same room, but finding one takes a minute instead of a week. That is what this lesson is about: how you arrange data (data modeling), how you build the card catalogue (indexes), and what kind of shelves the database uses underneath (storage engines). Lesson 10 helped you pick which kind of database to use. This lesson is about using it well.

Where this fits: In Database Management Systems (deep-cse-4-2) you learned tables, keys, normalization (lessons 14-15) and how B+ tree indexes and hashing work inside (lesson 17). We will only recap those. Here the question is practical: when a system serves millions of users, how do you shape tables and indexes so the busiest queries are fast, and which storage engine suits a write-heavy or a read-heavy workload?

Model for the queries, not just for the data: A beginner designs tables by asking "what things exist?": users, products, orders. That is a good start, but a system designer also asks "what will we ask the database, and how often?" Write down the top five queries with their rate. For a Daraz-style shop that might be: show a product page (50,000 per second), list a user's last 20 orders (2,000 per second), place an order (300 per second), search products by category and price (5,000 per second), and a nightly sales report (once a day). The page view and the search dominate, so the model and indexes must make them cheap. The nightly report can be slow; nobody is waiting on it. This list is called the access pattern, and it drives every decision below.

Normalization recap: Normalization means storing each fact once. The customer's address lives only in the customers table, and orders point to it with a customer_id. Why it is good: no duplicated data, so no chance of two copies disagreeing, and updates touch one row. The cost: to show an order with the customer's name you need a join, which means reading two tables and matching rows. On one machine with good indexes, joins are fast and normalization is the right default.

Deliberate denormalization: Denormalization means storing a copy of a fact where it is read, on purpose, to avoid joins or extra lookups. Example: a product page needs the seller's shop name. Normalized, you read the product row, then the seller row. Denormalized, you keep seller_name inside the product row too, so one read is enough. At 50,000 page views per second, removing one lookup per view removes 50,000 lookups per second. The price is paid on writes: when a seller renames the shop, every one of their products must be updated, maybe 10,000 rows, and for a short while some rows show the old name. That trade is fine when reads vastly outnumber writes and slight staleness is harmless. It is not fine for money: never copy an account balance into many places.

Precomputed values: A close cousin of denormalization is storing an answer you would otherwise compute. Instead of counting a post's likes with COUNT(*) over a likes table every time someone opens the post, keep a like_count column and add 1 when a like arrives. Counting 2 million like rows on every view is wasteful; reading one number is cheap. Summary tables for dashboards (sales per day per category) are the same idea. Rule of thumb: compute on write when reads are frequent and the computation is expensive; compute on read when writes are frequent and reads are rare.

Why an index makes reads fast: Without an index, finding phone number 01711223344 among 1 billion user rows means a full table scan: check row 1, row 2, all the way, up to a billion checks. An index is a separate sorted structure that maps a column's value to where the row lives, like the catalogue cards. Because it is sorted, you can do something like binary search: each step halves what is left. How many halvings to go from 1 billion to 1? log2 of 1,000,000,000 is about 29.9, so about 30 steps. One billion checks versus thirty. That is the whole magic.

B-tree indexes in real life: Disks and SSDs read in pages, often 4 to 16 KB, not single numbers. So databases use B-trees (B+ trees, deep-cse-4-2-17), where each node is one page holding hundreds of keys and pointers. With about 100 children per node, the number of levels for 1 billion keys is log base 100 of 1 billion, which is 4.5, so about 5 levels. The top one or two levels are almost always in memory, so a lookup costs maybe 2 or 3 disk page reads. That is why a well-indexed query on a huge table can still answer in a few milliseconds.

Indexes are not free: Every index is another sorted structure that must be kept up to date. Insert one order into a table with 5 indexes and the database writes the row plus 5 index entries, so roughly 6 writes instead of 1. Indexes also take disk and memory space. So the rule is: index the columns your frequent queries filter, join or sort on, and nothing else. A table with 15 indexes "just in case" will have slow inserts and a crowded memory cache. Check with the database's EXPLAIN command whether a query actually uses an index.

Composite indexes and column order: A composite index covers several columns, for example (category, price). It is sorted first by category, then by price inside each category, like a phone book sorted by surname, then first name. This index helps "category = 'phones' AND price < 20000" a lot: jump to the phones section, then read the cheap end. It also helps "category = 'phones'" alone. But it does not help "price < 20000" alone, because prices are scattered across all categories, just as a phone book cannot quickly find everyone named Rahim regardless of surname. This is the leftmost-prefix rule. Put the column you test with equality first and the range or sort column after it.

Covering indexes: If an index contains every column a query needs, the database can answer from the index alone without visiting the table row. For "list order id and date of user 42's last 20 orders", an index on (user_id, created_at, order_id) covers the query: jump to user 42, read the last 20 entries, done. This saves one random read per row, which for 20 rows can mean 20 fewer disk reads.

Storage engines, the shelves underneath: The storage engine is the part of the database that actually puts bytes on disk and gets them back. Two big families dominate: B-tree engines (used by most relational databases such as PostgreSQL and MySQL's InnoDB) and LSM-tree engines (used by Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB and HBase style stores). They make opposite trade-offs, and choosing between them is a real system design decision.

B-tree engines: The data lives in fixed-size pages arranged as a B-tree, and updates change pages in place. To update a row, find its page (a few reads), change it, and write the page back, plus a write-ahead log record for crash safety (deep-cse-4-2-23). Reads are predictable: one walk down the tree. The weakness is random writes: changing one 100-byte row may rewrite a whole 8 KB page somewhere random on disk, and pages split as the tree grows. B-trees shine for read-heavy, transaction-heavy workloads like orders, accounts and inventory.

LSM-tree engines, step by step: LSM stands for Log-Structured Merge tree. Step 1: every write is appended to a log on disk (for crash safety) and inserted into an in-memory sorted table called the memtable. Appending is the fastest thing a disk can do. Step 2: when the memtable reaches a size, say 64 MB, it is written to disk in one go as a sorted, never-changed file called an SSTable (Sorted String Table). Step 3: over time many SSTables pile up, so a background process called compaction merges them, like merging sorted card piles, keeping only the newest value of each key and dropping deleted ones. Step 4: a read checks the memtable first, then the SSTables from newest to oldest, until it finds the key.

Making LSM reads bearable: Checking many SSTables would be slow, so each SSTable keeps a small index of key ranges and a Bloom filter. A Bloom filter is a tiny bit array that can answer "this key is definitely not in this file" or "it might be". If it says definitely not, the file is skipped without a disk read. With compaction keeping the number of files small and Bloom filters skipping most of the rest, a typical read touches only one or two files.

Amplification, the honest cost: Write amplification is how many bytes the disk really writes for each byte you write. A B-tree rewriting an 8 KB page for a 100-byte change has an amplification of about 80 for that write. An LSM tree writes the data once to the log and once in the SSTable, but compaction rewrites it again several times as files merge, often an amplification of 10 or more overall, yet as big sequential writes. Read amplification is how many places a read must look: a B-tree looks in one path; an LSM tree may look in several files. Space amplification is extra disk used by old versions waiting for compaction. No engine wins all three; you choose which pain fits your workload.

Which workload suits which: Lots of small writes that rarely change, like chat messages, sensor readings, location pings, logs and activity events: LSM trees, because appending is cheap and they absorb huge write rates. Many reads, range scans and transactions with updates in place, like bank accounts, orders and product inventory: B-trees, because reads are predictable and transactions are mature. Many real systems use both: a relational database for orders and money, and an LSM-based store for the message history or event stream.

Counters and the hot row problem: Suppose a cricket match page shows a live view counter, and 20,000 people per second open it. If every view runs UPDATE matches SET views = views + 1 WHERE id = 7, all 20,000 updates fight for the lock on one single row. They queue up one behind another, and the row becomes a hot row that slows everything near it. Fixes: split the counter into, say, 10 sub-counters (rows 7-0 to 7-9), let each view add to a random one, and sum the 10 when displaying, so contention drops roughly tenfold; or count in memory (for example, an atomic increment in a cache) and flush the total to the database every few seconds; or batch the increments through a queue (lesson 13). Displayed numbers may lag by a second, which nobody minds for a view count.

Real-life example 1, a bKash-style statement page: The most common question users ask their wallet app is "show my last 10 transactions". The transactions table holds billions of rows. The designer creates a composite index on (account_id, created_at), so the database jumps to that account and reads the newest 10 entries, about 3 page reads instead of a scan. The balance itself stays normalized in exactly one place and is updated inside a transaction, because a copied balance could disagree. The table is stored in a B-tree engine, since every transfer is a transaction that updates rows in place.

Real-life example 2, a Pathao-style location history: Every active driver sends a location every few seconds. That is a stream of tiny writes that are never edited, only appended, and are read later by trip and time range. The designer chooses an LSM-based wide-column store, partitions the data by driver and day, and sorts each partition by timestamp, so "driver 55's path between 5 pm and 6 pm" is one sorted range read. Trips, fares and payments, which need transactions, live in a relational database next to it.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Designing tables without listing the queries first. Adding an index for every column, then wondering why inserts are slow. Forgetting the leftmost-prefix rule and expecting an index on (category, price) to speed up a price-only search. Denormalizing money or other facts that must never disagree. Saying "NoSQL is faster" without saying for which workload; the real answer is write-heavy append workloads often suit LSM engines, read-and-update workloads often suit B-trees. Exams ask: compute index lookup steps with logs, explain why indexes slow writes, compare B-tree and LSM tree (memtable, SSTable, compaction, Bloom filter), pick a composite index for a given query, and fix a hot counter.

Recap: Start from access patterns, the top queries and their rates. Normalize by default, denormalize and precompute deliberately when reads dominate and slight staleness is fine. An index turns a billion-row scan into about 30 comparisons, but each index adds write cost and space. Order composite index columns by the leftmost-prefix rule. B-tree engines update pages in place and favour reads and transactions; LSM engines append and compact, favouring heavy writes. Hot rows need split counters or batching. Next lesson: what to do when even one well-designed database machine is not enough.
key_points: List the top queries and their rates (access patterns) before designing tables.
Normalize by default; denormalize or precompute on purpose when reads dominate and slight staleness is fine, never for money.
An index turns a scan of 1 billion rows into about 30 comparisons (log2), and a B-tree with fan-out 100 into about 5 levels.
Every index speeds some reads but adds a write and uses space on every insert.
Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule: equality column first, range or sort column after.
B-tree engines update pages in place and suit read-heavy transactional data.
LSM-tree engines append to a memtable, flush sorted SSTables and compact; they suit huge write rates.
A hot counter row can be fixed with split sub-counters, in-memory counting or batching.
lessons.tip: For any table you design, write its three busiest queries next to it, then check that each one has an index that matches its leftmost columns.
lessons.task: Take your phone's contact list. Decide which index you would build for "find by number" and which for "list all contacts in the Family group sorted by name". Write the column order of each composite index and explain why in one line.

quiz.q: About how many comparisons does a binary-search-style index need to find one key among 1 billion sorted keys?
quiz.explain: log2 of 1,000,000,000 is about 29.9, so roughly 30 halvings.

quiz.q: A table has an index on (category, price). Which query does it NOT help much?
quiz.explain: By the leftmost-prefix rule, prices are scattered across categories, so a price-only search cannot use the index order.

quiz.q: In an LSM-tree engine, what is the memtable?
options: A sorted file on disk that never changes
An in-memory sorted table that collects new writes before they are flushed
The process that merges old files
A filter that says a key is definitely absent
quiz.explain: Writes go to the log and the in-memory memtable first; when it fills up it is flushed as an SSTable.

quiz.q: Why does adding many indexes slow down inserts?
options: Each insert must also update every index structure
quiz.explain: With 5 indexes, one insert means the row plus 5 index entries, so about 6 writes.

quiz.q: 20,000 viewers per second increment one row's view counter and it becomes slow. What is a good fix?
options: Add another index on the counter
Split it into several sub-counters and sum them when reading
Switch the counter to a string column
quiz.explain: Spreading increments over, say, 10 sub-counters reduces lock contention about tenfold; batching or in-memory counting also works.

lessons.title: Scaling the Database: Replicas, Shard Keys and Unique IDs
lessons.content:
Think of a famous kacchi biryani shop in Old Dhaka on Eid day. At first one cook and one cashier are enough. As the crowd grows, the owner first buys a bigger pot and a faster stove. Then he hires helpers who copy the cook's recipe and serve plates from extra counters, while the head cook alone decides the recipe. Finally the crowd is so big that he opens a second branch in Mirpur and a third in Uttara, each serving its own area. Bigger stove, copies, branches: that is exactly how databases scale. Bigger machine is vertical scaling, copies are replicas, branches are shards.

Where this fits: Distributed Systems (deep-cse-6-3) already explained the theory. Lessons 14 and 15 there covered primary-backup and leaderless replication, lesson 16 consistency models, and lesson 22 partitioning and consistent hashing. We will not re-teach those. This lesson is the practical playbook: in what order to scale, how many replicas you need, how to pick a shard key, what breaks when data is split, and how to make unique IDs when there is no single database to count for you.

First, do you really need to scale out? Splitting a database is expensive in engineering time, so first squeeze the single machine. Add the right indexes (lesson 11). Fix slow queries. Put a cache in front for hot reads (lesson 8). Then scale up: a modern server with 64 cores, 512 GB of memory and fast SSDs handles a surprising amount. Only when you hit a real ceiling do you scale out. And ask which ceiling it is: too many reads, too many writes, or too much data. Reads are fixed with replicas, writes and data size with sharding.

Read replicas: One machine, the primary (also called leader), accepts all writes. It streams its changes to several replicas (followers), which apply the same changes and serve read queries. Most apps read far more than they write, often 10 to 100 times more, so moving reads to replicas takes most of the load off the primary. Replicas also give a quick backup: if the primary dies, a replica can be promoted (failover, deep-cse-6-3-14).

Replicas worked: Suppose the app does 10,000 reads per second and 500 writes per second, and one database machine comfortably handles 4,000 queries per second. Reads need 10,000 / 4,000 = 2.5 machines, so 3 replicas, plus one spare so that losing a replica does not overload the rest: 4 replicas. The primary handles the 500 writes. But notice something important: every replica must also apply all 500 writes per second, because each holds a full copy. So replicas multiply read capacity but do not add any write capacity. If writes grow to 5,000 per second, more replicas will not help at all.

Replication lag: Replication is usually asynchronous: the primary says "done" to the user before the replicas have the change. The delay until a replica catches up is called replication lag. Normally it is milliseconds, but under heavy load it can grow to seconds or more. That creates odd bugs. Example: Nusrat changes her profile name, the write goes to the primary, then the page reloads and reads from a replica that is 2 seconds behind. She sees her old name and thinks the app is broken.

Fixing lag problems in practice: These fixes give the client-centric guarantees from deep-cse-6-3-16. Read-your-writes: for data the user can edit, such as their own profile, read from the primary, or read from the primary for, say, 10 seconds after that user's last write. Better: remember the primary's log position after the write, and only read from a replica that has reached that position. Monotonic reads: send each user's reads to the same replica (for example, choose it by hashing the user id), so they never see newer data and then older data. And for anything involving money, read from the primary or use synchronous replication, accepting slightly slower writes.

When writes or data outgrow one machine, shard: Sharding (partitioning, deep-cse-6-3-22) splits the data so each machine holds only a part, and each part takes only its share of writes. Every shard is usually itself a small primary-with-replicas group, so you get both: shards for write and size scale, replicas inside each shard for read scale and safety. The theory of hash, range and consistent hashing is in that lesson; here we focus on the decision that matters most in practice, the shard key.

Choosing the shard key: The shard key is the column that decides which shard a row lives on. A good one has four properties. High cardinality: many different values, so data can spread across many shards (gender has 2 or 3 values, useless). Even spread: no single value is huge. Present in most queries: so a query can go straight to one shard instead of asking all of them. Keeps related data together: so common operations touch one shard.
