You rarely get all four perfectly, so pick the one that fits your busiest queries.

Common shard keys: User id, for apps where most queries are about one user: their profile, their posts, their orders. Tenant id, for business software serving many organisations, such as a school-management system where every query is about one school. Geography, such as city, for ride-hailing or food delivery, where riders and drivers in Dhaka never need Chattogram data. Time, for logs and metrics, but beware: all of today's writes go to the newest shard, a hot spot, so time is usually combined with something else, like device id first, then time.

How many shards worked: A social app has 400 million users and 8 TB of data, growing. The team wants each shard to hold at most 1 TB so backups and restores stay quick, and wants room to double. 8 TB at 1 TB per shard is 8 shards; doubled for growth gives 16 shards. Each shard has a primary and 2 replicas, so 48 database machines. Such numbers are estimates to start the conversation, not laws.

Cross-shard queries: Sharding makes some queries painful. "Show user 42's orders" goes to one shard if orders are sharded by user id. But "top 10 best-selling products today across all users" must ask every shard and merge the answers, called scatter-gather; with 16 shards, one slow shard makes the whole query slow. Joins across shards are worse: the database cannot do them for you, so the application must fetch from several shards and combine. Practical answers: co-locate related tables by the same key (shard orders by customer_id, like customers), denormalize the few fields you need, and send heavy analytics to a separate data warehouse fed by a pipeline (Data Engineering, deep-cse-7-11).

Cross-shard writes: A money transfer between two accounts that live on different shards is now a distributed transaction. You either use two-phase commit with its blocking risk or a saga with compensating steps (deep-cse-6-3-21). That is a strong reason to choose a shard key that keeps the most important multi-row operations inside one shard.

Resharding without pain: Shards fill up and you need more. If you used hash mod N with N real machines, adding a machine moves most rows (worked in deep-cse-6-3-22). The common practical trick is many logical shards on few physical machines: create, say, 1,024 logical shards on 8 machines, 128 each. A row's logical shard never changes. To grow, move whole logical shards to new machines: copy the shard, let the copy catch up from the replication stream, briefly pause writes to that one shard, switch the routing map, resume. Each move touches only one small piece, and the rest of the system keeps running.

Hot shards and celebrities: Even a perfect hash cannot spread one super-popular key. If a famous cricketer's account is on shard 5, millions of followers reading his posts all hit shard 5. Fixes: cache his hot data aggressively, add extra read replicas to that shard, or give very large accounts special treatment, such as their own shard or splitting their data by adding a suffix to the key. Watch per-shard metrics, because a system's speed is set by its busiest shard.

Unique IDs without one counter: On one database, AUTO_INCREMENT hands out 1, 2, 3 and so on. With 16 shards, each shard counting by itself would produce order 1001 on shard 1 and another order 1001 on shard 2. Options: Offsets: shard i uses i, i + 16, i + 32..., which works but makes adding shards awkward. UUIDs: 128-bit random IDs that any machine can make with no coordination and practically no collisions, but they are big, not sorted by time, and random inserts scatter across a B-tree index. A ticket server: one central database hands out numbers, simple but a single point of failure and a bottleneck.

Snowflake-style IDs worked: Twitter popularised a 64-bit layout that many systems copy. 1 sign bit (always 0), 41 bits of milliseconds since a chosen start date (the epoch), 10 bits of machine id, 12 bits of sequence number. 41 bits of milliseconds is 2 to the power 41 ms, about 69.7 years before it runs out. 10 bits allow 1,024 machines. 12 bits allow 4,096 IDs per millisecond per machine, over 4 million per second. To build one: time 1,000 ms after the epoch, machine 3, sequence 5 gives (1000 shifted left 22 bits) OR (3 shifted left 12 bits) OR 5 = 4,194,316,293. Because time sits in the top bits, IDs sort roughly by creation time, which keeps B-tree inserts at the end and makes "newest first" easy. The danger: if a machine's clock jumps backwards, it could repeat IDs, so generators refuse to issue IDs until the clock catches up.

Connection pooling: Each database connection uses memory and a process or thread on the server. If 200 app servers each open 50 connections, that is 10,000 connections, far more than a typical relational database handles well (often a few hundred). A connection pooler sits in between and lets thousands of app requests share a few hundred real connections, handing one out only while a query runs. It is a small box in the diagram that prevents a big outage.

Real-life example 1, a school-management app: Imagine a Bangladeshi startup whose software runs attendance, results and fees for 5,000 schools. Every query is about one school, so school_id is the shard key: all of a school's students, classes and payments sit on one shard, and joins stay local. Big schools with 5,000 students and small ones with 200 share shards by being spread over 1,024 logical shards. On SSC result day, read traffic jumps, so each shard's replicas serve result pages while the primary keeps taking fee payments.

Real-life example 2, a wallet's transaction history: A bKash-style wallet keeps billions of transaction records. They are sharded by account number, so "my last 10 transactions" goes to one shard. Each transaction gets a Snowflake-style ID, so IDs are unique across all shards and sort by time. Money moves between accounts on different shards through a saga with idempotent steps, while balance reads for the account owner always go to the shard primary to avoid lag surprises.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Sharding before trying indexes, caching and a bigger machine. Thinking replicas increase write capacity. Ignoring replication lag, then chasing "random" bugs where users see old data. Picking a shard key with low cardinality or one that most queries do not include, so every query becomes scatter-gather. Using hash mod number-of-machines and dreading the day you add one. Using auto-increment IDs across shards. Exams and interviews ask: how many replicas for a given load, how to guarantee read-your-writes, pros and cons of candidate shard keys, how to handle a cross-shard join, how to design a unique ID generator with bit counts, and how to reshard online.

Recap: Scale up and tune first. Replicas multiply reads, not writes, and bring lag, which you tame with read-your-writes and sticky replicas. Shard when writes or size outgrow one machine, and choose a shard key with many values, even spread, present in most queries, keeping related data together. Expect scatter-gather, cross-shard transactions and hot shards. Use many logical shards for easy resharding, Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs (41 + 10 + 12 bits) for unique sortable IDs, and a connection pooler to protect the database. Next lesson: moving slow work off the request path with queues.
key_points: Tune queries, add indexes and caches and try a bigger machine before splitting the database.
Read replicas multiply read capacity but every replica still applies every write, so they add no write capacity.
Asynchronous replication causes lag; fix with read-your-writes (read primary after own write) and sticky replicas for monotonic reads.
Shard when writes or data size outgrow one machine; each shard is usually a primary with replicas.
A good shard key has high cardinality, even spread, appears in most queries and keeps related data together.
Cross-shard queries need scatter-gather and cross-shard writes need 2PC or sagas.
Many logical shards on few machines make resharding a matter of moving whole small pieces.
Snowflake-style IDs: 41-bit milliseconds (about 69.7 years), 10-bit machine id (1,024), 12-bit sequence (4,096 per ms).
lessons.tip: When you propose a shard key, immediately test it against your top three queries: if any of them must ask every shard, say so and explain how you will live with it.
lessons.task: On paper, design a Snowflake-style ID for your own app with 2 data centres and 50 machines each. Decide how many bits you give to time, data centre, machine and sequence (64 total), then compute how many years and how many IDs per millisecond per machine your layout allows.

quiz.q: An app has 500 writes per second. Adding 4 more read replicas will change its write capacity how?
options: Write capacity does not increase, because every replica must apply every write
quiz.explain: Each replica holds a full copy and applies all writes; replicas scale reads only.

quiz.q: A user edits her name and then sees the old name on reload. Which guarantee was missing?
quiz.explain: She read from a lagging replica; reading her own data from the primary or a caught-up replica fixes it.

quiz.q: Which is the weakest shard key for a large social app?
options: Tenant id for a multi-school app
quiz.explain: Gender has very few values, so data cannot spread across many shards.

quiz.q: In a 64-bit Snowflake-style ID with a 12-bit sequence, how many IDs can one machine make per millisecond?
quiz.explain: 2 to the power 12 is 4,096.

quiz.q: Why do many systems create 1,024 logical shards even when they have only 8 machines?
options: So growing means moving whole small logical shards instead of rehashing every row
Because databases require powers of two
quiz.explain: A row's logical shard never changes; only the shard-to-machine map changes when machines are added.

lessons.title: Message Queues and Asynchronous Processing in Practice
lessons.content:
Walk into a busy restaurant at iftar time. The waiter does not run into the kitchen and stand there until your haleem is cooked. He writes a slip, clips it on the kitchen rail, and goes back to take the next table's order. The cooks pull slips from the rail one by one. If fifty tables order at once, the rail just gets longer; the waiter keeps smiling, and the kitchen catches up. That rail of slips is a queue, and the idea is asynchronous processing: accept the work now, do it a little later, and do not make the customer wait for the slow parts.

Where this fits: Distributed Systems (deep-cse-6-3-06) explained message-oriented middleware: brokers, point-to-point queues and publish-subscribe topics, acknowledgements and redelivery, dead-letter queues, the append-only log and consumer groups. We only recap those. This lesson is about using queues as a system designer: deciding what goes async, sizing workers, getting duplicates and ordering right, and the patterns that keep data consistent between a database and a queue.

What to make async: Ask one question about each step of a request: does the user need this result before we reply? Saving an order and charging the payment: yes, the user must know it worked, so these stay synchronous. Sending the confirmation SMS and email, generating the invoice PDF, updating recommendations, recording analytics, resizing uploaded photos, transcoding video: no, these can happen seconds or minutes later. Also make work async when it is slow, when it calls an unreliable outside service (SMS gateways, email providers), or when it arrives in bursts.

Latency worked: Suppose placing an order does: save to database 20 ms, send email 300 ms, send SMS 500 ms, build invoice PDF 400 ms. Done one after another, the user waits 20 + 300 + 500 + 400 = 1,220 ms, over a second, and if the SMS gateway is down the whole order fails. With a queue: save the order (20 ms), drop three small jobs on the queue (about 5 ms), reply. The user waits about 25 ms. The slow parts still happen, just not on the user's clock, and a sick SMS gateway no longer breaks checkout.

The job queue and worker pattern, step by step: Step 1: the web server (producer) writes a small message, such as {"type": "send_sms", "order_id": 9001, "msg_id": "a7f3"}, to the queue. Keep messages small; put big data like images in storage and send only a link. Step 2: the broker stores the message durably. Step 3: one of many worker processes (consumers) takes the message. Step 4: the worker does the job. Step 5: the worker acknowledges, and the broker deletes or marks the message done. If the worker dies before step 5, the message becomes visible again after a timeout and another worker retries it.

Queues absorb spikes: A queue is a shock absorber between a bursty producer and a steady consumer. Worked example: during a flash sale, 1,000 jobs per second arrive for 60 seconds, but the workers can only finish 600 per second. Each second the backlog grows by 400, so after 60 seconds 24,000 jobs are waiting. Then arrivals drop back to 200 per second. Workers still finish 600, so the backlog shrinks by 400 per second and is gone in 24,000 / 400 = 60 seconds. Without the queue, those extra 400 requests per second would have been errors. With it, they were simply a bit late.

Sizing workers with Little's law: Little's law says L = lambda x W: the average number of items inside a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each item spends inside. It works for queues, shops and bank counters alike. Use it to size workers: if 200 jobs per second arrive and each takes 0.5 seconds to process, then on average 200 x 0.5 = 100 jobs are being worked on at any moment. So you need at least 100 concurrent worker slots, for example 10 machines with 10 threads each, plus headroom for peaks, say 30 to 50 percent more. You can also turn it around: if 24,000 jobs are queued and throughput is 600 per second, a new job waits about 24,000 / 600 = 40 seconds.

Fan-out, one event and many listeners: Often one thing happening interests several parts of the system. When an order is placed, inventory must reserve stock, notifications must tell the customer, analytics must count the sale, and loyalty must add points. Instead of the order service calling four services, it publishes one OrderPlaced message to a topic, and each interested service has its own subscription (its own consumer group) receiving its own copy. Next month, when a fraud-check team wants the same event, they subscribe; the order service does not change at all. That is decoupling in practice.

Delivery guarantees in practice: Almost every real queue gives at-least-once delivery: a message will be delivered, but sometimes more than once. Why: a worker sends the SMS, then crashes before acknowledging, so the message is redelivered and the SMS is sent again. Exactly-once delivery across a network is not something you can assume. The practical answer is idempotent consumers: design each consumer so that processing the same message twice has the same effect as once.

Making a consumer idempotent, worked: Give every message a unique id, such as msg_id "a7f3". The consumer keeps a processed_messages table. On receiving a message: check whether a7f3 is already there; if yes, acknowledge and skip; if no, do the work and insert a7f3, ideally in the same database transaction as the work itself, so both happen or neither does. Some actions are naturally idempotent: "set order 9001 status to SHIPPED" can run twice safely, while "add 50 loyalty points" cannot, so it needs the dedup check. For external calls like payment gateways, pass an idempotency key so the provider also ignores the duplicate.

Ordering: With one queue and many parallel workers, messages finish in a random order. Usually that is fine, but sometimes it is not: for order 9001, "created", "paid" and "shipped" must be processed in that order. The practical trick is partitioning by key: log-style brokers split a topic into partitions and keep order inside each partition, and messages with the same key (here order_id 9001) always go to the same partition, consumed by one worker at a time. So you get order per order, while different orders still run in parallel. Do not ask for a global order across everything; that forces a single consumer and kills throughput.

Retries, backoff and the dead-letter queue: Some failures are temporary, like an SMS gateway timeout; others are permanent, like a malformed message or a deleted user. Retry temporary failures with exponential backoff: wait 1, 2, 4, 8, then 16 seconds, 31 seconds in total over five retries, adding a little random jitter so thousands of jobs do not retry at the same instant (deep-cse-6-3-25). After the last attempt, move the message to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) instead of retrying forever. A message that crashes every worker that touches it is called a poison message; without a retry limit it can block a queue for hours. Someone must watch the DLQ, fix the cause and replay the messages.

Visibility timeouts: When a worker takes a message, many brokers hide it from other workers for a visibility timeout, say 30 seconds. If no acknowledgement arrives in time, the message reappears for someone else. Set the timeout comfortably longer than the job usually takes; if a job takes 45 seconds and the timeout is 30, a second worker will start the same job while the first is still running, creating duplicates on every message. Long jobs can extend their timeout while they work.

Backpressure: A queue hides slowness, but it cannot make it disappear. If consumers are slower than producers for hours, the queue grows until memory or disk runs out, and messages become so old they are useless (an OTP that arrives after 20 minutes). Backpressure means pushing back on producers: cap the queue length and reject new work with a clear error, slow producers down, drop or delay low-priority work, or scale consumers automatically based on queue depth. Always monitor two numbers: queue depth (how many waiting) and age of the oldest message (how late you are).

Event-driven architecture: When services mainly talk by publishing events, the design is called event-driven. An event is a fact in past tense, like OrderPlaced or PaymentFailed, and the publisher does not know or care who listens. A command, like SendInvoice, is a request to one specific receiver. Event-driven designs are loosely coupled and easy to extend, but the flow of one business process is spread across many consumers, so it is harder to see and debug, and data across services becomes eventually consistent. Correlation ids and tracing (lesson 16) are essential.

The dual-write problem and the transactional outbox: The order service must save the order in its database and publish OrderPlaced to the queue. These are two different systems, so it cannot do both atomically. If it saves and then crashes before publishing, the order exists but nobody is notified; if it publishes and then the database save fails, everyone hears about an order that does not exist. The outbox pattern fixes this: in the same database transaction, insert the order row and an outbox row containing the event. A separate relay process reads new outbox rows and publishes them, marking each as sent. If the relay crashes, it publishes again later, which is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent. This was introduced briefly in deep-cse-6-3-21; here it is a standard building block.

Delayed and scheduled jobs: Some work must happen later at a specific time: cancel an order if not paid within 30 minutes, remind a user tomorrow at 9 am, expire a seat reservation after 10 minutes. Options: a queue that supports delayed delivery, or a jobs table with a run_at column that a scheduler polls every few seconds, picking rows whose time has come. Beware the classic cron trap: if the scheduler runs on 3 servers for safety, each may fire the same job, so use a lock or a single elected leader, and keep jobs idempotent anyway.

Choosing the kind of queue: A classic job queue (RabbitMQ-style, or a simple queue built on an in-memory store) is good for tasks: each message is handled once and deleted. A log-based broker (Kafka-style) keeps messages for days, lets many consumer groups read the same stream at their own pace, and allows replay, which suits event streams and very high throughput. Cloud providers offer managed versions of both (Cloud Computing, deep-cse-7-3). Pick by need: tasks, replay, throughput and ordering.

Real-life example 1, a Daraz-style checkout: The checkout request validates the cart, reserves stock and records the payment in the database, all synchronously, and also writes an OrderPlaced outbox row in the same transaction. The relay publishes it. The notification service sends SMS and email, the invoice service builds a PDF, analytics updates the sales dashboard and the seller service alerts the seller, each from its own subscription. On 11.11 the topic backlog grows during the first minutes, workers autoscale on queue depth, and the backlog drains while customers keep checking out.

Real-life example 2, e-KYC verification: A wallet app asks a new user to photograph their NID card and take a selfie. Checking the text, matching the face and running fraud rules can take 20 to 60 seconds, too long to hold an HTTP request open. So the upload request stores the images, enqueues a verify_kyc job with the user id, and replies "We are verifying, we will notify you". Workers process the job, retrying the face-match service with backoff if it times out, and on success publish KycApproved, which triggers a push notification. If a job fails five times it lands in the DLQ for a human reviewer.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Putting the money-critical step in a queue when the user needs its result immediately. Assuming exactly-once delivery and writing non-idempotent consumers, so customers get two SMS or double loyalty points. Retrying forever without a DLQ, letting a poison message block everything. Setting the visibility timeout shorter than the job. Ignoring queue age, so a backlog silently grows for hours. Publishing to a queue and writing to the database separately without an outbox. Exams ask: which steps of a flow should be async, compute backlog growth and drain time, use Little's law to size workers, make a consumer idempotent, keep per-key ordering, and explain the outbox pattern.

Recap: Make work async when the user does not need its result right away, when it is slow or flaky, or when it comes in bursts. A queue absorbs spikes; Little's law (L = lambda x W) sizes the workers. Expect at-least-once delivery and make consumers idempotent with message ids. Partition by key for per-key ordering. Retry with backoff and jitter, then dead-letter. Watch queue depth and oldest-message age, and push back when needed. Use the outbox to publish events reliably. Next lesson: protecting the system from too many requests with rate limiting.
key_points: Make a step async if the user does not need its result before the reply, or if it is slow, flaky or bursty.
Moving slow side jobs to a queue cut an order request from about 1,220 ms to about 25 ms in the worked example.
Queues absorb spikes: backlog grows by (arrival rate minus service rate) each second and drains with the spare capacity.
Little's law L = lambda x W sizes workers: 200 jobs/s x 0.5 s = 100 concurrent workers.
Real queues are at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent, using message ids and a processed table.
Partition by key (such as order id) to keep order per key while still running in parallel.
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, then move failures to a dead-letter queue; monitor queue depth and oldest-message age.
The transactional outbox writes the data and the event in one database transaction, then a relay publishes it.
lessons.tip: For every arrow you draw into a queue, say aloud what happens if the message is delivered twice, delivered late, or never processed; your design should have an answer for all three.
lessons.task: Write down every step that happens when you order food on a delivery app. Mark each step S (must finish before the app says "order placed") or A (can be done later by a worker), then for one A step write how you would make its consumer idempotent.

quiz.q: Which step of placing an order should usually stay synchronous?
quiz.explain: The user must know whether payment succeeded before the reply; the others can run later from a queue.

quiz.q: Jobs arrive at 1,000 per second for 60 seconds while workers finish 600 per second. How big is the backlog after 60 seconds?
quiz.explain: It grows by 1,000 - 600 = 400 per second, so 400 x 60 = 24,000.

quiz.q: 200 jobs per second arrive and each takes 0.5 seconds. By Little's law, how many jobs are in progress on average?
quiz.explain: L = lambda x W = 200 x 0.5 = 100, so you need at least 100 concurrent worker slots.

quiz.q: Why must queue consumers usually be idempotent?
options: Because real queues often deliver a message more than once
quiz.explain: At-least-once delivery means duplicates happen, for example after a crash before the acknowledgement.

quiz.q: What problem does the transactional outbox pattern solve?
options: Messages arriving out of order across partitions
Saving data and publishing its event cannot be atomic across two systems
Workers being too slow during spikes
quiz.explain: Writing the event into an outbox table in the same database transaction makes the save and the event succeed or fail together; a relay publishes later.

lessons.title: Rate Limiting: Token Buckets, Windows and Distributed Limiters
lessons.content:
Think of the ticket counter at Kamalapur railway station two days before Eid. If one person could buy 200 tickets, a few touts would empty the train and everyone else would go home without a seat. So the rule is: at most four tickets per person per day. The rule is not there to annoy honest travellers; it is there so that the counter stays fair and does not collapse. Rate limiting is that rule for software: a cap on how many requests someone may send in a period of time, with everything above the cap politely refused.

What it is: A rate limiter counts requests per client (a user, an IP address, an API key, a phone number) and, when the count passes a limit such as 100 requests per minute, rejects the extra requests, usually with HTTP status 429 Too Many Requests. It sits in front of the work, so rejected requests cost almost nothing.

Why it is needed: First, abuse: bots guessing passwords, scraping prices, or spamming sign-ups. Second, fairness: one buggy client looping in a tight loop should not starve thousands of normal users. Third, cost: some requests spend real money, such as each SMS or each call to a paid map service. Fourth, protecting downstream systems: a database that comfortably handles 5,000 queries per second will fall over at 50,000, and it is better to refuse some requests cleanly at the door than to let everyone time out. Rate limiting is different from load shedding (lesson 15): a rate limit is a per-client rule decided in advance; load shedding drops work when the whole system is overloaded, whoever sent it.

Where to put it: On the client, a limit is polite but untrusted, since anyone can modify an app. At the edge or API gateway, it stops abusive traffic before it reaches your servers; this is the most common place. Inside a service, for limits that need business knowledge, such as "at most 5 money transfers per minute per wallet". Many systems use several layers: a coarse per-IP limit at the edge and fine per-user limits in the services.

Who to count: Per user or per API key is the fairest, but needs the request to be authenticated first. Per IP works before login, but is crude: mobile operators in Bangladesh, like in many countries, put many customers behind shared public IP addresses (carrier-grade NAT), and a whole university campus may appear as one IP, so a strict per-IP limit can block hundreds of innocent users at once. Per phone number or device is useful for OTP flows. A global limit protects a fragile dependency regardless of who calls. Choose the key that matches what you are protecting.

Algorithm 1, token bucket: Picture a bucket that holds at most C tokens and is refilled at R tokens per second. Each request takes one token; if the bucket is empty, the request is rejected. Worked: C = 10, R = 1 per second, bucket starts full. At time 0 a user fires 10 requests: all allowed, bucket now 0. At 0.5 s another request: only half a token has refilled, so rejected. At 3 s, 3 tokens have refilled, so 3 more requests are allowed. Over any long stretch the user averages 1 request per second, but short bursts of up to 10 are fine. In the first 60 seconds the most they can get is 10 + 60 = 70. You only store two numbers per user, the token count and the last refill time, and compute refills lazily when a request arrives. Token bucket is the most widely used algorithm because it allows natural bursts, like an app loading a screen with 6 calls at once.

Algorithm 2, leaky bucket: Requests enter a bucket (a queue) of fixed size and leak out to be processed at a constant rate, say 5 per second, like water dripping from a hole. If the bucket is full, new requests are dropped. The output is perfectly smooth, which is great when a downstream system needs a steady pace, such as an SMS gateway that accepts at most 5 messages per second from you. The drawback: a burst of good requests waits in line or is dropped, and old requests can wait behind new ones.

Algorithm 3, fixed window counter: Cut time into windows, say each clock minute, and keep a counter per client per window, for example key "user42:12:01". Each request adds 1; if the counter passes 100, reject until the next minute starts. It is the simplest and cheapest: one counter and an expiry. Its known flaw is the boundary burst: a user sends 100 requests at 12:00:59 and another 100 at 12:01:00. Both windows are within limit, yet the system took 200 requests in about 2 seconds, double the intended rate.

Algorithm 4, sliding window log: Keep a list of timestamps of each client's recent requests. When a request arrives, delete timestamps older than 60 seconds, count what remains, and allow the request only if the count is below the limit, then add its timestamp. This is exact: there is no boundary burst. The cost is memory: with a limit of 100 per minute, each busy user can hold 100 timestamps of 8 bytes, so 1 million active users need about 800 MB just for the log. Fine for small limits or few clients, heavy for a big public API.

Algorithm 5, sliding window counter: A clever middle ground. Keep only two counters: the previous window and the current one, and assume requests in the previous window were spread evenly. Estimate = current count + previous count x (fraction of the previous window still inside the sliding 60 seconds). Worked: limit 100 per minute; the previous minute had 80 requests; we are 15 seconds into the current minute, which so far has 30. The sliding window still covers the last 45 seconds of the previous minute, which is 0.75 of it. Estimate = 30 + 80 x 0.75 = 90, below 100, so allow. At 45 seconds in, with still 30 in the current window, the estimate would be 30 + 80 x 0.25 = 50. Two counters per client, smooth limits and only a small error from the evenly-spread assumption: that is why many large systems use it.

Comparing them: Token bucket: allows bursts up to C, smooth average, tiny memory; the usual default for APIs. Leaky bucket: smooth output rate, good in front of a fixed-speed dependency. Fixed window: simplest, but allows up to double at boundaries. Sliding log: exact, memory-heavy. Sliding counter: nearly exact, cheap. In an interview, name two, explain the trade-off, and pick one for the case at hand.

Rate limiting across many servers: A real system has many gateway servers. If each keeps its own counters in memory and the limit is 100 per minute, a user whose requests are spread over 4 gateways can send up to 400. So counters usually live in a shared fast store, such as an in-memory key-value store like Redis, which all gateways consult. For fixed windows the operation is: increment the key "user42:12:01", set it to expire after 60 seconds, and reject if the new value is above 100.

Race conditions and atomicity: A naive implementation reads the count, checks it, then writes count + 1. Two gateways handling the same user at the same moment may both read 99, both decide "allowed", and both write 100, letting 101 requests through. Over many gateways the error grows. The fix is to make the check-and-update atomic: use the store's atomic increment command, which returns the new value, and decide based on that; for token bucket or sliding log, run the whole logic as one script inside the store so no other request can interleave.

Speed and failure of the limiter: The shared store adds one network round trip, usually under a millisecond inside a data centre, to every request, so keep it close and simple. Some systems also keep a small local allowance per gateway and sync with the central store every so often, trading a little accuracy for speed. And decide what happens if the limiter's store goes down: fail open (allow everything, so an outage of the limiter does not take down the product) or fail closed (reject everything, safer for very sensitive actions such as login or OTP). Most choose fail open for general traffic and fail closed for security-critical paths.

Telling the client: Reject with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, and include a Retry-After header saying how many seconds to wait. Many APIs also return headers showing the limit, how many requests remain and when the window resets, so well-behaved clients can slow down before hitting the wall. Clients, in turn, should back off with jitter when they see 429 rather than retry immediately, otherwise the retries themselves become a flood.

Real-life example 1, protecting OTP SMS: A wallet or e-commerce app sends a one-time password by SMS at login. Attackers sometimes run bots that request OTPs for thousands of numbers, either to annoy people or to make the company pay for SMS. Suppose each SMS costs the company 0.30 taka; one million fake requests would cost 300,000 taka. Layered limits stop this: at most 3 OTPs per phone number per 15 minutes (sliding window), at most 10 per device per hour, a coarse per-IP limit that is generous enough for shared mobile IPs, and a global ceiling on total SMS per minute that alerts the team when crossed. The OTP verify endpoint gets its own strict limit, say 5 wrong attempts and then a lock, so the 6-digit code cannot be guessed by trying all 1,000,000 values.

Real-life example 2, a payment gateway's public API: A Bangladeshi payment gateway lets online shops create payments through its API. Each merchant gets an API key and a plan: small shops 20 requests per second, large marketplaces 500. The gateway uses a token bucket per key with C equal to twice the rate, so a shop can burst briefly when a campaign starts. Counters live in a shared in-memory store with atomic scripts. Responses carry the remaining quota, and on 429 the official client library waits for Retry-After plus jitter. A separate global limit protects the bank connection behind the gateway, which can only accept a fixed rate.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Relying only on client-side limits. Counting per IP only and blocking whole campuses or mobile operators. Keeping counters in each server's memory and forgetting the effective limit multiplies by the number of servers. Read-then-write races. Forgetting what happens when the limiter's store fails. Returning a vague 500 error instead of 429 with Retry-After. Exams ask: explain and trace token bucket and leaky bucket, show the fixed-window boundary problem with numbers, compute the sliding window counter estimate, design a distributed rate limiter, and choose keys and limits for a scenario such as login or OTP.

Recap: Rate limiting caps requests per client per time to stop abuse, keep fairness, control cost and protect downstream systems. Put it at the gateway and inside services where business rules need it, and pick the counting key carefully. Token bucket allows bursts with a steady average; leaky bucket smooths output; fixed window is cheap but can double at boundaries; sliding log is exact but memory-heavy; sliding counter (current + previous x overlap) is the practical compromise. Share counters across servers with atomic operations, decide fail-open or fail-closed, and answer with 429 and Retry-After. Next lesson: keeping the whole system up when parts of it fail.
key_points: Rate limiting caps requests per client per time window to stop abuse, keep fairness, control cost and protect downstream systems.
Put it at the edge or API gateway, plus service-level limits for business rules; client-side limits are not trusted.
Choose the key carefully: per user or API key is fair; per IP can block many users behind shared mobile or campus IPs.
Token bucket (capacity C, refill R) allows bursts up to C with a long-run average of R; it is the usual default.
Fixed windows are cheap but allow up to double the limit at a boundary (100 at 12:00:59 plus 100 at 12:01:00).
Sliding window counter estimate = current + previous x overlap fraction, e.g. 30 + 80 x 0.75 = 90.
Across many servers use a shared store with atomic increments or scripts to avoid read-then-write races.
Reject with HTTP 429 and Retry-After; decide whether the limiter fails open or closed.
lessons.tip: When you add a rate limiter to a design, always state four things: what key you count by, which algorithm, where the counters live, and what happens if that store is down.
lessons.task: Take a sheet of paper and simulate a token bucket with capacity 5 and refill 1 token every 2 seconds. Write the times of 12 imaginary requests (some bunched, some spread) and mark each one allowed or rejected, tracking the token count after each.

quiz.q: A token bucket has capacity 10 and refills 1 token per second, starting full. What is the most requests a client can get through in the first 60 seconds?
quiz.explain: 10 tokens at the start plus 60 refilled over 60 seconds gives 70.

quiz.q: What is the known weakness of the fixed window counter?
options: It needs a timestamp for every request
A client can send up to double the limit across a window boundary
It cannot be stored in memory
quiz.explain: 100 requests at the end of one window and 100 at the start of the next pass both checks, 200 in about 2 seconds.

quiz.q: Limit 100 per minute. Previous minute had 80 requests; we are 15 seconds into the current minute with 30 so far. What is the sliding window counter estimate?
quiz.explain: 30 + 80 x 0.75 = 90, since 45 of the previous 60 seconds still fall in the window.

quiz.q: Four gateway servers each keep their own in-memory counter with a limit of 100 per minute. What can go wrong?
options: Requests are processed out of order
A client spread across all four can send up to 400 per minute
quiz.explain: Each server counts separately, so the effective limit multiplies by the number of servers; a shared store fixes it.

quiz.q: Which HTTP response should a rate limiter return when a client is over its limit?
options: 429 Too Many Requests, ideally with Retry-After
quiz.explain: 429 tells the client exactly what happened and Retry-After tells it how long to wait.

lessons.title: Reliability and Resilience: Redundancy, Failure Patterns and Disaster Recovery
lessons.content:
A good hospital in Dhaka does not trust the power line alone. When the electricity goes, an IPS keeps the lights on for a few seconds, then a diesel generator starts, and the operating theatre never goes dark. Nobody hopes for a blackout; they simply assume one will come and plan for it. Reliable systems are built the same way. Disks die, servers reboot, networks split, a bad deploy ships a bug, a cloud region has a bad day. Reliability engineering is not about preventing every failure, which is impossible, but about making sure that when a part fails, the users barely notice.

Where this fits: Distributed Systems (deep-cse-6-3-20) defined faults, errors and failures, failure models, MTTF and MTTR, and lesson 25 there introduced retries with backoff, timeouts, circuit breakers and SLOs. Lesson 02 of this course explained availability nines. Here we turn those ideas into a designer's checklist: find single points of failure, do the availability math, add redundancy, and use the standard resilience patterns, plus backups and disaster recovery. Fault Tolerant Systems (deep-cse-7-10) goes deeper into the theory.

Single points of failure: A single point of failure (SPOF) is any part whose failure alone takes the whole service down. To find them, walk your diagram box by box and ask: "If this one dies right now, what happens?" Obvious ones: one load balancer, one database primary with no standby, one cache everyone depends on. Less obvious ones: one DNS provider, one data centre, one payment provider, a TLS certificate that expires on a forgotten date, or the one engineer who knows the production password. Each SPOF you find gets one of three answers: make it redundant, make its failure harmless (degrade), or accept the risk on purpose and write that down.

Availability in series: When a request must pass through several components one after another, all of them must work, so their availabilities multiply. Worked: a load balancer at 99.99 percent, an app tier at 99.9 percent and a database at 99.9 percent give 0.9999 x 0.999 x 0.999, about 0.9979, which is 99.79 percent, or roughly 18.4 hours of downtime a year, worse than any single part. Three components each at 99.9 percent give 0.999 cubed, about 99.70 percent, around 26.3 hours a year instead of 8.76. Lesson: every extra box on the critical path lowers availability, so keep the critical path short.

Availability in parallel: When you have redundant copies and any one of them can serve, the system fails only if all fail at once. For two independent copies each 99 percent available, the chance both are down is 0.01 x 0.01 = 0.0001, so availability is 1 - 0.0001 = 99.99 percent. Two mediocre machines together beat one excellent machine. The big catch is the word independent. Two servers in the same rack share a power supply and a network switch; two copies running the same buggy code crash on the same bad input; two regions configured by the same faulty script break together. Real redundancy means spreading copies across racks, zones and sometimes regions, and rolling out changes gradually so a bug cannot hit every copy at once.

Kinds of redundancy: Active-active: all copies serve traffic all the time, like several app servers behind a load balancer; failure of one just shifts load to the others. Active-passive: one copy serves while a standby waits, like a database primary and its replica; on failure the standby is promoted. The standby can be hot (running and in sync, takes over in seconds), warm (running but needs some catching up) or cold (must be started and loaded, takes much longer). Capacity rule N+1: if peak traffic needs 4 servers, run 5, so losing one at peak is harmless; N+2 lets you also take one out for maintenance.

Timeouts, the first defence: Every network call must have a timeout, because a remote service that hangs is worse than one that fails fast. Worked with Little's law (lesson 13): a service has a pool of 200 worker threads and makes 100 calls per second to a downstream service. If that service hangs and the timeout is 30 seconds, threads stuck waiting = 100 x 30 = 3,000, far more than 200, so the pool is exhausted in about 2 seconds and the whole service stops answering, even for requests that never needed the sick downstream. With a 1-second timeout, at most 100 x 1 = 100 threads are stuck, and the service survives. Set timeouts from measured latency, a bit above the p99, not from library defaults.

Retries, carefully: Retries fix brief glitches, but they can also multiply load exactly when a system is struggling. Recap from deep-cse-6-3-25: use exponential backoff with jitter, retry only idempotent operations or ones protected by idempotency keys, and cap the attempts. Watch for retry amplification across layers: if the app retries 3 times, its client library retries 3 times, and the gateway retries 3 times, one user click can become 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 calls to a failing database. Retry at one layer only, and use a retry budget, for example retries may add at most 10 percent on top of normal traffic.

Circuit breakers: Recap: a circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and watches failures. Closed: calls flow normally. If, say, more than 50 percent of calls fail within 10 seconds, it opens: calls fail immediately without touching the dependency, giving it room to recover and saving your threads. After a cool-down, say 30 seconds, it goes half-open and lets a few trial calls through; if they succeed it closes, if not it opens again. Pair it with a fallback, such as cached data or a friendly message.

Bulkheads: Ships are divided into watertight compartments, so a hole floods one section, not the whole ship. In software, a bulkhead gives each dependency its own limited pool of threads or connections. If a service has 200 threads and gives 50 to calls to an outside payment provider, then when that provider hangs only those 50 get stuck; the other 150 keep serving browsing, login and order history. Without the bulkhead, the one sick dependency would eat all 200 threads.

Graceful degradation: Not every feature is equally important. When a part fails, switch off or simplify the less important features and keep the core working. A product page whose reviews service is down shows the product, price and buy button, and quietly hides the reviews section. A home feed whose recommendation engine is slow shows a cached list of popular items. A ride app whose ETA service fails shows "a few minutes" instead of crashing. Decide in advance which features are core and which can be dropped, and build the fallbacks before the bad day.

Load shedding: When total demand exceeds total capacity, trying to serve everyone means serving everyone slowly and then nobody at all, as queues grow and requests time out after work was already spent on them. Load shedding means rejecting some requests early and cheaply, usually with HTTP 503, so the rest get good service. Shed by priority: keep payments and logins, drop analytics events, prefetching and background refreshes first. A common signal is queue length or request age: if a request has already waited longer than the client will wait, drop it rather than process it uselessly. The goal is to keep goodput, the useful completed work, high.

Health checks: The load balancer needs to know which instances to send traffic to. A liveness check asks "is the process alive?", and if not, restart it. A readiness check asks "can it serve traffic right now?", for example it has finished warming its cache and can reach what it needs. Be careful with deep checks: if every app instance reports unhealthy whenever the shared database is slow, the load balancer may remove all instances at once and turn a slowdown into a full outage. Keep readiness focused on the instance itself and handle dependency trouble with timeouts, breakers and degradation.

Backups and the 3-2-1 rule: Replication is not a backup. If someone runs a bad DELETE, or a bug corrupts data, replication faithfully copies the damage to every replica within milliseconds. Backups are point-in-time copies you can go back to. A classic guideline is 3-2-1: keep 3 copies of the data, on 2 different kinds of storage, with 1 copy offsite, in another location. Many teams add that one copy should be immutable or offline, so ransomware or a compromised account cannot delete it. And a backup you have never restored is only a hope: test restores regularly and time them.

RPO and RTO: Two numbers define how bad a disaster may be. Recovery Point Objective (RPO): how much recent data you can afford to lose, measured in time. If you back up once a night at 2 am and disaster strikes at 11 pm, you lose up to about 21 hours of data, so nightly backups mean an RPO of up to 24 hours; continuous replication or log shipping brings it down to seconds or minutes. Recovery Time Objective (RTO): how long the service may be down before it is restored. Restoring 5 TB from backup might take hours; failing over to a hot standby takes minutes. A wallet ledger might need RPO near zero and RTO of minutes; a blog can live with RPO of a day and RTO of hours. Lower numbers cost more money.

Disaster recovery strategies: From cheapest and slowest to most expensive and fastest. Backup and restore: only backups in another region; recovery takes hours. Pilot light: the core data is continuously replicated to a second region, but the servers there are off or tiny; start and scale them on disaster, tens of minutes. Warm standby: a scaled-down but fully working copy runs in the second region; scale it up and switch traffic, minutes. Active-active (multi-site): both regions serve real users all the time; losing one only shifts traffic, near-zero RTO, but it is the most expensive and makes data consistency hard. Match the strategy to the RPO and RTO the business actually needs.

Multi-region trade-offs: Running in two regions protects against a whole data centre or city outage, but brings new problems. Round trips between regions take tens of milliseconds, so synchronous writes to both slow every write; asynchronous writes risk losing the last seconds of data on failover. Two regions accepting writes for the same data can conflict, the CAP and PACELC choices from deep-cse-6-3-17 in practice. Some data may legally have to stay in the country. A common compromise is to keep each user's data homed in one region, serve reads nearby, and fail over whole regions only when needed.

Chaos testing and game days: You only know your failover works when you have seen it work. Chaos engineering deliberately injects failures, such as killing instances, adding network delay or blocking a dependency, to check that the system degrades as designed. Netflix's Chaos Monkey, which randomly terminates production instances, is the famous example. Start small: in a staging environment, during working hours, with a clear stop button. A game day is a planned drill where the team simulates a disaster, such as "the primary database is gone", and practises the runbook while measuring the real RTO.

Real-life example 1, a wallet on Eid eve: A bKash-style wallet expects five times normal traffic. The app tier runs N+1 per zone across two zones; the ledger database has a synchronous standby in another zone for RPO near zero, and backups go to another city every hour. Calls to each partner bank go through a separate bulkhead with a 2-second timeout and a circuit breaker; when one bank's link fails, transfers to that bank show "temporarily unavailable" while all other features keep working. Promotional banners and cashback calculations are the first things shed if load climbs too high.

Real-life example 2, a public results website: On the day board exam results are published, millions of students hit the site within minutes. The team makes results read-only and precomputed, serves them from a CDN and a cache, and keeps the database off the hot path. A queue-based waiting page and load shedding protect the origin when the CDN misses spike. Health checks are shallow so a slow database does not drain the load balancer. A rehearsal a week earlier, with synthetic traffic at twice the expected peak, revealed that the old timeout was 60 seconds; it was cut to 2.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Calling a system highly available while it has one database and no standby. Adding redundant copies that share the same rack, power or deployment, so they fail together. Calling remote services without timeouts, or with library defaults of 30 to 60 seconds. Retrying at every layer. Treating replication as a backup, and never testing restores. Using deep health checks that pull every instance out at once. Exams ask: compute availability in series and in parallel, identify SPOFs in a diagram, explain circuit breaker states and bulkheads, define RPO and RTO with numbers, and compare DR strategies.

Recap: Assume failure and design so users barely notice. Find SPOFs by asking "what if this dies?" for every box. Series availability multiplies down (0.999 cubed is about 99.7 percent); independent parallel copies multiply failure chances down (1 - 0.01 squared = 99.99 percent). Use N+1 capacity, active-active or hot standby, short timeouts, careful retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads, graceful degradation and load shedding. Back up with 3-2-1 and test restores, set RPO and RTO, choose a DR strategy that matches them, and prove it with chaos tests. Next lesson: seeing inside the system, shipping safely, and securing it.
key_points: A single point of failure is any part whose failure alone brings the service down; find them by asking "what if this dies?" for every box.
In series availabilities multiply: three parts at 99.9 percent give about 99.7 percent (about 26 hours down a year).
Independent parallel copies: two at 99 percent give 1 - 0.01 x 0.01 = 99.99 percent, but only if failures are truly independent.
Every remote call needs a timeout; 100 calls/s x 30 s timeout = 3,000 stuck threads, enough to kill a 200-thread service.
Retry at one layer with backoff, jitter and a budget; 3 retries at 3 layers can become 27 calls.
Circuit breakers, bulkheads, graceful degradation and load shedding stop one failure from spreading.
Replication is not a backup: follow 3-2-1 and test restores.
RPO is how much data you may lose, RTO how long you may be down; DR strategies trade cost for lower RPO and RTO.
lessons.tip: For every design, draw the request's critical path, write an availability number on each box, multiply them, and then ask which single box, made redundant, would raise the total the most.
lessons.task: Pick an app you use daily. List five things it depends on (for example login, payment, maps, notifications, images). For each, write what the app should still let you do if that one part fails, which is your graceful degradation plan.

quiz.q: A request passes through three components in series, each 99.9 percent available. What is the overall availability, roughly?
quiz.explain: 0.999 x 0.999 x 0.999 is about 0.997, so about 99.7 percent, roughly 26 hours of downtime per year.

quiz.q: Two independent servers each 99 percent available, and either can serve. What is the availability?
quiz.explain: Both must fail together: 0.01 x 0.01 = 0.0001, so 1 - 0.0001 = 99.99 percent.

quiz.q: A service with 200 threads calls a hung dependency 100 times per second with a 30-second timeout. What happens?
options: About 3,000 threads would be needed, so the pool is exhausted in about 2 seconds
quiz.explain: Little's law: 100 x 30 = 3,000 waiting calls, far above 200 threads.

quiz.q: Why is database replication alone not a backup?
options: A bad delete or corruption is copied to every replica too
quiz.explain: Replication copies every change, including mistakes; backups let you go back to an earlier point in time.

quiz.q: Nightly backups at 2 am and disaster at 11 pm. Which statement about RPO is correct?
options: Up to about 21 hours of data can be lost, so the RPO is up to about a day
RPO is zero because a backup exists
RPO measures how long restore takes
quiz.explain: RPO is the window of data you can lose; with nightly backups it can approach 24 hours. Restore duration is RTO.

lessons.title: Observability, Deployment and Security in Design
lessons.content:
Imagine you run a busy restaurant kitchen in Dhaka. You need three things to keep it going. First, eyes: you must see which stove is overheating, which order is late and how long customers are waiting. Second, a safe way to change the menu: you would not throw out every old dish and serve a brand-new menu to 500 guests at once; you would let a few tables taste the new dish first. Third, locks and guards: only the cook enters the kitchen, only the cashier opens the cash box, and the back door stays shut. A large software system needs exactly the same three things. Watching it is called observability, changing it safely is called deployment, and protecting it is security. This lesson puts all three into your system design toolbox.

Where this fits: Distributed Systems (deep-cse-6-3-25) already introduced logs, metrics, traces, correlation ids, SLIs, SLOs and error budgets. Web Engineering (deep-cse-5-3-20 to 22) taught sessions, tokens, password hashing and the OWASP Top 10. We will only recap those and focus on the design questions: what should you measure, which alerts actually help, how do you ship new code to millions of users without breaking them, and where do security controls go in the boxes-and-arrows diagram.

Observability in one breath: Observability means you can answer "what is going on inside, and why?" just by looking at what the system sends out. Three signals do the job. Logs are timestamped lines describing single events, like "payment 8812 failed: insufficient balance". Metrics are numbers counted over time, like "1,240 requests per second" or "error rate 0.3 percent"; they are cheap to store and great for graphs and alerts. Traces follow one request as it hops through many services, so you can see that a 900 ms checkout spent 700 ms waiting for the inventory service. A correlation id, one unique id attached to the request at the front door and passed along every hop, ties the logs and the trace together.

The four golden signals: Google's SRE book suggests four signals to watch for every user-facing service. Latency: how long requests take, and you should track failed requests separately, since a fast error is not a happy user. Traffic: how much demand there is, such as requests per second. Errors: the rate of failed requests, including ones that return 200 but with wrong content. Saturation: how full the system is, like CPU at 85 percent, a queue with 50,000 waiting jobs or a database at 95 of 100 connections. If you can only build one dashboard, build these four for each service.

Percentiles, not averages: Averages hide pain. Suppose 100 requests take 50 ms each except 5 slow ones that take 2,000 ms. The average is (95 x 50 + 5 x 2,000) / 100 = (4,750 + 10,000) / 100 = 147.5 ms, which sounds fine. But the 95th percentile, the time under which 95 percent of requests finish, is 50 ms, and the 99th percentile is 2,000 ms. That p99 tells the truth: one user in a hundred waits two seconds. And a page that calls 20 services will hit somebody's slow 1 percent quite often, so big systems watch p99 and even p999. Lesson 02 showed how to compute percentiles from a sorted list.

Alerts that matter: An alert should wake a human only when users are hurting or soon will be, and only when the human can do something. Alerting on symptoms is better than alerting on causes. "Checkout error rate above 2 percent for 5 minutes" is a good alert. "CPU above 80 percent on one server" is usually noise, because the load balancer may simply route around it. Too many noisy alerts cause alert fatigue: engineers start ignoring the pager, and then miss the real fire. A common pattern is two levels: pages for urgent user pain, and tickets for things to fix during office hours, like a disk that will be full in 3 days. Every alert should link to a runbook, a short page that says what to check first.

SLO-based alerting recap: In deep-cse-6-3-25 you saw that an SLO like "99.9 percent of requests succeed over 30 days" gives an error budget of 0.1 percent. If the service gets 100 million requests a month, the budget is 100,000 failed requests. Instead of alerting on every blip, teams alert on burn rate: how fast the budget is being used. If it is burning so fast that the whole month's budget would be gone in two days, page someone now. If slowly, open a ticket.

Deployment, the problem: Most outages in real companies are caused by changes: a new code version, a config edit, a database migration. So how you release is part of the design. The old way was big-bang: stop the site at midnight, copy new code to every server, start again and pray. Downtime and huge risk. Modern systems release often in small pieces, and they choose a strategy that limits how many users a bad change can touch.

Rolling deployment: Suppose 10 servers sit behind a load balancer. Take server 1 out of the pool, update it, check its health, put it back, then server 2, and so on. At every moment at least 9 servers serve traffic, so there is no downtime. The downside: for a while, old and new versions run side by side, so they must be compatible, for example both must understand the same database columns and API fields. Rolling back means rolling forward again with the old version, which takes time.

Blue-green deployment: Keep two identical environments. Blue runs the current version and gets all traffic. You install the new version on green, test it quietly, then flip the load balancer or DNS so all traffic goes to green. If something is wrong, flip back to blue in seconds. Rollback is instant, which is the big win. The costs: you need double the servers during the switch, and shared things such as the database are not duplicated, so database changes still need care.

Canary deployment, worked: Named after the canary birds miners carried to detect bad gas early. Send a small slice of real traffic to the new version and compare. Say the service takes 2,000 requests per second. Step 1: 5 percent goes to the canary, which is 2,000 x 0.05 = 100 requests per second; 1,900 still go to the old version. Watch for 15 minutes. The old version shows an error rate of 0.1 percent and p99 of 300 ms. If the canary shows 0.1 percent and 310 ms, it is healthy, so step up to 25 percent, then 50, then 100. If the canary shows 2 percent errors, that is 20 times worse, so the system rolls it back automatically. Only 5 percent of users for 15 minutes saw the problem, instead of everyone. Many teams also roll out region by region, for example first one data center, then the rest.

Feature flags: A feature flag is an if-statement controlled from outside the code: if flag("new_checkout", user) then new flow else old flow. You can deploy code with the feature switched off, then turn it on for staff, then for 1 percent of users, then for everyone, without another deployment. If it misbehaves, turn the flag off in seconds. Flags also allow A/B tests. The trap is flag debt: old flags that nobody removes, making the code a maze of branches. Delete a flag once the feature is fully launched.

Database changes without downtime, expand and contract: Code can roll back in seconds, but data cannot. Imagine renaming the column phone to mobile_number while old and new code run together. If you rename in one step, old servers crash looking for phone. The safe way has phases. Expand: add the new column mobile_number, and let new code write to both columns. Migrate: copy old rows from phone to mobile_number in small batches, so the database is not locked for an hour. Switch: make code read from mobile_number. Contract: once no code uses phone, drop it. Each step is backward compatible, so you can stop or roll back at any point.

Security in the design: Security is not a box you add at the end; it shows up on almost every arrow. Start with two words that people mix up. Authentication answers "who are you?", for example by password plus an OTP. Authorization answers "what are you allowed to do?", for example a customer may see only their own orders, while a support agent may see any order but may not refund more than 5,000 taka. In a design, authentication usually happens once at the edge, often at the API gateway, which then passes a verified identity to inner services. Authorization must be checked by the service that owns the data, every time.

Tokens recap: After login, the server gives the client a token. A session id is a random string that points to session data stored on the server or in a shared cache. A signed token such as a JWT carries the user id and expiry inside it, signed so nobody can change it; any service can verify it without a database lookup, which scales well. The catch: a signed token cannot easily be cancelled before it expires, so keep access tokens short-lived, like 15 minutes, and use a longer refresh token that the server can revoke. OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect are the standard flows for "log in with Google" style sign-in (deep-cse-5-3-20).

Encrypt everywhere: Encryption in transit means TLS on every connection, not just from phone to load balancer but also between internal services, because internal networks get breached too. Encryption at rest means disks, backups and database files are encrypted, so a stolen disk or a leaked backup is useless. The keys themselves live in a key management service, not in the code. Very sensitive fields, like national ID numbers, can get extra field-level encryption, so even a database admin sees only scrambled bytes.

Secrets and least privilege: Passwords for databases, API keys for SMS gateways and signing keys are secrets. They must never be written in source code or pushed to Git, because repositories get copied and leaked. Store them in a secrets manager and inject them at runtime. Least privilege means every person and every service gets only the permissions it needs: the notification service can read phone numbers but cannot touch balances. If it is hacked, the damage stays small. This is also called limiting the blast radius.

DDoS and abuse in layers: A distributed denial-of-service attack floods you with traffic from thousands of machines. Defence comes in layers. The CDN and cloud edge absorb huge network floods (lesson 09). A web application firewall blocks known bad patterns such as SQL injection attempts. Rate limiting (lesson 14) slows down any single user, IP or API key. Inside, autoscaling and load shedding (lesson 15) keep the core alive. The OWASP Top 10 (deep-cse-5-3-22) covers code-level bugs like injection and broken access control, which no firewall can fully fix.

Real-life example 1, a wallet's Friday release: A bKash-style wallet team wants to release a new "send money" screen. The backend change goes out by canary: 2 percent of traffic in one data center for 20 minutes. Dashboards show the four golden signals for both versions side by side, and a trace sample shows each transfer's path. The new screen is behind a feature flag, first enabled for employees. On the second day the flag reaches 10 percent of users, and the team notices p99 latency rose from 400 ms to 900 ms for that group. Traces show a new call to the rewards service on the critical path. They turn the flag off in seconds, move the rewards call to an async queue, and try again the next week. No customer lost money, and most never noticed.

Real-life example 2, a university result portal: On SSC result day, a results website gets a sudden flood. The team watches traffic and saturation and sees the database connection pool at 98 percent. An alert based on the error-rate SLO pages the on-call engineer, whose runbook says: turn on the static cached result page and enable stricter rate limits. Meanwhile security is in place: the admin panel that uploads results sits on a separate internal network, requires two-factor login and is allowed only for three named staff accounts. Thousands of students hammering the public site cannot even reach it.

Common mistakes: Logging everything at full detail, then paying a fortune for storage while the useful line is buried. Logging passwords, OTPs or full card numbers, which turns logs into a security leak. Watching averages instead of p99. Alerting on causes like CPU instead of user symptoms, creating alert fatigue. Deploying a database rename in one step. Treating the internal network as safe and skipping TLS inside. Using long-lived JWTs that cannot be revoked. Hard-coding API keys in the app.

What exams and interviews ask: Name the three pillars of observability and what each is good for. List the four golden signals. Explain why p99 matters more than the average, with numbers. Compare rolling, blue-green and canary deployments on downtime, rollback speed and cost. Explain feature flags and expand-and-contract migrations. Distinguish authentication from authorization and say where each is checked. Explain encryption in transit versus at rest. In a design interview, saying "we roll out by canary with automatic rollback on SLO burn" and "auth at the gateway, authorization in each service, TLS everywhere" shows maturity.

Recap: Observability uses logs, metrics and traces, joined by a correlation id, and the four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Watch percentiles, alert on user pain, and give every alert a runbook. Release in small, reversible steps: rolling for no downtime, blue-green for instant rollback, canary to limit the blast of a bad change, and feature flags to separate deploy from launch. Change databases with expand and contract. Build security into every arrow: authenticate at the edge, authorize at the data, encrypt in transit and at rest, keep secrets out of code, give least privilege, and defend against floods in layers. Next lesson, we look at how to split a system into microservices, and when not to.
key_points: Logs, metrics and traces, tied together by a correlation id, let you see inside a running system.
Watch the four golden signals for every service: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
Use percentiles like p99, not averages: 95 requests at 50 ms and 5 at 2,000 ms average 147.5 ms but p99 is 2,000 ms.
Alert on user-facing symptoms and SLO burn rate, with a runbook for each alert, to avoid alert fatigue.
Rolling avoids downtime, blue-green gives instant rollback, canary limits a bad change to a small slice of traffic.
Feature flags separate deploying code from launching a feature; expand and contract changes databases safely.
Authenticate at the edge, authorize in the service that owns the data, and use TLS everywhere plus encryption at rest.
Keep secrets out of code, give least privilege, and defend against DDoS in layers: CDN, firewall, rate limits, load shedding.
lessons.tip: When you draw any design, add three small labels before you finish: which four numbers you would put on its dashboard, how a new version reaches users, and where the login check and the permission check happen.
lessons.task: Take 20 response times from a stopwatch or invent them (make 2 of them very slow). Sort them, compute the average, the median and the p95 on paper, and write one sentence on which number best describes the unhappy users.

quiz.q: Which set lists the four golden signals?
quiz.explain: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation describe how a user-facing service is doing; CPU and RAM are only parts of saturation.

quiz.q: 95 requests take 50 ms and 5 take 2,000 ms. Why is the average of 147.5 ms misleading?
options: Averages are always larger than p99
It hides that 1 in 100 users waits 2 seconds, which p99 shows
quiz.explain: The average looks fine, but p99 = 2,000 ms reveals the slow tail that real users feel.

quiz.q: A team wants the fastest possible rollback if a new version misbehaves, and can afford double servers briefly. Which strategy fits best?
options: Editing code directly on production servers
quiz.explain: Blue-green keeps the old environment ready, so switching traffic back takes seconds, at the cost of running two environments.

quiz.q: You must rename a database column while old and new code run side by side. What is the safe approach?
options: Rename it in one step during peak hours
Delete the column and recreate it
Expand and contract: add the new column, write both, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old one
quiz.explain: Each expand-and-contract step stays compatible with both versions, so nothing crashes and you can stop at any point.

quiz.q: Where should the check "may this support agent refund 8,000 taka?" happen?
options: In the service that owns the refund data, as an authorization check
quiz.explain: Login proves who you are (authentication). What you may do (authorization) must be enforced by the service owning the data, every time.

lessons.title: Microservices in Practice: When and How to Split
lessons.content:
Think of a small family shop in Mirpur. One person takes orders, packs bags, keeps accounts and handles delivery. It works because everything is in one head and one room. Now imagine the shop grows into a supermarket chain with 200 staff. If every decision still went through one person, the whole chain would crawl. So they split into departments: purchasing, warehouse, billing, delivery, each with its own team, own records and a clear way to send requests to the others. A software system can grow the same way. One big program is called a monolith; a set of small, separately deployed services, each owning one business job, is called microservices. This lesson is about when and how to split, and when not to.

Where this fits: Distributed Systems (deep-cse-6-3) already taught RPC (05), message queues (06), sagas (21) and retries, timeouts and circuit breakers (25). Here we use them as tools. The question in this lesson is a design question: where do you draw the lines between services, how do the services talk, and what does the split cost you?

The monolith: A monolith is one codebase, built and deployed as one unit, usually with one database. Inside, it can still be neatly organised into modules. Its strengths are real: one place to search code, function calls instead of network calls, one database transaction can update orders and payments together, one deployment to manage, easy local testing. Many very large websites ran as monoliths for years. Its problems show up with size: a 2-million-line codebase where a change in one corner breaks another, 100 engineers stepping on each other's toes, a build that takes 40 minutes, and the whole app must scale together even if only search is busy.

Microservices: In a microservice architecture, each service does one business job, such as users, catalog, orders, payments or notifications. Each is deployed on its own schedule, runs as its own process, and talks to others only over the network through an API or events. Each is usually owned by one small team. The wins: teams move independently, a bug in recommendations cannot crash payments if boundaries are well designed, and you can scale just the busy part, for example 30 copies of search and 3 copies of the profile service. Each service can even pick the language or database that fits it.

Monolith first: Martin Fowler and others advise starting most new products as a monolith. Early on, you do not yet know where the natural boundaries are, and the product changes every week. Drawing service boundaries in the wrong places is very expensive to undo, because moving a line now means changing APIs, databases and teams. A small team of 5 engineers with 10 services spends its time on plumbing instead of features. Split later, when real pain appears: teams blocking each other, parts with very different scaling needs, or parts that change at very different speeds.

The modular monolith: A middle path is a modular monolith: one deployable app, but strictly divided into modules with clear interfaces, and each module owning its own tables. Orders may not read the payments tables directly; it must call the payments module's public functions. You keep the simplicity of one deployment and in-process calls, but the code is already shaped like services. If one module later needs to become its own service, the cut line is already drawn.

Splitting by business capability: The best boundaries follow what the business does, not technical layers. A bad split is "frontend service, logic service, database service": every feature then touches all three, and they must be deployed together, which is a distributed monolith with all the costs and none of the benefits. A good split follows capabilities, like catalog, cart, ordering, payment, delivery tracking. Domain-driven design calls such a boundary a bounded context: inside it, words have one clear meaning. "Order" in the kitchen context means dishes to cook; in the payment context it means an amount to charge.

Database per service: Each service owns its data, and no other service touches its tables directly. If the delivery service needs a customer address, it asks the user service's API or keeps its own copy updated by events. Why so strict? Shared tables couple services secretly: if orders changes a column, delivery breaks, and you lose the freedom to deploy separately. The price is real: no cross-service joins, no single transaction spanning services, and some data is duplicated and only eventually consistent.

Synchronous communication: One service calls another and waits for the reply, using REST over HTTP or gRPC (lesson 06). It is simple to reason about and right when you need the answer now, such as "is this coupon valid?" before showing the price. The danger is chains. If service A calls B, B calls C, and each has 99.9 percent availability, the chain's availability is 0.999 x 0.999 x 0.999, about 99.7 percent. With 10 services in a row it falls to about 99.0 percent, which means roughly 7 hours of trouble a month instead of 43 minutes. Latency also adds up: five sequential calls of 20 ms each already cost 100 ms. So keep call chains short, and protect each call with timeouts, limited retries and circuit breakers (deep-cse-6-3-25).

Asynchronous communication: A service publishes an event, like "OrderPlaced", to a message broker and moves on (lesson 13). Any interested service subscribes: notifications sends an SMS, analytics counts the sale, loyalty adds points. The publisher does not need to know who listens, and if notifications is down for 10 minutes, the events wait in the queue. This loose coupling is the main reason async is preferred for anything that does not need an immediate answer. The cost: the flow is harder to follow, so you need good tracing, and consumers must handle duplicates and out-of-order events.

API gateway: Mobile apps should not know about 20 internal services. An API gateway is the single front door. It routes "/orders/..." to the order service and "/products/..." to the catalog service, and handles shared chores: authentication, rate limiting, TLS termination, request logging. A variant called backend-for-frontend gives the mobile app and the web app separate gateways, each shaping responses for its screen, for example combining product, price and stock into one response so the phone on a slow 4G link makes one call instead of three.

Service discovery: Services run as many copies that start, stop and move all the time, so their IP addresses change. Service discovery is a live phone book. When an instance starts, it registers itself ("orders, 10.0.3.17:8080, healthy") in a registry; callers look up the name and get a healthy address. In client-side discovery, the caller queries the registry and picks an instance itself. In server-side discovery, the caller talks to a load balancer that does the lookup. Container platforms such as Kubernetes give each service a stable DNS name that does this for you (deep-cse-6-3-07 covered naming).
