Transactions across services, sagas recap: Placing a food order may need: create order, charge payment, assign rider. With database per service, there is no single ACID transaction. Instead use a saga (deep-cse-6-3-21): a chain of local transactions, each with a compensating action. If assigning a rider fails, the saga runs the compensations: refund payment, cancel order. In orchestration, a central coordinator tells each service what to do next; in choreography, each service reacts to the previous service's event. Orchestration is easier to follow for long flows; choreography has no central point but can become a tangle of events.

Containers and orchestration, briefly: Microservices are usually packaged as containers: the code plus everything it needs, so it runs the same on a laptop and in production. An orchestrator such as Kubernetes places containers on machines, restarts crashed ones, scales copies up and down, and does rolling deployments (lesson 16). Service meshes add a small proxy beside each service to handle retries, TLS between services and metrics without changing code. Cloud Computing (deep-cse-7-3) covers these properly.

The costs, honestly: Every arrow between services is a network call that can be slow, fail or arrive twice. Debugging a slow request means tracing it across many services. Data is duplicated and eventually consistent, so users may briefly see an old address. You need mature automation: CI/CD for every service, centralized logs, tracing, dashboards. Testing changes that touch three services is hard, so teams use contract tests to check that each API still matches what callers expect. And the infrastructure bill rises, since each service runs several copies for redundancy.

Worked split, a food-delivery app: Imagine a Foodpanda-style app in Dhaka that started as a monolith. After two years it has 60 engineers and these pains: lunch-hour search traffic is 10 times the rest, payments must be audited carefully and changes slowly, and the restaurant menu team ships ten times a day. A sensible split: Catalog and search service (restaurants, menus; read-heavy, cached, scaled to many copies). Order service (cart and order state machine). Payment service (talks to card and wallet gateways; strict, slow-changing, its own audited database). Rider and dispatch service (rider locations, assignment). Notification service (SMS and push, fed by events). User service (profiles, addresses). The flow: the app calls the gateway; order service checks prices with catalog synchronously, asks payment to charge, then publishes OrderPlaced; dispatch, notification and the restaurant tablet all react to that event. If notification is down, orders still go through.

Real-life example 2, a university portal that should not split: A private university's student portal handles registration, results and fees for 12,000 students, built by a team of 4. Someone suggests microservices. The numbers say no: peak load is maybe a few hundred requests per second during registration week, which one well-tuned app with a database replica handles easily. Splitting would add gateways, discovery, tracing and 8 deployment pipelines for 4 people. A modular monolith with clear modules for registration, results and accounts is the better design, and it leaves the door open if the university grows into a multi-campus platform.

When not to use microservices: small team, early product, unclear domain, low traffic, no automation or monitoring culture yet, or when most features need strong consistency across many tables. Splitting just because big tech companies do it is cargo-culting: they adopted microservices to solve problems of hundreds of teams, which you may not have.

Common mistakes: Splitting by technical layer instead of business capability. Services sharing one database, which makes the split fake. Making services so tiny, one per function, that a single request crosses 15 hops. Long synchronous chains without timeouts, so one slow service freezes everything. Forgetting that events may be delivered twice. Splitting before having CI/CD, logging and tracing. Moving to microservices to fix messy code; a messy monolith usually becomes a messy distributed system.

What exams and interviews ask: Compare monolith and microservices with pros and cons. Explain database per service and its consequences. Compute the availability of a call chain. Compare sync and async communication and when to use each. Explain the role of an API gateway and service discovery. Describe a saga with compensation for a multi-service flow. In interviews, a strong answer often says "I would start with a modular monolith and split out search and payments first, because..." and names the trade-offs.

Recap: A monolith is simple and fast to build; microservices let many teams and differently loaded parts move and scale independently, at the cost of network calls, eventual consistency and operational complexity. Start with a monolith or a modular monolith, split by business capability, give each service its own data, prefer async events where no instant answer is needed, keep sync chains short and protected, front everything with an API gateway, find services through discovery, and coordinate multi-service work with sagas. Next, we start the case studies, beginning with a URL shortener.
key_points: A monolith is one deployable unit; microservices are small services, each owning one business capability and deployed separately.
Start with a monolith or modular monolith and split only when real pain appears.
Split by business capability (bounded context), not by technical layer, or you get a distributed monolith.
Each service owns its database: no shared tables, so no cross-service joins or single transactions.
Sync calls multiply failure: three 99.9 percent services in a chain give about 99.7 percent, ten give about 99.0 percent.
Prefer async events for work that needs no instant answer; consumers must handle duplicates.
An API gateway is the single front door; service discovery finds healthy instances; sagas coordinate multi-service flows.
Costs: network failures, harder debugging, eventual consistency, more automation and infrastructure.
lessons.tip: Before splitting anything, write down the specific pain the split fixes and the new failure it adds. If you cannot name the pain with a number, keep it in the monolith.
lessons.task: Pick an app you use, such as a food-delivery or ride app. On paper, list 5 to 7 business capabilities it has, draw each as a service box, and mark each arrow between them as sync (needs an answer now) or async (an event).

quiz.q: Which split creates a "distributed monolith"?
options: Catalog, orders, payments and delivery services
Frontend service, logic service and database service that every feature must change together
A separate notification service fed by events
quiz.explain: Splitting by technical layer means every feature touches all services and they deploy together, so you pay the network costs without independence.

quiz.q: Four services in a synchronous chain each have 99.9 percent availability. About what is the chain's availability?
quiz.explain: 0.999 to the power 4 is about 0.996, so the chain is about 99.6 percent available.

quiz.q: Why does each microservice usually own its own database?
options: Shared tables secretly couple services, so one change breaks another and independent deployment is lost
It makes joins across services faster
quiz.explain: Owning data keeps services independent; the price is no cross-service joins and some eventual consistency.

quiz.q: A team of 4 builds a portal for 12,000 students with a few hundred requests per second at peak. What is the best starting design?
options: A separate data center per module
A modular monolith with clear module boundaries
quiz.explain: The load and team size do not justify microservice overhead; a modular monolith keeps it simple and ready to split later.

quiz.q: After an order is placed, the app must send an SMS and add loyalty points. Which communication fits best?
options: The order service calls both synchronously and waits
Publish an OrderPlaced event; notification and loyalty services consume it
Both services read the orders table directly
The phone sends the SMS itself
quiz.explain: These tasks need no instant answer, so an event decouples them and the order still succeeds if one consumer is down.

lessons.title: Case Study: Designing a URL Shortener
lessons.content:
Have you ever seen a link like bit.ly/3xYz9Ab on a poster or in an SMS? You tap it and land on a page with a huge address like https://shop.example.com/campaign/eid-2026/offers?ref=sms&utm_source=gp. A URL shortener is a service that turns a long web address into a short one and, when someone visits the short one, sends them to the long one. It is the most famous warm-up question in system design interviews, because it is small enough to finish in 40 minutes but touches almost every building block: requirements, estimation, API, ID generation, database choice, caching and scaling. This lesson walks through it with the step framework from lesson 01.

Step 1, functional requirements: Ask before you draw. A good set: given a long URL, create a short URL. Visiting the short URL redirects to the long URL. Optionally, users may choose a custom alias such as /eidsale. Links may have an expiry date. The owner can see simple analytics, like how many clicks per day. Out of scope for now: user accounts with dashboards, link editing, QR codes.

Step 1, non-functional requirements: Redirects must be very fast, say under 50 ms at p99 from the server, because they sit in front of every visit. The service must be highly available: if it is down, every printed poster and SMS with a short link is broken. Short codes must not be guessable in sequence if links can be private. Once created, a mapping must never be lost or changed. The workload is read-heavy: a link is created once and clicked many times.

Step 2, estimation: Assume 100 million new short URLs per month and a read-to-write ratio of 100 to 1. Writes per second: 100 million divided by (30 x 86,400 seconds) is about 39 per second on average. Reads: 100 times that, about 3,900 redirects per second on average; with a peak factor of around 5, plan for roughly 20,000 per second. Storage: keep links for 10 years, which is 100 million x 12 x 10 = 12 billion records. If each record (code, long URL, creation time, expiry, owner) takes about 500 bytes, that is 12 billion x 500 bytes = 6 TB, before replication. Cache: daily reads are about 3,900 x 86,400, roughly 333 million. If we cache the hottest 20 percent of those requests at 500 bytes each, we need about 33 GB of memory, which fits in a few cache servers.

Step 3, API: Two endpoints are enough. POST /api/v1/urls with body {longUrl, customAlias (optional), expiresAt (optional)} returns {shortUrl: "https://sho.rt/2TX"}. GET /{code} returns a redirect to the long URL, or 404 if it does not exist or has expired. The POST should accept an idempotency key (lesson 06), so a retry on a flaky mobile network does not create two different codes. An API key per client lets us rate limit (lesson 14), which matters because shorteners are popular with spammers.

How long should the code be: The code uses base62: digits 0-9, lowercase a-z and uppercase A-Z, which are 62 characters that are safe in a URL. With 6 characters there are 62 to the power 6, about 56.8 billion codes. With 7 characters there are 62 to the power 7, about 3.52 trillion codes. We need 12 billion over 10 years, so 6 characters would already fit, but 7 gives huge room for growth and makes random guessing far harder. Each extra character multiplies the space by 62.

Approach A, hash and truncate: Compute a hash of the long URL, say MD5 or SHA-256, and take the first 7 base62 characters. Nice property: the same long URL always gives the same code. The problem is collisions: two different URLs may share the same first 7 characters. So on every insert you must check whether the code already exists; if it does and belongs to a different URL, append a salt such as a counter to the URL and hash again. As the table fills, collisions become more frequent, and each check is an extra database read. A Bloom filter, a compact in-memory structure that answers "definitely not present" or "maybe present", can make most checks cheap.

Approach B, unique ID plus base62, worked: Give every new link a unique integer ID, then convert the number to base62. Conversion is just repeated division, like converting to binary but with base 62. Take ID 11,157. Divide by 62 squared (3,844): 11,157 = 2 x 3,844 + 3,469. Then 3,469 = 55 x 62 + 59. So the digits are 2, 55, 59. Using the alphabet 0-9 for 0 to 9, a-z for 10 to 35 and A-Z for 36 to 61: 2 is "2", 55 is "T" (55 - 36 = 19, the 20th capital letter), 59 is "X". The short code is "2TX". Decoding reverses it: 2 x 3,844 + 55 x 62 + 59 = 11,157. No collisions are possible, because every ID is unique.

Where the unique IDs come from: A single auto-increment column in one database works at first but becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure. Options from lesson 12: a Snowflake-style 64-bit ID made of time, machine id and sequence, generated locally on each server; or a range allocator, where a small coordination service hands each app server a block of 1,000 IDs at a time, so the server can create 1,000 links with no network call. If a server crashes, a few unused IDs in its block are wasted, which is fine. One downside of plain counters: sequential codes are guessable, so someone can walk through 2TX, 2TY, 2TZ and discover private links. Fixes include shuffling the ID with a reversible scrambling function before encoding, or using random codes with a collision check.

Step 4, data model and database choice: The core table is tiny: code (primary key), long_url, created_at, expires_at, owner_id. The access pattern is a simple key lookup by code, there are no joins, and we need billions of rows spread across machines. A key-value or wide-column store, such as a DynamoDB- or Cassandra-style database, fits naturally and shards by code (lesson 10). A relational database sharded by code also works fine; the point is that the lookup is by primary key. Replicate each shard three times for durability. For custom aliases, the insert must be conditional: "insert only if this code does not exist", so two users cannot grab /eidsale at the same moment.

Step 5, the redirect: 301 or 302: HTTP 301 means "moved permanently"; browsers and some proxies remember it and next time skip our server completely. That saves us load and makes repeat visits faster, but we lose the ability to count those clicks, and we cannot change the target later. HTTP 302 (or 307) means "found, temporarily elsewhere"; the browser asks us every time, so every click reaches our server and can be counted, at the cost of more load. Services that sell analytics usually prefer 302; a service that just wants to save bandwidth may choose 301. Saying this trade-off out loud in an interview is a strong signal.

High-level design: A client calls the load balancer, which spreads requests across stateless web servers (lesson 07). For a create: the server validates the URL, gets the next ID from its local block, encodes it in base62, writes the row to the database and returns the short URL. For a redirect: the server looks up the code in the cache first; on a hit it returns the redirect at once; on a miss it reads the database, puts the result in the cache and redirects. Each click also sends a small event to a message queue (lesson 13) for analytics, so counting clicks never slows the redirect.

Caching hot links: Clicks follow a heavy-tailed pattern: a link in a viral Facebook post or an operator's SMS campaign gets millions of clicks in an hour, while most links are rarely clicked. Cache-aside with LRU eviction (lesson 08) handles this well: the hot codes stay in memory, cold ones fall out. Because a code-to-URL mapping never changes, cached entries never go stale, which is the easiest kind of caching there is. Only deleted or expired links need care: set the cache TTL no longer than the time until expiry, or delete the cache entry when the link is removed. A CDN or edge cache can even serve the redirect for the very hottest links.

Analytics: Each redirect publishes an event like {code, time, country, device, referrer} to the queue. Workers aggregate them into counts per code per hour and store those in a separate analytics database. With 20,000 clicks per second at peak, writing each click directly to the main database would compete with redirects, so the queue absorbs the spikes. For very hot links, workers keep counters in memory and flush every few seconds instead of one write per click.

Expiry and cleanup: Expired links should return 404 or a friendly "link expired" page. You do not need to delete them the moment they expire: check expires_at on each read, and let a background job sweep expired rows slowly at night. Some designs also recycle codes from deleted links; most do not, because an old printed poster could then point to someone else's page.

Abuse and safety: Shorteners hide where a link goes, so attackers use them for phishing and malware. Defences: rate limit link creation per API key and per IP, check new long URLs against a list of known bad sites, show a preview page for suspicious links, let users report abuse, and block http links to known scam domains. Without this, your domain gets blacklisted by browsers and email providers, and all your users' links stop working.

Bottlenecks and scaling: Web servers are stateless, so add more behind the load balancer. The database is sharded by code, so add shards as data grows (lesson 12, with consistent hashing from deep-cse-6-3-22). The cache absorbs most reads; if one viral code becomes a hot key, replicate that entry to several cache nodes or cache it in the web servers' own memory for a few seconds. The ID allocator is a small service, run three copies behind consensus or simply hand out large blocks. For global users, run read replicas and caches in several regions; writes can go to one home region since there are only about 39 per second on average.

Real-life example 1, a telecom SMS campaign: A mobile operator sends an Eid offer SMS to 20 million subscribers with one short link. Within 10 minutes, maybe 2 million people tap it, a burst of over 3,000 redirects per second for a single code. Because the mapping is cached in memory and even at the edge, the database barely notices. The click events pile into the queue, workers count them, and the marketing team sees a live chart of clicks by district.

Real-life example 2, links on a government notice: An education board prints a short link on a notice board for admission forms. Here, durability and predictability matter more than analytics: the link must work for years and must never be reused. The team uses a 301 redirect for speed, a custom alias like /admission2026, a non-expiring record, and three replicas across two data centers. A periodic checker visits the long URL and alerts if the target page breaks.

Common mistakes: Jumping to the database before estimating, then choosing something that cannot hold 12 billion rows. Using hash-and-truncate without collision handling. Using a single auto-increment database as the only ID source. Forgetting the 301 versus 302 trade-off. Writing a database row for every click. Making codes sequential and guessable for private links. Ignoring abuse, which is the real-world reason many free shorteners shut down.

What exams and interviews ask: Estimate QPS and storage for given numbers. How many codes does base62 with length 6 or 7 give? Convert an ID to base62. Compare hash-based and counter-based code generation. Explain 301 versus 302. Show where the cache goes and why it never goes stale here. How would you handle custom aliases, expiry and analytics without slowing redirects?

Recap: A URL shortener maps short codes to long URLs. Requirements show it is read-heavy and must be fast and always up. Estimation gives about 39 writes and 3,900 reads per second on average, 12 billion links and about 6 TB over 10 years. Seven base62 characters give about 3.5 trillion codes. Generate codes from unique IDs encoded in base62, or from hashes with collision checks. Store the mapping in a sharded key-value style database, cache hot codes, choose 301 or 302 deliberately, send click analytics through a queue, and guard against abuse. Next, a much busier real-time system: chat.
key_points: A URL shortener maps short codes to long URLs; it is read-heavy, latency-sensitive and must be highly available.
100 M new links a month at 100:1 reads gives about 39 writes and 3,900 reads per second on average, and about 6 TB over 10 years.
Base62 with 7 characters gives about 3.52 trillion codes; 6 characters give about 56.8 billion.
Counter or Snowflake-style IDs encoded in base62 never collide; hash-and-truncate needs collision checks.
Store mappings in a sharded key-value style store by code; use conditional inserts for custom aliases.
301 lets browsers skip you next time (less load, no counting); 302 brings every click back (analytics, more load).
Cache hot codes with LRU; mappings never change, so the cache never goes stale.
Send click analytics through a queue and protect the service with rate limits and malicious-URL checks.
lessons.tip: Practise the whole case on a timer: 5 minutes requirements, 5 estimation, 5 API and data model, 15 diagram and deep dives, 5 trade-offs. Saying the numbers out loud is half the answer.
lessons.task: By hand, convert the IDs 125 and 11,157 to base62 using the alphabet 0-9, a-z, A-Z, then decode your answers back to check them. Then compute how many 5-character base62 codes exist.

quiz.q: About how many different codes do 7 base62 characters give?
quiz.explain: 62 to the power 7 is about 3,521,614,606,208, roughly 3.52 trillion.

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of hash-and-truncate code generation?
options: Two different long URLs can produce the same short code, so collisions must be checked
quiz.explain: Taking only the first few characters of a hash can collide, so every insert must check and re-hash with a salt if needed.

quiz.q: A company sells click analytics for its short links. Which redirect status should it usually use?
options: 302 or 307, so every click reaches the server
quiz.explain: With a temporary redirect the browser asks every time, so every click can be counted; 301 lets browsers skip the server.

quiz.q: Why can cached short-code mappings be kept without worrying about stale data?
options: A code's target never changes once created, apart from deletion or expiry
quiz.explain: The mapping is immutable, so a cached copy stays correct; only deleted or expired links need a TTL or explicit removal.

quiz.q: Where should click counting happen so that it never slows down redirects?
options: In a synchronous database write before redirecting
Asynchronously: publish a click event to a queue and let workers aggregate
quiz.explain: A queue absorbs click spikes and keeps the redirect path short; workers aggregate counts in the background.

lessons.title: Case Study: Designing a Chat System
lessons.content:
When you send "Ami rasta-y, 5 min" to a friend on Messenger or WhatsApp, the message usually appears on their phone in well under a second, with one tick, then two ticks, then maybe blue ticks when they read it. If their phone is off, the message waits and arrives the moment they reconnect. Behind that tiny moment is one of the most interesting designs in this course: a chat system. Unlike the URL shortener, chat is real-time, two-way and stateful: the server must push messages to you without you asking, keep millions of connections open, remember who is online and never lose or reorder a conversation.

Step 1, functional requirements: one-to-one chat; group chat with a size limit (say up to 500 members); sent, delivered and read receipts; online and last-seen status; message history on any device; offline delivery when the user comes back; push notifications when the app is closed; text first, with images and files as a later deep dive. Out of scope for now: voice and video calls, which need very different media servers.

Step 1, non-functional requirements: low latency (a message should reach an online friend in about a few hundred milliseconds), high availability, durability (a sent message is never lost), messages shown in the correct order within each conversation, and scale to tens of millions of daily users. Privacy matters too: many apps use end-to-end encryption, which changes what the server can see.

Step 2, estimation: Assume 50 million daily active users, each sending 40 messages a day. That is 50 million x 40 = 2 billion messages per day, or about 23,000 messages per second on average, and several times that at peak, for example the minute after a big cricket match or at midnight on Eid. If an average text message with metadata is about 100 bytes, storage is 2 billion x 100 bytes = 200 GB per day, about 73 TB per year before replication, and roughly 220 TB with 3 copies. Connections: if 10 million users are online at once and one chat server can hold, as an assumption, 50,000 open connections, we need about 200 chat servers, plus spares.

Why plain HTTP is not enough: In normal HTTP the client asks and the server answers. But in chat, the server must speak first: "you have a new message". Lesson 05 compared the options. Short polling (ask every 2 seconds) wastes huge bandwidth and battery: 10 million users polling every 2 seconds is 5 million requests per second, nearly all answered "nothing new". Long polling holds each request open until there is news, which is better but awkward. WebSockets open one long-lived, two-way connection over TCP after an HTTP upgrade, and both sides can send messages any time. Chat systems use WebSockets (or similar persistent connections) for online users.

The building blocks: Chat servers hold the WebSocket connections and relay messages; they are stateful, because each one knows which users are connected to it. API servers handle ordinary stateless things: login, profile, contact list, creating groups, fetching old history. A session or presence store, a fast in-memory key-value store, records which chat server each online user is connected to. A message store keeps the history. A message queue or internal pub/sub carries messages between chat servers. A push notification service reaches users whose app is closed (lesson 21). A service discovery component tells a connecting client which chat server to use, usually a nearby, lightly loaded one.

Connecting: When Rafi opens the app, it logs in through the API servers, asks discovery for a chat server, gets, say, chat-17 in the Singapore region, and opens a WebSocket to it. Chat-17 writes into the session store: rafi -> chat-17. When Rafi's connection drops, the entry is removed or expires. The load balancer in front of chat servers must support long-lived connections and must not cut them every 60 seconds.

Message flow, step by step: Rafi (on chat-17) sends a message to Mitu. Step 1: Rafi's app sends {to: mitu, client_msg_id: "r-8812", text} over the WebSocket. The client_msg_id is generated on the phone so a retry does not create a duplicate (idempotency again). Step 2: chat-17 assigns a server message ID, saves the message in the message store, and acknowledges to Rafi, which shows one tick, meaning "the server has it". Step 3: chat-17 looks up Mitu in the session store and finds mitu -> chat-42. Step 4: it forwards the message to chat-42 through the internal queue or pub/sub. Step 5: chat-42 pushes it down Mitu's WebSocket. Mitu's app acknowledges, and a "delivered" receipt travels back the same way, so Rafi sees two ticks. Step 6: when Mitu opens the chat, her app sends a "read up to message X" receipt. Note the order: save first, then deliver, so a crash between steps never loses the message.

Offline users: If the session store says Mitu is not connected, the message is still saved in step 2, and the server sends a push notification through the phone platform's push service. When Mitu reconnects, her app asks: "give me all messages in my conversations after the last message ID I have". This sync-by-cursor design means the server does not need a separate "undelivered" pile per user; each device just remembers how far it has read in each conversation. It also makes multiple devices easy: a laptop and a phone each keep their own cursor.

Message IDs and ordering: Ordering by the sender's phone clock is unreliable, since phone clocks can be minutes wrong (deep-cse-6-3-08). What users need is a consistent order within each conversation, not a global order of all messages in the world. Common approach: the server assigns each message an ID that increases within the conversation, for example a per-conversation sequence number kept by the shard that owns that conversation, or a time-ordered Snowflake-style ID (lesson 12). All participants sort by that ID, so everybody sees the same order. Two messages sent at nearly the same moment by Rafi and Mitu will be ordered by whichever the server processed first, and both phones will agree.

Storing billions of messages: The access pattern is simple and huge: write a message to a conversation, and read the latest N messages of a conversation, scrolling backwards. Messages are almost never updated. Old messages are rarely read; recent ones constantly. This fits a wide-column store like Cassandra or HBase very well (lesson 10): partition key = conversation_id, clustering key = message_id in descending order. All messages of one chat sit together on one partition, sorted, so "latest 50 messages" is one fast sequential read. Write throughput scales by adding nodes, which matters at 23,000 writes per second. Very large or very old conversations can be split by time bucket, such as conversation_id plus month, so one partition never grows without limit.

Group chat and fan-out: In a group of 200 people, one message must reach 199 others. The chat server looks up the member list, then for each member finds their chat server in the session store and forwards, or sends a push if offline. So one message becomes 199 deliveries, which is why apps cap group size. Storage is done once per group: the message is written once to the group's conversation, and each member reads from there, rather than copying it into 199 inboxes. For very large broadcast-style groups or channels with thousands of members, systems switch to a pull model where clients fetch new posts, the same trade-off as fan-out on write versus read in the next lesson.

Presence, who is online: A naive design marks a user online when they connect and offline when they disconnect. But mobile connections drop silently: walking into a lift or a weak signal in a bus kills the connection without a goodbye. So clients send a heartbeat, say every 30 seconds. If no heartbeat arrives for, say, 60 seconds, the user is marked offline and last-seen is set. With 10 million online users and a 30-second heartbeat, that is about 333,000 small heartbeats per second, which is why presence lives in a fast in-memory store and is often handled by its own service. Broadcasting every status change to all contacts is expensive, so many apps only send presence to people who currently have that chat open, or fetch it lazily.

Media messages: Photos and videos never travel through the chat servers' message path. The phone uploads the file to object storage, often through a pre-signed URL, receives a file ID, and then sends a normal small chat message containing that ID and a thumbnail. The receiver downloads the file from the CDN (lesson 09). This keeps chat servers light and fast.

End-to-end encryption, briefly: With end-to-end encryption, messages are encrypted on the sender's phone with keys only the participants have, and decrypted only on the receiver's phone. The server stores and forwards ciphertext it cannot read. Phones publish public keys to a key server, and protocols like the Signal protocol create fresh keys for each message. Design consequences: the server cannot search message text, cannot show content in notifications by itself, and multi-device sync requires each device to have its own keys. Details belong to Computer Security (deep-cse-6-2).

Scaling and failures: Chat servers scale by adding more; discovery spreads new connections. If chat-42 crashes, its 50,000 users' apps notice the broken connection, reconnect to another server after a short random delay (jitter, so 50,000 phones do not all reconnect in the same second), and sync any messages they missed by cursor. Because messages were saved before delivery, nothing is lost. The message store is sharded by conversation and replicated. The session store is replicated too, and if it loses data, clients re-register on their next heartbeat.

Real-life example 1, Eid midnight: At midnight on Eid, millions of Bangladeshi users send "Eid Mubarak" to family groups within minutes. Messages per second jump many times above average. The design copes because messages go into a horizontally scaled store partitioned by conversation, group fan-out is limited by group size caps, chat servers were added in advance based on last year's peak, and push notifications are queued, so if the push provider slows down, messages still save and deliver to online users.

Real-life example 2, a customer support chat: A bank adds live chat in its app so customers can talk to support agents. The same design applies, with twists: an agent may handle 5 conversations at once, so a routing service assigns new chats to the least busy agent; the full history must be kept for audit, so messages are not end-to-end encrypted against the bank itself but are encrypted in transit and at rest; and when the customer is offline, a reply arrives as a push notification and an SMS fallback.

Common mistakes: Using HTTP polling for real-time delivery. Forgetting that chat servers are stateful and need a session map to route messages. Delivering before saving, so a crash loses messages. Ordering by phone timestamps. Storing a copy of every group message per member. Treating disconnect as the only offline signal, without heartbeats. Pushing large media through the chat path. Letting all clients reconnect at once after a server crash.

What exams and interviews ask: Why WebSockets over polling, with numbers. Walk through sending a message to an online and an offline user. How do you know which server a user is on? How are messages ordered? Which database fits message history and with what keys? How does group chat fan out, and why limit group size? How is presence detected? What changes with end-to-end encryption?

Recap: A chat system keeps persistent WebSocket connections on stateful chat servers, records which server each user is on in a fast session store, saves every message before delivering it, assigns per-conversation increasing IDs for order, and stores history in a wide-column store partitioned by conversation. Offline users get push notifications and sync by cursor on reconnect. Groups fan out to members, presence uses heartbeats, media goes through object storage and a CDN, and end-to-end encryption keeps the server blind to content. Next lesson, the news feed, where fan-out becomes the main problem.
key_points: Chat is real-time and two-way, so online users keep a persistent WebSocket connection to a stateful chat server.
50 M users x 40 messages a day is 2 billion messages, about 23,000 per second and 200 GB per day at 100 bytes each.
A fast session store maps each online user to their chat server so messages can be routed.
Save a message before delivering it; receipts (sent, delivered, read) travel back as small messages.
Order messages by server-assigned, per-conversation increasing IDs, never by phone clocks.
Store history in a wide-column store partitioned by conversation id and sorted by message id.
Offline users get a push notification and sync by cursor; groups fan out once per member, so group size is capped.
Presence uses heartbeats; media goes via object storage and CDN; end-to-end encryption keeps content unreadable to the server.
lessons.tip: Draw the send-message path as numbered arrows (1 to 6) and say for each arrow what happens if that hop fails. Interviewers love the answer "save first, then deliver".
lessons.task: Open a chat app with a friend. Turn your phone's data off, have your friend send you 3 messages, then turn it back on. Write down what ticks your friend saw at each stage and explain each one using the message flow from this lesson.

quiz.q: Why do chat systems use WebSockets instead of short polling for online users?
options: WebSockets are encrypted and polling is not
The server can push messages instantly on one open connection, instead of millions of mostly empty poll requests
quiz.explain: Short polling by 10 million users every 2 seconds means 5 million mostly useless requests per second; a WebSocket lets the server push when there is news.

quiz.q: How does chat-17 know where to forward a message for Mitu?
options: It looks up Mitu's chat server in the session/presence store
It broadcasts to every chat server
It asks Mitu's phone by SMS
quiz.explain: The session store maps each online user to the chat server holding their connection, so the message can be routed directly.

quiz.q: What is the safest order of steps when a chat server receives a message?
options: Deliver to the receiver, then save if they read it
Save only on the sender's phone
Save it in the message store, acknowledge the sender, then deliver
quiz.explain: Saving first means a crash after the ack never loses the message; the receiver can always sync it later.

quiz.q: Which storage layout fits chat history best?
options: One relational row per user holding all messages as text
A wide-column store with partition key conversation_id and messages sorted by message_id
A file per message on one disk
quiz.explain: All messages of a conversation sit together and sorted, so reading the latest 50 is one fast read, and writes scale by adding nodes.

quiz.q: Why do chat apps send heartbeats every 30 seconds or so?
options: Mobile connections can drop silently, so missing heartbeats reveal that a user went offline
quiz.explain: A lift or weak signal can kill a connection without a clean disconnect; heartbeats let the server detect it and set last-seen.

lessons.title: Case Study: Designing a News Feed
lessons.content:
Open Facebook, Instagram or LinkedIn and the first thing you see is a feed: a scrolling list of posts from friends, pages and people you follow, newest or most interesting first, ready in about a second. It feels simple, like reading a notice board. But think about it: you might follow 500 people, each posting at random times, and 300 million other users want their own personal notice board at the same moment. Building that board is the news feed problem, and its heart is one question: do we do the work when someone posts, or when someone reads?

Step 1, functional requirements: a user can publish a post (text, maybe images or video); a user sees a feed of posts from people and pages they follow; the feed is sorted, either by time or by a ranking; the user can scroll to load more; posts show like and comment counts. Out of scope for now: comments threading, ads, stories, search.

Step 1, non-functional requirements: the feed should load fast, say under 500 ms for the first screen; the system is extremely read-heavy, since people scroll far more than they post; a new post may take a few seconds to appear in friends' feeds, so eventual consistency is acceptable (deep-cse-6-3-16); and the system must stay up when a celebrity with millions of followers posts.

Step 2, estimation: Assume 300 million daily active users, each opening the feed 10 times a day: 3 billion feed reads per day, about 34,700 per second on average, several times more at peak. Assume each user posts 0.5 times a day: 150 million posts per day, about 1,740 per second. Assume an average of 200 friends or followers. If every post is copied into every follower's feed, that is 150 million x 200 = 30 billion feed insertions per day, about 347,000 per second. These three numbers drive the whole design.

Step 3, API: POST /v1/posts with {text, media_ids} creates a post. GET /v1/feed?limit=20&cursor=... returns the next 20 feed items plus a new cursor. As lesson 06 explained, use a cursor, such as the ID or score of the last item seen, not an offset: new posts keep arriving at the top, so "page 3" by offset would show duplicates or skip posts.

Step 4, the publishing path: When Nadia posts, the request goes through the load balancer to the post service. It checks auth and rate limits, stores the post in the post store (post_id, author_id, text, media ids, created_at), and returns success quickly. Media was uploaded earlier to object storage and is served through the CDN (lesson 09). Then the post service publishes a "PostCreated" event to a queue (lesson 13). Everything after this, building friends' feeds, sending notifications, indexing for search, happens asynchronously in workers.

The data: Besides the post store, we need the social graph: who follows whom. It is queried constantly with two questions, "who are Nadia's followers?" for publishing and "whom does Rafi follow?" for reading. It can live in a graph database or simply in a sharded key-value store with two lists per user, followers and following. The feed itself is a third piece: for each user, a list of post IDs that should appear in their feed.

Option A, fan-out on write (push): When Nadia posts, a fan-out worker gets her 200 followers from the graph and inserts the new post ID at the top of each follower's feed list, stored in a fast cache. When Rafi opens his feed, the list is already built: read 20 post IDs from his feed cache, fetch those posts (mostly from the post cache), and return. Reads are extremely fast, which is great because reads are 20 times more common than posts here. The cost is on write: 200 inserts for an ordinary user, 347,000 inserts per second overall, and a lot of wasted work for followers who never log in.

Option B, fan-out on read (pull): Do nothing extra when Nadia posts. When Rafi opens his feed, look up the 500 people he follows, fetch the recent posts of each, merge them by time or score, and return the top 20. Writes are cheap and nothing is wasted on inactive users. But every feed open now costs hundreds of lookups and a merge, at 34,700 feed opens per second, so reads get slow and expensive. Pull alone is fine for small systems but struggles at this scale.

The celebrity problem, worked: Fan-out on write breaks for a cricket star with 10 million followers. One post means 10 million feed insertions. If the fan-out workers can do 100,000 insertions per second in total, that single post keeps them busy for 10 million / 100,000 = 100 seconds, while ordinary users' posts wait in the queue behind it. If the star posts five times during a match, the backlog grows quickly. Meanwhile most of those 10 million followers are not even online.

The hybrid: Real systems mix both. For ordinary users, fan out on write, so their posts land in friends' feeds ready to read. For accounts above a threshold, say 100,000 followers, do not fan out; instead, at read time, the feed service fetches recent posts from the few celebrities that user follows and merges them into the pre-built list. Rafi's feed = his precomputed list (from normal friends) merged with the latest posts of the 8 celebrities he follows. Merging a handful of celebrity timelines is cheap, and the 100-second storm disappears. Some systems also skip fan-out to users who have been inactive for weeks and rebuild their feed by pull when they return.

Feed cache layout: For each active user, keep only a list of post IDs, with maybe a score or timestamp, not the full posts. If we keep 500 IDs of 8 bytes each per user, that is 4 KB per user; for 300 million users it would be about 1.2 TB, which a cluster of in-memory cache nodes can hold, and in practice only recently active users need a list at all. Keeping only IDs means a post edit or deletion changes one place, the post store, not millions of feeds. The full posts come from a separate post cache keyed by post_id, and user names and photos from a user cache. Assembling a feed page is called hydration: turn 20 IDs into 20 complete items.

Ranking, briefly: Most big platforms no longer sort purely by time. A ranking step scores candidate posts by signals like how close you are to the author, how much you interacted with similar posts, the post's age, and how many likes and comments it is getting. Typically a cheap stage picks a few hundred candidates, and a heavier machine learning model orders them. For system design, the key point is placement: candidates come from the fan-out list plus celebrity pulls, ranking happens in the feed service at read time or slightly ahead of time, and the model's details belong to Machine Learning (deep-cse-6-1) and Information Retrieval (deep-cse-7-9).

Likes and counters at scale: A popular post can get thousands of likes per second. Running UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1 on one database row for each like turns that row into a hot spot (lesson 11). Better: record each like event (user, post) in a likes store so each user can like only once, and keep the count separately with sharded counters, for example 10 sub-counters per hot post that are summed on read, or buffer increments in memory and flush every few seconds. Users accept that a count shows 12,403 when the true number is 12,410. This is the eventual consistency trade-off made on purpose.

Notifications and other consumers: The same PostCreated event feeds other workers: one sends "Nadia posted a photo" pushes to close friends, one updates the search index, one checks the content against community rules. Because each is a separate consumer of the queue, a slow search indexer cannot slow down feed building.

Putting it together, a feed read: Rafi opens the app. The feed service reads his top 200 post IDs from the feed cache, fetches recent posts of the celebrities he follows, merges them, removes posts from people he has since unfollowed or blocked, ranks the candidates, takes the top 20, hydrates them from the post and user caches, and returns them with a cursor. Images load separately from the CDN. If the feed cache is cold, for example after he returns from a long break, the service rebuilds it by pull and stores it for next time.

Real-life example 1, a cricket final: Bangladesh wins a close match at night. Within minutes, millions of users post and react, and star players post photos to millions of followers. The hybrid model means the stars' posts are pulled at read time instead of fanned out; ordinary posts fan out through a queue that grows for a few minutes and then drains; like counters on viral posts are sharded so no single row melts; and feed reads keep being served from the cache even if fan-out runs a minute behind. Users see slightly delayed posts, but nobody sees an error page.

Real-life example 2, a campus social app: A university club app has 15,000 students and maybe 50 posts an hour. Here the simplest design wins: fan-out on read with a single relational database, an index on (author_id, created_at), and a 30-second cache per user's feed. Each student follows maybe 100 clubs and friends, so a feed query merges a few hundred recent rows in milliseconds. The lesson: the hybrid push-pull machinery is a solution to a scale problem; do not build it until the numbers demand it.

Common mistakes: Choosing push or pull without doing the arithmetic. Forgetting the celebrity problem. Storing full post copies in every feed instead of IDs. Using offset pagination on a feed that changes every second. Updating a single like-count row for every like. Doing fan-out synchronously inside the post request, so posting takes seconds. Ignoring inactive users who make push wasteful. Forgetting to filter blocked or deleted content at read time.

What exams and interviews ask: Compare fan-out on write and fan-out on read with their costs, and compute insertions per second. Explain the celebrity problem with numbers and describe the hybrid fix. Describe what the feed cache stores and why only IDs. How do you paginate a feed? How would you count likes on a viral post? Where would ranking fit?

Recap: A news feed is an extremely read-heavy, eventually consistent system. Posts are stored once; a queue triggers fan-out work asynchronously. Push precomputes each follower's feed for fast reads but costs heavy writes; pull is cheap to write but slow to read. The hybrid pushes for ordinary users and pulls for celebrities, whose 10 million followers would otherwise jam the workers for 100 seconds per post. Feed caches hold post IDs, pages use cursors, posts are hydrated from caches, counters are sharded, and ranking orders the candidates. Next lesson, the notification system that tells people about all this.
key_points: A news feed is extremely read-heavy and can be eventually consistent: a post may appear a few seconds late.
300 M users x 10 feed opens is about 34,700 reads per second; 150 M posts x 200 followers is about 347,000 fan-out inserts per second.
Fan-out on write (push) precomputes feeds for fast reads but costs many writes; fan-out on read (pull) is cheap to write but slow to read.
A celebrity with 10 M followers would occupy 100,000-inserts-per-second workers for 100 seconds per post.
The hybrid pushes ordinary users' posts and pulls celebrity posts at read time, then merges.
Feed caches store only post IDs (about 4 KB for 500 IDs); posts are hydrated from post and user caches.
Use cursor pagination, asynchronous fan-out through a queue, and sharded counters for likes.
Ranking scores candidates from the fan-out list and celebrity pulls; its model details belong to ML courses.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a "one writes, many read" system, compute both the reads per second and the fan-out writes per second before choosing push or pull. The numbers usually pick for you.
lessons.task: Count how many accounts you follow on one social app and estimate how many of them post daily. Then compute how many feed insertions your follows cause per day under push, and how many lookups one feed open would need under pull.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of fan-out on write (push)?
options: Feeds are precomputed, so reading a feed is very fast
quiz.explain: Push does the work at post time, so a feed read is just reading a ready list; the cost moves to writes.

quiz.q: A star with 10 million followers posts, and fan-out workers manage 100,000 inserts per second. About how long does pure push take for that post?
quiz.explain: 10,000,000 / 100,000 = 100 seconds of worker time for one post, delaying everyone else's posts.

quiz.q: How does the hybrid approach handle celebrities?
options: Their posts are not fanned out; followers pull them at read time and merge them in
quiz.explain: Ordinary users are pushed; the few celebrities a user follows are pulled and merged at read time, which is cheap.

quiz.q: Why does the feed cache store post IDs instead of full posts?
options: It saves memory and an edit or delete changes only the post store, not millions of feeds
quiz.explain: IDs are small and the post content lives in one place, so updates are cheap; pages are hydrated from the post cache.

quiz.q: A viral post gets thousands of likes per second. What is a good way to count them?
options: UPDATE one likes row for every like
Recalculate likes by scanning all users
Store the count only on users' phones
Use sharded counters or buffered increments, accepting a slightly stale count
quiz.explain: A single row becomes a hot spot; sharded or buffered counters spread the writes, and a slightly stale count is acceptable.

lessons.title: Case Study: Designing a Notification System
lessons.content:
Think of the school bell and the class captain at the same time. When the principal wants every student to know that tomorrow is a holiday, she does not walk into each class herself. She hands one note to the office, the office copies it, the peons carry copies to every room, and a captain reads it aloud. If one class is empty because the students are at the playground, the peon comes back later. A notification system is that office for an app: one part of the system says "tell Rahim his parcel has shipped", and a dedicated service makes sure the message actually reaches Rahim, on the right channel, once, at a sensible time.

What it is: A notification system is a service that other services call to send messages to users through push notifications, SMS and email (and sometimes in-app inbox messages). The order service, the payment service and the marketing team all use it, so none of them has to know how SMS gateways or phone push services work. It is a perfect case study because it uses almost every building block from this course: APIs (lesson 06), queues and workers (lesson 13), rate limiting (lesson 14), retries and resilience (lesson 15) and monitoring (lesson 16).

The three channels: Push notifications are the small pop-ups on your phone. The app cannot send them straight to the phone; it must go through the phone platform's service: Apple Push Notification service (APNs) for iPhones and Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) for Android. Each installed app gets a device token, a long string that says "this app on this phone". Our server sends the message plus the token to APNs or FCM, and they deliver it. SMS goes through an SMS gateway or aggregator, a company connected to mobile operators like Grameenphone or Robi, and each SMS costs money. Email goes through an email provider over SMTP or an HTTP API (deep-cse-4-3 lesson 07 covers SMTP). Push is nearly free but not guaranteed to be seen; SMS reaches even basic phones without internet but costs money; email is cheap and good for long receipts but slow to be noticed.

Requirements, functional: Other services can send a notification to a user on one or more channels. Users can choose what they receive (for example, turn off promotional SMS but keep transaction alerts). Messages use templates with variables, such as "Your order {order_id} is on the way". The system supports both instant messages (an OTP, a payment alert) and scheduled or bulk campaigns (an Eid offer to two million users). We can see whether each message was sent, delivered, opened or failed.

Requirements, non-functional: Scale: say 10 million notifications a day normally, with campaign spikes many times higher. Latency: an OTP or payment alert should leave our system within a few seconds; a marketing message can wait minutes. Reliability: no important message lost, which means at-least-once delivery inside our system. No spamming: avoid sending the same message twice and avoid sending too many to one person. Respect quiet hours, for example no promotional push between 11 pm and 8 am.

Estimation: 10 million a day divided by 86,400 seconds is about 116 notifications per second on average. With a peak factor of 5 that is about 580 per second, and an Eid campaign that pushes 2 million messages in 10 minutes needs about 3,333 per second. Each notification record (ids, channel, status, timestamps, a short body) is maybe 500 bytes, so 10 million a day is about 5 GB of logs per day, roughly 1.8 TB a year before replication. These numbers say: one database row write per message is fine, but sending must be spread over many workers.

High-level design: Callers send a request to the notification service API, for example POST /notifications with user_id, type, template_id, variables and an idempotency key. The service validates the request, looks up the user's preferences and contact details (device tokens, phone number, email), renders the template, and drops one message per channel into a separate queue: a push queue, an SMS queue and an email queue. Workers for each channel pull from their queue, call the outside provider, and record the result in a notification log database. A scheduler service holds future and bulk jobs and releases them into the queues at the right time and speed.

Why separate queues per channel: Providers fail independently. If the SMS gateway is slow tonight, SMS messages pile up in the SMS queue, but push and email keep flowing. This is the bulkhead idea from deep-cse-6-3 lesson 25 applied to channels. It also lets us scale each worker pool on its own: SMS workers are limited by the gateway's allowed rate, push workers can run much faster. Many designs go further and give urgent traffic its own queue, so a 2-million-message campaign never sits in front of someone's OTP.

Priorities: Not every message is equal. A simple scheme has three levels: critical (OTP, security alerts, payment confirmations), normal (order updates), and low (marketing). Critical messages go to a high-priority queue with dedicated workers. Low-priority campaigns are released slowly by the scheduler. Here is the worked reason: if a campaign of 2 million messages is ahead of an OTP in one queue and workers send 3,000 per second, the OTP waits about 2,000,000 / 3,000 = 667 seconds, over 11 minutes, and the OTP expires. With a separate critical queue, it waits milliseconds.

Templates and preferences: A template store holds texts like "Dear {name}, your {amount} taka payment to {merchant} was successful", in both Bangla and English, with a version number. The service fills in variables at send time. The preference store records per user and per category which channels are allowed and the user's language and time zone. Legal and trust rules live here too: promotional messages need consent, and transactional ones (like a payment alert) are usually allowed always. Checking preferences before queuing saves money, because an SMS that the user blocked should never reach the gateway.

Deduplication: Because queues give at-least-once delivery (deep-cse-6-3 lesson 06), a worker may crash after sending but before acknowledging, so the message is redelivered. To avoid sending twice, every notification gets a unique id, and the caller passes an idempotency key (lesson 06). Before sending, the worker checks a fast store: "have I already sent notification n-8841?" It uses an atomic set-if-not-exists with an expiry of, say, 24 hours. If the key already exists, it skips. This cannot remove every duplicate (if the provider accepted the message but our reply was lost, we cannot know for sure), but it removes almost all of them, and for OTPs a rare duplicate is harmless.

Retries and fallbacks: Providers fail: a gateway times out, FCM returns a temporary error. The worker retries with exponential backoff and jitter (deep-cse-6-3 lesson 25), for example after 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds plus a little random time. Permanent errors are not retried: an invalid device token means the app was uninstalled, so we delete that token. After the maximum number of retries, the message goes to a dead-letter queue for inspection (lesson 13). For critical messages there is a fallback: if push fails or the user has no device token, send an SMS instead. Some systems even keep two SMS providers and switch when one has an outage.

Rate limits: Two kinds. First, outbound limits set by providers: a gateway might allow, say, 500 SMS per second on our account, so SMS workers use a token bucket (lesson 14) to stay under it. Second, per-user limits to protect people: for example, at most 3 marketing pushes per user per day, and at most 5 OTPs per phone number per hour to stop attackers from burning our SMS budget. The per-user counters live in a shared store with atomic increments.

Tracking: Each notification moves through states: created, queued, sent (provider accepted), delivered (the provider reported delivery), opened or clicked (the app or a tracking link reported it), or failed. Providers report delivery later through callbacks to our webhook, so the log row is updated after the send. These states feed dashboards: delivery rate per channel, latency from request to send, failure reasons. An alert fires if, say, SMS delivery rate drops from 97 percent to 60 percent, which usually means a gateway problem.

Cost worked: Suppose an SMS costs about 0.35 taka (an invented round figure for the example; real prices vary by provider and volume). An Eid campaign to 2 million users by SMS costs 2,000,000 x 0.35 = 700,000 taka. The same campaign as push costs almost nothing beyond servers. That is why many systems send push first and use SMS only for critical messages or users without the app. Even a small bug that sends every SMS twice doubles the bill, which makes deduplication a money feature, not just a nicety.

Bulk campaigns: For 2 million users, the marketing tool does not call the API 2 million times in a loop and hope. It creates a campaign job: a segment (users who bought in the last 90 days), a template, a start time and a send rate. The scheduler reads the user list in pages (cursor pagination, lesson 06), checks preferences and quiet hours, and feeds the low-priority queue at a steady rate, such as 3,000 per second. Pacing protects our servers, the providers and also the app's own backend: if 2 million people tap a push at the same second, the app servers get a stampede, so spreading sends over 10 to 20 minutes spreads the clicks too.

Real-life example 1, a bKash-style payment alert: You pay 500 taka at a shop. The payment service, after committing the transaction, writes an event, and the notification service receives "payment_success" for your user id with an idempotency key equal to the transaction id. It is critical priority, so it goes straight to the critical push queue. Push fails because your phone is offline, so after the retry window the fallback sends an SMS. If the payment service resent the event during a retry, the dedup check on the transaction id stops a second SMS. You get exactly the one alert you expect.

Real-life example 2, an Eid campaign for a Daraz-style shop: Marketing schedules "Eid sale starts at 8 pm" for 2 million users. The scheduler starts at 7:50 pm, skips users who turned off promotions, uses Bangla or English templates based on preference, and pushes about 3,333 messages per second so all 2 million go out in 10 minutes. Meanwhile, a customer's order OTP travels on the critical queue and arrives in under two seconds, completely unaffected by the campaign traffic.

Common mistakes: Sending directly from the order service to the SMS gateway inside the user's request, so a slow gateway makes checkout slow. Putting OTPs and marketing in one queue. Retrying forever, or retrying permanent errors like invalid numbers. Forgetting user preferences and quiet hours, which annoys users until they uninstall. Forgetting that providers have their own rate limits. Assuming push "delivered" means "seen". Not tracking costs, so a loop bug sends a million SMS overnight.

What exams and interviews ask: Draw the architecture with per-channel queues; explain how you prevent duplicates; how you handle a provider outage; how you prioritise OTPs over marketing; how you would send 2 million messages in 10 minutes and the per-second rate that requires; how users opt out. Good answers name the trade-off: at-least-once plus dedup instead of impossible exactly-once.

Recap: A notification system is a shared service that turns "tell this user" into delivered push, SMS or email. Separate queues per channel and per priority keep failures and campaigns from hurting urgent messages. Preferences, templates, dedup keys, retries with backoff, fallbacks and rate limits make it polite, cheap and reliable, and a status log with dashboards tells you it is actually working. Next, lesson 22 designs search autocomplete, where the challenge is not reliability but answering in under 100 milliseconds on every keystroke.
key_points: A notification system is a shared service that sends push, SMS and email so other services don't have to.
Push goes through APNs or FCM using device tokens; SMS goes through paid gateways; email through providers.
Separate queues per channel act as bulkheads, so one slow provider doesn't block the others.
Critical messages like OTPs need their own priority queue; a 2-million campaign ahead of an OTP means an 11-minute wait.
At-least-once queues need deduplication with notification ids or idempotency keys.
Retry temporary errors with backoff and jitter, drop bad tokens, fall back from push to SMS for critical alerts.
Rate limits protect providers, users and the SMS budget; campaigns are paced by a scheduler.
Track states (queued, sent, delivered, opened, failed) and alert when delivery rates drop.
lessons.tip: When you design any notification feature, ask two questions first: what happens if this is sent twice, and what happens if it is sent 11 minutes late?
lessons.task: Look at the last 10 notifications on your phone. Classify each as critical, normal or marketing, and note which channel it came by (push, SMS, email). Which ones would you put in the high-priority queue?

quiz.q: Why does the design give push, SMS and email separate queues?
options: To make every message cost the same
So a slow or failing provider on one channel does not block the other channels
Because queues can only hold one message type by law
quiz.explain: Per-channel queues are bulkheads: an SMS gateway outage piles up only SMS messages, while push and email keep flowing.

quiz.q: A campaign of 2,000,000 messages sits ahead of an OTP in the same queue, and workers send 3,000 per second. Roughly how long does the OTP wait?
quiz.explain: 2,000,000 / 3,000 = about 667 seconds. That is why OTPs get their own critical queue.

quiz.q: A worker crashes after sending an SMS but before acknowledging the queue message. What prevents a second SMS?
options: Checking a dedup store keyed by the notification id or idempotency key before sending
quiz.explain: Queues redeliver unacknowledged messages, so the worker checks whether that notification id was already sent.

quiz.q: FCM says a device token is invalid. What should the worker do?
options: Delete or mark the token as dead and not retry that push
Send the push to a random user
quiz.explain: An invalid token is a permanent error, usually an uninstalled app. Retrying wastes effort; remove the token.

quiz.q: At about 0.35 taka per SMS, what does an SMS campaign to 2 million users cost?
quiz.explain: 2,000,000 x 0.35 = 700,000 taka, which is why push is preferred for campaigns and duplicates cost real money.

lessons.title: Case Study: Search Autocomplete (Typeahead)
lessons.content:
Picture a very fast shopkeeper at a Gausia market stall. You start to say "I want a sh..." and before you finish, he holds up a shirt, a shawl and shoes, the three things people ask for most that start with "sh". He has not read your mind; he simply remembers what customers usually want. Search autocomplete, also called typeahead, is that shopkeeper inside a search box: after every letter you type, it shows the few most popular searches that start with what you have typed so far.

What it is and why it matters: Autocomplete saves typing, fixes spelling before it happens and guides users toward searches that actually return good results. On a shopping app or a search engine it is used on almost every keystroke, which makes it one of the highest-traffic features in the whole system. The interesting design problem is not storing data safely, as in the notification system of lesson 21; it is answering in a tiny time budget, again and again, from a huge list of possible queries.

Requirements: Functional: as the user types a prefix, return the top 5 suggestions that start with it, ranked by popularity. Suggestions should reflect real searches, update over time, and never show offensive or illegal text. Non-functional: very low latency, the usual target is that suggestions appear within about 100 milliseconds of a keystroke, or typing feels laggy. High availability, because a broken autocomplete makes the whole search box feel broken, but some staleness is fine: if today's suggestions are based on yesterday's counts, nobody is hurt. That last point is a gift: we can trade freshness for speed. We will assume only lowercase letters and spaces for the worked examples, and discuss Bangla later.

Estimation: Say 10 million daily active users, each doing 10 searches a day, and each search sends about 6 autocomplete requests while typing. That is 10,000,000 x 10 x 6 = 600 million requests a day, divided by 86,400 seconds gives about 6,944 requests per second on average, and perhaps 14,000 per second at peak with a factor of 2. A simple client trick cuts this a lot: debouncing, which means waiting until the user pauses typing for, say, 100 milliseconds before sending a request, so fast typists send fewer requests. The data side: if we keep the 10 million most popular queries of around 20 characters, the raw text is about 200 MB; with trie nodes and stored suggestion lists it grows several times, but it still fits comfortably in the memory of a single large server, and we replicate it for load.

Why not just use the database: The naive way is a SQL query like SELECT query FROM searches WHERE query LIKE 'sh%' ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 5. With an index on the query column, finding the rows starting with "sh" is fast, but there may be hundreds of thousands of them, and they must all be sorted by count for every keystroke. At 14,000 requests per second, that is a lot of disk and CPU work for answers that rarely change. We want a structure that has the answer prepared in advance.

The trie: A trie (from "retrieval", recap from data structures, deep-cse-2-2) is a tree where each edge is one character and each path from the root spells a prefix. The words "tea", "ten" and "to" share the node "t"; "tea" and "ten" also share "te". To find all queries starting with a prefix, you walk down one node per character, then everything below that node is a match. Walking the prefix costs only its length, p steps, no matter how many millions of queries are stored.

A trie worked example: Suppose our logs contain these queries with counts: to 70, tea 50, tech 45, ten 30, team 20, toy 15. For prefix "te", walk t then e. Below "te" we find tea 50, tech 45, ten 30 and team 20. The top 2 are tea and tech. For prefix "t", everything is below it, and the top 2 are to 70 and tea 50. For prefix "tea", below are tea 50 and team 20. Notice the problem: for a short prefix like "t" or "s", the subtree contains a huge share of all queries, so collecting and sorting them at request time is slow.

Storing top-k at each node: The key optimisation is to precompute the answer. At every node, store the list of the top k queries in its subtree, for example k = 5. In our example, node "t" stores [to 70, tea 50, tech 45, ten 30, team 20], node "te" stores [tea 50, tech 45, ten 30, team 20], node "to" stores [to 70, toy 15]. Now a request for prefix "te" is: walk 2 nodes and return the stored list. The time is just the prefix length plus reading 5 items. The cost is extra memory, since each popular query is copied into the list of every ancestor node, and extra work whenever counts change. It is the classic trade: spend memory and build time to make reads almost free.

Limiting prefix length: Real users rarely need suggestions after 50 characters, and very long prefixes have few matches anyway. Capping the trie depth at, say, 50 keeps memory bounded and stops a giant pasted text from creating a deep useless path.

Building the trie offline: Updating the trie on every search would mean 14,000 writes per second fighting with reads. Instead, separate the write path from the read path. Step 1, the search service writes each search to a log. Step 2, a batch job, for example weekly or daily, counts queries, a classic MapReduce job (deep-cse-6-3 lesson 24): map emits (query, 1), reduce sums per query. Step 3, a builder program creates a fresh trie with top-k lists from these counts. Step 4, the new trie is saved as a snapshot and loaded by the serving machines, which then switch from the old trie to the new one in one step. Reads never wait for writes.

Sampling and trending: Logging every single keystroke-level request is wasteful. Counting only completed searches, and even only 1 in 10 of them, still keeps the ranking accurate for popular queries, because popular ones appear thousands of times. For news-like trends ("cyclone warning" during a storm), a weekly rebuild is too slow, so systems add a fast path: a streaming job counts the last hour, and recent counts get extra weight. A common approach is time decay: an older search counts less, for example its weight halves every few days, so last week's spike fades instead of sitting at the top forever.

Serving path: The browser sends GET /suggest?q=te. A load balancer (lesson 07) picks one of many suggestion servers, each holding the trie in memory. The server walks the trie and returns the list as small JSON. Because results for a prefix change only when the trie is rebuilt, they are very cacheable: the response can carry Cache-Control: max-age=3600, so the browser reuses the answer if you type "te" again, and a CDN or reverse proxy (lessons 08 and 09) can cache popular prefixes too. Many requests never reach our servers at all.

Sharding by prefix: If the trie grows too big for one machine, split it by prefix: queries starting with a to m on shard 1, n to z on shard 2. But letters are not equal; far more words start with "s" or "c" than with "x" or "q", so equal letter ranges give unequal shards, a hot spot (deep-cse-6-3 lesson 22). The fix is to split by measured load, for example "s" alone gets two shards ("sa" to "sm" and "sn" to "sz"), while "u" to "z" share one. A small shard map tells the gateway where each prefix lives.

Filtering: A blocklist filter sits between the trie and the response, removing hateful, adult or dangerous suggestions and personal data like phone numbers. Removing an entry from the next trie build is the lasting fix; the filter handles it instantly until then. Personalisation (your own recent searches first) is usually stored separately per user and merged with the global list at request time.

Bangla and multiple languages: In Bangladesh people search in Bangla script, in English, and in Banglish typed with English letters, like "bkash offer" or "borsha". A trie works on any characters, including Unicode Bangla letters, but there are details: one Bangla letter as you see it can be several Unicode code points, keyboards differ, and the same word has many Banglish spellings. Practical systems keep separate tries per script, normalise text (lowercase, trim spaces, normalise Unicode forms), and can map common Banglish spellings to one canonical query. Deeper search ranking and language handling belong to Information Retrieval (deep-cse-7-9).

Failures and safety nets: Every suggestion server holds a full copy of the trie (or of its shard), so if one dies, the load balancer's health checks simply stop sending it traffic and the others carry on. If the nightly build job fails or produces a broken trie, the servers keep serving yesterday's snapshot; a quick sanity check, such as "the new trie must have at least 90 percent as many queries as the old one", stops a bad build from going live. And if the whole suggestion service is down, the search box still works, it just shows no suggestions. That is graceful degradation from lesson 15: the feature fails softly instead of taking search with it.

Real-life example 1, a Daraz-style shopping search: A user types "ph". The phone app waits 100 ms after the last keystroke, sends the request, and gets [phone cover, phone, phone holder, photo frame, philips trimmer] from the nearest edge cache in under 50 ms. Sales during an Eid sale shift popularity, so the shop rebuilds the trie daily, with an hourly trending boost so "eid panjabi" rises the same evening it becomes popular.

Real-life example 2, a city directory app: A Dhaka restaurant directory has only 30,000 names. Here the whole thing is small: one trie with top-5 lists fits in a few MB, so it can even be shipped inside the app and searched offline on the phone, with a weekly update download. This shows good design is about scale: the same idea, a trie with top-k, runs on a phone or on a cluster.

Common mistakes: Querying the database with LIKE on every keystroke. Rebuilding or updating the trie live on the read path. Forgetting the top-k cache at each node, so short prefixes are slow. Sharding by first letter without looking at real load. No debouncing or caching, so traffic is many times larger than needed. Forgetting the filter. Assuming suggestions must be perfectly fresh, when slight staleness is acceptable and is exactly what makes the design simple.

What exams and interviews ask: Draw a trie for given words and counts and show the top-k at each node; explain why lookup cost depends on prefix length, not on the number of stored queries; separate the data-gathering path from the query path; explain how to handle trending searches; how to shard unevenly distributed prefixes; estimate requests per second with and without debouncing.

Recap: Autocomplete returns the top suggestions for a prefix within about 100 ms. A trie gives O(prefix length) lookup, and storing the top k queries at every node turns each request into a short walk and a ready list. Counts come from search logs through offline (and some streaming) aggregation, the trie is rebuilt and swapped in, results are cached in browsers and edges, and shards follow real load, not the alphabet. Next, lesson 23 moves from tiny text responses to the heaviest traffic of all: video streaming.
key_points: Autocomplete returns the top few popular queries starting with the typed prefix, within about 100 ms.
Slight staleness is acceptable, which lets us trade freshness for speed.
A trie finds a prefix in steps equal to its length, regardless of how many queries are stored.
Storing the top-k list at every node turns a request into a short walk plus reading a ready answer.
Counts come from search logs via batch (and streaming for trends); the trie is rebuilt offline and swapped in.
Debouncing on the client and caching in browsers and CDNs cut request volume sharply.
Shard by measured prefix load, not equal alphabet ranges, because letters are uneven.
Filter offensive suggestions and normalise Bangla, English and Banglish text.
lessons.tip: For read-heavy features that can be a little stale, always ask: can I precompute the answer offline and just look it up at request time?
lessons.task: Write 8 searches you might type with made-up counts. Draw the trie on paper and write the top-3 list at each node. Then count how many nodes you walk for the prefix of length 2.

quiz.q: With the counts to 70, tea 50, tech 45, ten 30, team 20, toy 15, what are the top 2 suggestions for prefix "te"?
quiz.explain: Below node "te" are tea 50, tech 45, ten 30 and team 20, so the top 2 are tea and tech.

quiz.q: Why store a top-k list at every trie node?
options: So short prefixes do not need to scan and sort a huge subtree at request time
Because tries cannot hold more than k words
To make writes faster during the day
quiz.explain: Precomputing the answer at each node makes reads a short walk; the cost is extra memory and rebuild work.
