quiz.q: 10 M users x 10 searches x 6 requests per search is about how many requests per second on average?
Why is splitting the trie into equal alphabet ranges (a-m, n-z) a problem?
options: Letters are uneven, so some shards (like ones holding s or c) get far more load
quiz.explain: Uneven first-letter popularity makes hot shards; split by measured load instead.

quiz.q: What does debouncing in the client do?
options: Rebuilds the trie in the phone
Waits for a short typing pause before sending a request, reducing request count
Sends each keystroke twice for safety
quiz.explain: Waiting about 100 ms after the last key means fast typists send fewer requests.

lessons.title: Case Study: Designing a Video Streaming Platform
lessons.content:
Think of how a big cooking show reaches a whole country. The chef cooks once in the studio, but the recording is not sent as one giant file to every home. It is cut into pieces, copied into a few sizes for big screens and small phones, and stored in TV stations all over the country, so every viewer gets it from somewhere nearby. A video streaming platform, a YouTube-style or Bioscope-style service, works the same way: one upload, many processed versions, many copies close to viewers, and a player that keeps choosing the size your connection can handle.

What makes video special: Video is the heaviest thing most systems ever serve. A 10-minute HD video is hundreds of megabytes, and popular platforms stream to millions of people at once. So the design is dominated by three things: processing (turning one raw upload into many playable versions), storage (keeping all those versions safely), and above all bandwidth (pushing bits to viewers without buffering). Most of the money goes to bandwidth, which is why CDNs (lesson 09) are at the heart of this design.

Requirements: Functional: users can upload videos, watch them on phones, laptops and TVs, and see titles, thumbnails, view counts and comments. Playback must start fast and adapt to the network, from 4G in Dhaka to a weak village connection. Non-functional: smooth playback with little buffering, high availability for watching, durable storage (an uploaded video must not be lost), and reasonable cost. Uploads can take minutes to process, and that is acceptable; users expect a short "processing" message, but they do not accept a frozen video while watching. That tells us where to spend effort.

Estimation, storage: Assume 10,000 uploads a day, each 10 minutes long. We store five renditions (versions) at these bitrates: 1080p at 5 Mbps, 720p at 2.5 Mbps, 480p at 1 Mbps, 360p at 0.6 Mbps and 240p at 0.3 Mbps, together 9.4 Mbps. A 10-minute video is 600 seconds, so all renditions take 9.4 x 600 / 8 = 705 MB. Per day: 10,000 x 705 MB = 7.05 TB. With 3 replicas for durability that is about 21 TB a day, and over a year about 7.7 PB. Plus the original uploads, if we keep them. Storage is big but predictable.

Estimation, bandwidth: Now viewing. If 1 million people watch at the same moment, each at an average of 2.5 Mbps, the outgoing traffic is 1,000,000 x 2.5 Mbps = 2.5 Tbps. No single data center link serves that comfortably, and paying long-distance transit for every byte would be ruinous. The only sane answer is to serve most bytes from CDN edge servers near viewers, often inside or next to local internet providers.

High-level design: There are two separate paths. The upload path: client, upload service, object storage for the raw file, a transcoding pipeline, object storage for the processed renditions, and the CDN. The watch path: client asks the API for video metadata and a manifest, then fetches video segments from the CDN, which fetches from object storage only on a miss. A metadata database stores titles, owners, durations, status and rendition locations. Separating the two paths means a flood of uploads never slows down watching.

Uploading big files: A 600 MB upload through our API servers would tie them up for minutes. Instead the client asks the upload service for permission, and the service returns a pre-signed URL: a temporary link that lets this client upload one object directly into object storage, valid for, say, 15 minutes. The API servers stay light. Large files go in parts, a multipart or resumable upload: 600 MB in 10 MB parts is 60 parts, and if the bus Wi-Fi drops at part 41, the app resumes from part 41 instead of starting over. When the last part arrives, storage notifies the system, which creates a "processing" job.

Transcoding, what and why: The raw file can be in any format, size and quality from any phone or camera. Transcoding converts it into standard formats: several resolutions and bitrates, a widely supported codec, and short segments for streaming. A codec is the compression method; H.264 plays almost everywhere, while newer codecs such as H.265, VP9 and AV1 give similar quality at a lower bitrate but cost more computing power to encode and are not supported on every old device. Platforms often encode popular videos in a newer codec too, because the bandwidth saved on millions of views pays for the extra encoding.

The transcoding pipeline as a DAG: The work is a directed acyclic graph of tasks, where arrows mean "must finish before". First inspect the file and validate it. Then split the video into chunks, for example 10-second pieces. Then, in parallel, encode every chunk into every rendition, separately extract and encode the audio, generate thumbnails, and optionally run checks like copyright or content moderation. Finally merge and package everything into segments and manifests and mark the video ready. Worked parallelism: a 600-second video in 10-second chunks is 60 chunks, and with 5 renditions that is 300 independent encoding tasks. Spread over 300 workers, a job that would take an hour on one machine finishes in a few minutes. A queue (lesson 13) feeds tasks to workers, and a failed task is simply retried.

Adaptive bitrate streaming: The player does not download one big file. Each rendition is cut into small segments, say 4 seconds each, so a 10-minute video has 600 / 4 = 150 segments per rendition. A manifest file lists the renditions and their segment URLs; HLS and MPEG-DASH are the two common formats (deep-cse-4-3 lesson 09 introduced DASH). The player measures how fast recent segments arrived and how many seconds are buffered, then picks the bitrate of the next segment. Example: you are watching 720p at 2.5 Mbps on a bus, the network drops to 1.5 Mbps, the buffer starts shrinking, so the player switches to 480p at 1 Mbps for the next segments. The picture gets a bit softer, but it never freezes. When the network recovers, it climbs back up.

Why small segments help: Small segments let the player switch quality every few seconds, let playback start after the first segment instead of the whole file, make seeking to minute 7 cheap (fetch segment 105 onwards), and are perfect cache objects: each is a plain file with a stable URL, ideal for a CDN. The trade-off: smaller segments mean more requests and more overhead; very large ones adapt slowly. A few seconds is the usual compromise.

The CDN and the long tail: Popularity is extremely uneven. A small number of videos get most of the views, and a very long tail of videos is watched rarely. Popular videos live in edge caches near viewers and are often pushed there before a big release. Tail videos are pulled on demand from object storage when someone asks, and may not be cached at the edge for long. This keeps edge storage for what matters. A trailer for a new Eid movie might be pre-loaded to edges in Dhaka, Chattogram and Sylhet, while a ten-year-old school concert video is fetched from origin the rare time someone watches it.

Metadata and view counts: Video metadata is ordinary structured data and fits a relational database, sharded by video id when it grows (lesson 12), with a cache in front for popular videos. View counts are a hot-key problem: a viral video may get thousands of views per second, and updating one database row that often would melt it. Instead, views are sent as events to a queue, aggregated in memory or by a stream processor every few seconds, and added to the stored count in batches. The displayed count may lag slightly, and that is fine.

Protecting content and cost thinking: Paid content is often encrypted and played with DRM, and links to segments can be signed so they expire. On cost: bandwidth is the largest bill, so platforms use better codecs for popular videos, cap the default quality on mobile data, and peer with local internet providers. Storage of tail videos can move to cheaper, slower storage classes. Transcoding compute can use spare cheaper machines, since uploads are not urgent.

Video states and failures: Each video moves through simple states in the metadata database: uploading, uploaded, processing, ready, or failed. The transcoding workers update the state as tasks finish, so the app can show "processing" honestly. If a worker dies halfway through a chunk, the queue redelivers the task to another worker; because encoding the same chunk twice produces the same output file at the same path, a retry is harmless, which is idempotency again (lesson 13). If the original file is corrupt, the job ends in failed and the uploader is notified through the notification system of lesson 21. Watching keeps working throughout, because the watch path never touches the pipeline.

Live streaming in brief: Live video, like a cricket match, follows the same ideas with tighter timing. The broadcaster sends one high-quality stream to an ingest server, which transcodes it into renditions in real time, cuts it into segments of a few seconds, and keeps updating the manifest as new segments appear. Viewers lag a few seconds behind the real moment; shorter segments reduce that delay but increase requests. Because everyone watches the same latest segments at the same time, CDN caching works extremely well for live events.

Real-life example 1, a Bangladeshi OTT service on Eid: A streaming service releases a new drama at 9 pm on Eid. Days before, the drama is transcoded into all renditions and pushed to CDN edges inside the country. At 9 pm, hundreds of thousands press play. Their players fetch the manifest from the API, then segments from nearby edges; viewers on weak connections automatically get 360p, those on home broadband get 1080p. The origin barely notices the rush, because the edges absorb it.

Real-life example 2, a teacher uploading a lecture: A teacher in Rajshahi uploads a 40-minute class from her phone. The app gets a pre-signed URL and uploads in parts; a network drop only costs one part. The video shows "processing" while the DAG splits it into chunks, encodes renditions in parallel and creates thumbnails. In a few minutes it is ready, and students on 2G-like speeds still watch at 240p instead of seeing an error.

Common mistakes: Sending uploads through application servers. Serving video from the origin with no CDN. Storing one big file per video with no segments or renditions, so weak connections buffer forever. Transcoding a whole long video on one machine serially. Updating the view count row on every view. Forgetting the cost of bandwidth in the estimate. Treating upload processing as if it must be instant, when the real latency requirement is on playback.

What exams and interviews ask: Estimate storage for N uploads with given bitrates and replicas; estimate peak bandwidth; draw upload and watch paths separately; explain transcoding as a DAG and why chunking speeds it up; explain adaptive bitrate streaming with a manifest and segments; explain how a CDN handles popular versus long-tail videos; how to count views at scale.

Recap: A video platform has a slow, heavy upload path and a fast, enormous watch path. Uploads go straight to object storage with pre-signed, resumable uploads, then a parallel transcoding DAG produces several renditions cut into few-second segments. Players use a manifest to switch bitrate segment by segment, so video adapts instead of freezing, and CDNs serve the popular bytes from near viewers. Storage is measured in petabytes and bandwidth in terabits per second, which is why estimates guide every choice. Next, lesson 24 designs ride-hailing, where the hard part is finding nearby moving things fast.
key_points: Video design is dominated by processing, storage and above all bandwidth.
Separate the upload path from the watch path so uploads never slow viewing.
Clients upload directly to object storage with pre-signed, resumable multipart uploads.
Transcoding is a DAG: split into chunks, encode chunks and renditions in parallel, then package.
Five renditions totalling 9.4 Mbps make a 10-minute video about 705 MB; 10,000 a day with 3 replicas is about 21 TB a day.
Adaptive bitrate streaming uses a manifest and few-second segments so the player switches quality instead of freezing.
CDNs serve popular videos from edges; long-tail videos are pulled from origin on demand.
View counts are aggregated from events in batches, not written per view.
lessons.tip: In any media design, compute bytes per second at peak first; that one number tells you whether you need a CDN, how many renditions you can afford and what the bill will look like.
lessons.task: Open any video app, start a video and switch between Wi-Fi and mobile data or turn on data saver. Watch whether the quality changes after a few seconds instead of stopping. Write down which resolution you saw before and after.

quiz.q: Why do clients upload videos with a pre-signed URL straight to object storage?
options: It keeps big uploads off the API servers, which stay light and fast
It removes the need for transcoding
quiz.explain: A pre-signed URL lets the client upload one object directly to storage for a limited time, so app servers are not tied up.

quiz.q: Renditions totalling 9.4 Mbps for a 600-second video take about how much space?
quiz.explain: 9.4 x 600 / 8 = 705 MB. 5,640 is megabits, not megabytes.

quiz.q: A 600-second video is split into 10-second chunks and encoded into 5 renditions. How many independent encoding tasks are there?
quiz.explain: 600 / 10 = 60 chunks, times 5 renditions = 300 tasks that can run in parallel.

quiz.q: Your network drops while watching 720p. What does adaptive bitrate streaming do?
options: Asks the user to reload the page
Picks a lower-bitrate rendition for the next segments so playback continues
quiz.explain: The player measures throughput and buffer, then fetches the next segments at a lower quality.

quiz.q: Why should view counts not be updated in the database on every single view?
options: A viral video becomes a hot row with thousands of writes per second; batching events avoids it
The CDN does not allow it
quiz.explain: Send view events to a queue, aggregate them, and add totals in batches; a slightly delayed count is fine.

lessons.title: Case Study: Ride-Hailing and Proximity Service
lessons.content:
Imagine you are standing on Mirpur Road waving for a CNG. You can only see the few drivers on your corner. A ride-hailing app is like standing on a tall tower above the whole city: it sees every free driver, picks the ones closest to you, asks one of them, and tells both of you where to meet. The tricky part is not storing trips; it is that every driver is a moving dot, the dots move every few seconds, and the question "who is near me?" must be answered for thousands of riders at once in a fraction of a second.

What this case study is about: A Pathao-style or Uber-style app has two kinds of users: riders, who request trips, and drivers, who share their location and accept trips. The core of the design is a proximity service, the part that answers "which available drivers are within 2 km of this point?", plus a matching flow that assigns exactly one driver to each trip. The same proximity ideas power food delivery, "restaurants near me" and finding the nearest ATM.

Requirements: Functional: drivers send their location regularly while online; a rider sees nearby cars on the map, requests a ride with pickup and drop-off; the system finds and offers the trip to suitable nearby drivers; one driver accepts; both see each other's live location; the trip is tracked to completion and payment. Non-functional: matching should feel quick, a few seconds; the location map can be a few seconds stale; a driver must never be assigned to two trips at once, and a trip must never get two drivers; the system must keep working in rush hour. Notice the mix: locations can be slightly stale (availability and speed first), but assignment must be strictly correct (consistency first). That split shapes everything.

Estimation: Say 500,000 drivers are online at peak and each phone sends its location every 4 seconds. That is 500,000 / 4 = 125,000 location writes per second. Each update is small, about 100 bytes (driver id, latitude, longitude, time, status), so the incoming data is about 12.5 MB per second, but the count of writes is what hurts. If we kept every update for history, that is about 1.08 TB a day. Riders asking "who is near me" might add tens of thousands of reads per second. Conclusion: a disk-based database updating an index 125,000 times a second is the wrong home for live locations.

Why a plain SQL range scan struggles: The obvious query is SELECT driver_id FROM drivers WHERE lat BETWEEN a AND b AND lng BETWEEN c AND d. An index on lat narrows rows to a thin horizontal strip of the whole country; an index on lng gives a vertical strip; the database must intersect two big sets to get the small box where they cross. A normal B-tree index (lesson 11) is one-dimensional, so it cannot find "close in two dimensions" directly. On top of that, every location update rewrites index entries 125,000 times a second. We need a way to turn two-dimensional closeness into something a one-dimensional key can handle.

Geohash, the idea: Geohash divides the world into a grid and gives each cell a short string. Start with the whole map. Split longitude in half: east half gets bit 1, west half bit 0. Then split latitude: north 1, south 0. Keep alternating, adding bits, and every 5 bits become one character from a 32-symbol alphabet (digits and letters, skipping a, i, l and o). Each extra character makes the cell 32 times smaller. The magic property: places that share a longer prefix are in the same smaller cell, so they are near each other. "Near" becomes "same prefix", and prefixes work with ordinary indexes and hash maps.

Geohash worked: Computing with the standard algorithm, a point in Dhanmondi (about 23.7465 N, 90.3760 E) gets the 7-character geohash wh0r0dc, Gulshan (about 23.7925 N, 90.4078 E) gets wh0r372, and Motijheel (about 23.7330 N, 90.4172 E) gets wh0r12r. All three share "wh0r", the 4-character cell covering most of Dhaka. Cell sizes at the equator are roughly: 4 characters, 39 km by 19.5 km; 5 characters, 4.9 km by 4.9 km; 6 characters, 1.2 km by 0.6 km; 7 characters, 153 m by 153 m. Cells get a little narrower east-west as you go away from the equator. To find drivers within about 1 km in a city, precision 6 is a good fit.

The boundary problem and neighbours: Two drivers 50 metres apart can sit on opposite sides of a cell border and have different prefixes. So we never search only the rider's own cell. We search the rider's cell plus its 8 neighbours, a 3 by 3 block, which is easy to compute from the geohash. Then we compute the real distance for each candidate and drop those too far away. If too few drivers are found, widen the search by using a shorter prefix (a bigger cell), for example from 6 to 5 characters.

Quadtree, the alternative: A quadtree starts with one square covering the city and splits any square into four children when it holds too many points, say more than 100 drivers. Dense areas like Motijheel at noon end up with many small squares; empty fields stay as one big square. Searching means walking down the tree to the rider's square and checking nearby squares. Its strength is that cells adapt to density; its weakness is that the tree must be rebuilt or rebalanced as drivers move, and it lives in memory on a server. Geohash is simpler to shard and store in a key-value store; quadtrees give more even cell sizes. Both are valid interview answers if you explain the trade-off.

The in-memory location store: Live locations go to a fast in-memory store, not the main database. A simple layout: a key per geohash-6 cell holding the set of available driver ids in that cell, plus a key per driver holding its latest position and status with a short expiry, say 30 seconds, so a driver whose phone died disappears automatically. On each update, if the driver changed cell, remove it from the old cell's set and add it to the new one. Stores like Redis even provide built-in geo commands that use geohash-like encoding internally. Location history, if needed for trip records or analytics, is written asynchronously through a queue to cheaper storage, never on the hot path.

Matching flow step by step: Step 1, the rider requests a trip; the trip service creates a trip record with status requested and an idempotency key so a double tap does not create two trips. Step 2, the matching service reads the 3 by 3 cells around the pickup point and gets, say, 12 available drivers. Step 3, it ranks them by estimated arrival time on real roads, not straight-line distance, because a driver across a canal or on a one-way road may be close in metres but far in minutes. Step 4, it offers the trip to the best driver, with a timeout of around 15 seconds. Step 5, if the driver declines or the timer expires, offer the next. Step 6, when a driver accepts, assign atomically.

Making assignment safe: Two dangers: two riders' requests may pick the same driver at the same moment, and a driver may tap accept on a trip that another driver already took. The fix is an atomic compare-and-set on the driver's status: "set status to reserved only if it is currently available", and on the trip: "set driver only if driver is empty". Only one of two racing operations can succeed; the loser simply moves on to the next candidate. This is a tiny piece of strong consistency inside a mostly eventually consistent system, and it can be done in one partition because a trip and its candidate drivers belong to one city shard.

The trip state machine: A trip moves through clear states: requested, driver_assigned, driver_arriving, in_progress, completed, or cancelled. Only certain moves are allowed; for example, you cannot jump from requested to completed. Storing the trip as a state machine in a durable database, with each change as an event, makes it easy to recover after crashes, show the right screen in both apps, start billing at in_progress, and send notifications (lesson 21) at each step. Payment after completion uses the idempotent payment patterns from lesson 06 and sagas from deep-cse-6-3 lesson 21.

Surge pricing and ETA in brief: Surge pricing compares demand and supply per area: if a geohash-5 area has 300 open requests and only 60 free drivers, prices rise to attract drivers and calm demand. The ratio is recomputed every minute or so from the same location data. ETA and routing use a road map stored as a graph and shortest-path algorithms such as Dijkstra (deep-cse-3-1), adjusted with live traffic speeds; big systems precompute shortcuts so routes compute in milliseconds. Each of these is a whole system by itself; in an interview, naming them and their inputs is enough.

Sharding and hot zones: A natural shard key is the city or region: Dhaka, Chattogram and Sylhet trips rarely interact, so each region's location store and matching service can run independently, close to its users. Inside a big city, shard by geohash prefix. Hot zones are the catch: Gulshan and Motijheel at office hours, or Bashundhara on a concert night, receive far more requests than quiet areas. The fix is the same as lesson 22: split busy prefixes into more shards and merge quiet ones, based on measured load.

Real-life example 1, an Eid-eve rush in Dhaka: At 6 pm before Eid, requests triple near bus terminals and shopping malls. Location writes stay steady (drivers already sent updates), but matching reads jump. Because locations live in memory per cell, each request still checks only nine small cells. The Gabtoli area's shard gets more replicas, surge pricing raises fares there, more drivers head that way, and the atomic assignment guarantees that even in the rush no driver gets two passengers.

Real-life example 2, a food-delivery app: A rider wants biriyani. "Restaurants near me" uses geohash on restaurant locations, which barely move, so a database index on the geohash string plus a cache is enough. Delivery riders, however, move like ride-hailing drivers and use the in-memory cell store. The same app uses two proximity designs because one dataset is static and the other is constantly moving.

Common mistakes: Storing live locations in the main relational database and updating it 125,000 times a second. Searching only the rider's own cell and missing drivers just across the border. Ranking by straight-line distance instead of road ETA. Forgetting to remove stale drivers whose phones went offline. Assigning drivers without an atomic check, causing double assignment. Sharding by driver id, which scatters a single neighbourhood across all shards. Making the map display strongly consistent when a few seconds of staleness is fine.

What exams and interviews ask: Estimate location writes per second; explain why geohash or quadtree is needed; compute or explain geohash prefixes and the neighbour search; compare geohash and quadtree; draw the matching flow; how to prevent double booking; what consistency each part needs; how to handle hot zones.

Recap: Ride-hailing is a proximity problem plus a correct assignment problem. Drivers send locations every few seconds, about 125,000 writes per second for 500,000 drivers, so live positions live in memory, grouped by geohash cells with expiry. A search checks the rider's cell and its 8 neighbours, then ranks by road ETA. Assignment uses atomic compare-and-set so each driver gets one trip and each trip one driver, and trips follow a durable state machine. Regions and busy prefixes become shards. Next, lesson 25 brings everything together in a flash-sale capstone and an interview playbook.

A plain lat/lng B-tree index is one-dimensional and struggles to find nearby points in two dimensions.

Search the rider's cell plus its 8 neighbours, then filter by real distance and rank by road ETA.

lessons.tip: In any location problem, separate what moves fast and can be a bit stale (positions) from what must be exactly right (who got the job), and design each part for its own need.
lessons.task: Open a map app, drop pins at your home and three nearby places, and note their latitude and longitude. Using the rule 1 degree of latitude is about 111 km, estimate how far north-south each pin is from home, then check with the app's distance tool.

quiz.q: 500,000 online drivers each send a location every 4 seconds. About how many writes per second is that?
quiz.explain: 500,000 / 4 = 125,000 writes per second, too many for index updates in a disk database.

quiz.q: Why does a search check the rider's geohash cell plus its 8 neighbours?
options: Because a nearby driver can be just across a cell border with a different prefix
To make the map look nicer
quiz.explain: Points 50 m apart can fall in different cells, so the 3 by 3 block avoids missing them.

quiz.q: Dhanmondi is wh0r0dc and Gulshan is wh0r372. What does their shared prefix "wh0r" tell you?
options: They lie in the same 4-character cell, roughly 39 km by 19.5 km at the equator
quiz.explain: A shared prefix means the same larger cell; longer shared prefixes mean closer points.

quiz.q: Two ride requests pick the same free driver at the same instant. What prevents double assignment?
options: Showing the driver on both maps
An atomic compare-and-set: reserve the driver only if status is still available
quiz.explain: Only one of two racing operations succeeds; the other moves to the next candidate.

quiz.q: Why rank candidate drivers by road ETA rather than straight-line distance?
options: A driver close in metres may be far in minutes because of rivers, one-way roads or traffic
quiz.explain: Real arrival time depends on the road network and traffic, not just the crow-flies distance.

lessons.title: Capstone: Designing a Flash Sale, and the System Design Interview Playbook
lessons.content:
Think of a bakery that announces: "At exactly 12 noon, the first 1,000 people get a cake for 10 taka." By 11:55 a crowd of thousands is pushing at the door. If the baker simply opens the door, people trample each other, the counter collapses, two people grab the same cake and someone pays for a cake that does not exist. A smart baker puts barriers outside, hands out numbered tokens, lets people in a few at a time, keeps an exact count of cakes behind the counter, and puts a cake aside for each token holder for ten minutes while they pay. A flash sale on a Daraz 11.11-style shopping app is that bakery, with two million people instead of a few thousand. It is the perfect capstone, because almost every lesson in this course shows up in it.

The problem in one line: Sell a small, fixed stock (say 1,000 phones at a big discount) to a huge crowd that arrives at the same second, without crashing, without overselling, without charging anyone twice, and while the rest of the shop keeps working normally.

Step 1, requirements (lesson 02): Functional: users see the product page and a countdown; at the start time they can add the item and check out; each user may buy at most one; stock must never go below zero; unpaid reservations return to stock; buyers get confirmation. Non-functional: the system must survive a spike many times normal traffic; product pages must load fast; correctness of stock and payment is non-negotiable (consistency over availability for the stock counter); the rest of the site, including normal orders, must not suffer. A fair queue matters too, because angry users who lost to bots hurt the brand.

Step 2, estimation (lesson 03): Suppose 2 million users show up in the first 10 minutes. On average that is 2,000,000 / 600 = about 3,333 users per second, but the real shape is a wall: most of them press the button within the first few seconds after noon, so the first seconds may see tens of thousands of requests per second, far above average. Only 1,000 can win, which is 1,000 / 2,000,000 = 0.05 percent of visitors. That single ratio is the key insight: 99.95 percent of the traffic will not buy anything, so the design must answer them cheaply and quickly, and only let a tiny fraction touch the expensive, consistent parts. Page weight: if a product page is 1.5 MB, 2 million views is 3 TB of transfer, so it must come from a CDN.

Step 3, the read side, product pages: The product page is the same for everyone: images, description, price. Serve the static parts and images from the CDN (lesson 09) with versioned file names, and the page data from a cache (lesson 08), pre-warmed before the sale so the first request does not stampede the database. The countdown runs in the browser using the server's time sent with the page, so millions of clients do not ask "has it started?" every second. Stock shown on the page ("only a few left") can be approximate and refreshed every few seconds; it is display only, not the source of truth.

Step 4, protecting the front door (lessons 07 and 14): Load balancers spread the traffic. Rate limiting at the gateway stops one user or one IP from sending hundreds of requests, and bot detection blocks scripts. A per-user limit enforces "one checkout attempt every few seconds". Most importantly, a virtual waiting room: when the sale opens, each arriving user gets a place in a queue and a page that says "you are in line". The system lets users through at a rate the checkout can handle, for example 2,000 per second, by giving each admitted user a short-lived signed token. Checkout accepts only requests with a valid token. The waiting room turns a wall of traffic into a steady stream, the token-bucket idea applied to people.

Step 5, the stock counter, preventing overselling: Here is the race. Two users read stock = 1 at the same moment, both see "available", both subtract one and both write: stock becomes 0 but two phones were sold, or with a naive write, minus 1. The fix is an atomic operation. Option A, in the database: UPDATE stock SET count = count - 1 WHERE product_id = 77 AND count > 0, then check whether one row was changed; if zero rows changed, the item is sold out. The database's row lock (deep-cse-4-2) makes this correct. Option B, for higher speed: keep the counter in an in-memory store and use an atomic decrement; if the result is negative, add it back and reply "sold out". Atomic means no other request can sneak in between read and write.

Worked overselling check: Stock starts at 3. Five requests arrive: A, B, C, D, E. With atomic decrement the counter goes 3 to 2 (A wins), 2 to 1 (B wins), 1 to 0 (C wins), 0 to minus 1 for D, so D's decrement is undone and D gets "sold out", and the same for E. Exactly 3 winners, never 4. Without atomicity, A and B could both read 3 and both write 2, and the shop would sell 4 phones from 3. In the interview, saying this race out loud and naming the atomic fix is worth a lot.

Step 6, reservations with expiry: Winning the decrement does not mean paying. So the winner gets a reservation: an order in state reserved with an expiry time, say 10 minutes. If payment succeeds, the order becomes paid. If the timer expires or payment fails, a background job cancels the reservation and adds the unit back to stock, and the next person in the waiting room may get it. This is why "stock" really has two numbers: available and reserved. Without expiry, people who walk away would lock up stock forever.

Step 7, the queue-based order pipeline (lesson 13): After the reservation, the heavy work is asynchronous: the reservation event goes into a queue, and workers create the full order record, call the payment service, and later trigger warehouse picking and notifications (lesson 21). The user sees "reserved, complete payment within 10 minutes" immediately. If workers fall behind, the queue grows but nothing collapses, and every step is idempotent so redelivered messages are harmless.

Step 8, payment correctness: The payment request carries an idempotency key, the order id, so a double tap or a retry never charges twice (lesson 06). The flow across services is a saga (deep-cse-6-3 lesson 21): reserve stock, charge payment, confirm order; if the charge fails, the compensating action releases the stock. Calls to the outside payment gateway use timeouts, retries with backoff and a circuit breaker (lesson 15): if the gateway is struggling, we stop hammering it, keep orders in reserved, and let them expire cleanly rather than leave money and stock in a confused state.

Step 9, isolating the sale from the rest of the shop: The flash sale gets its own resources: separate service instances, a separate queue and a separate counter store, so even if the sale is overwhelmed, normal shoppers buying rice and soap are unaffected. This is the bulkhead pattern. Data is also partitioned: the hot product's counter is one tiny hot key, so it lives alone on a fast node rather than sharing a shard with thousands of other products (lesson 12).

Step 10, observability and failure drills (lessons 15 and 16): Before the sale, the team runs a load test at more than the expected peak and watches the golden signals: traffic, errors, latency percentiles and saturation. Drills: if a counter node dies, a replica takes over, and the database remains the source of truth, so a reconciliation job compares counted sales against paid and reserved orders. If the payment gateway slows, the circuit breaker opens and reservations wait. If the waiting room itself fails, the safe default is to admit fewer people, not everyone. Feature flags let the team pause the sale instantly. A dashboard shows remaining stock, admitted users per second and payment success rate in real time.

The whole picture: Users hit the CDN for the page, pass the rate limiter and the waiting room, get a token, call checkout, which does an atomic decrement and creates a reservation, then a queue drives order creation, payment through a saga, and notifications. A reservation-expiry job returns unpaid stock. Every arrow has a reason you learned in an earlier lesson.

Real-life comparison, a bKash-style Eid salami spike: A wallet on Eid morning also faces a huge spike, but the shape differs: almost every request is a real transfer, so you cannot turn 99.95 percent away. There the answer is more capacity, partitioning by account, strongly consistent ledgers and queues for notifications, rather than a waiting room. Same toolbox, different design, because the requirements and numbers differ. That is the main lesson of system design.

The interview playbook, time plan: In a 45-minute interview, a good split is about 5 minutes for requirements and scope, 5 for estimation, 5 for the API and data model, 15 for the high-level design, 10 for deep dives into one or two hard parts, and 5 for bottlenecks, failures and trade-offs. That adds up to 45. Ask questions before drawing; write the numbers on the board; draw the simple version first, then evolve it; pick the hard part yourself (like overselling here) and go deep.

What to say: Use trade-off phrases, because there is no single right answer: "I choose X because our requirement is Y; the cost is Z, which is acceptable because ...". For example: "The stock counter must be strongly consistent, so I accept that it is a small single hot key on one fast node; product pages can be stale for a few seconds, so I cache them aggressively." Mention failures without being asked: "If this node dies, ...". Interviewers grade reasoning, not memorised diagrams.

Common mistakes in interviews: Jumping to boxes without requirements; no numbers; adding microservices, Kafka and sharding to a problem that needs one database; ignoring the read-to-write ratio; forgetting the race condition; treating every piece as needing the same consistency; never mentioning monitoring or failure; going silent instead of thinking out loud; and arguing with the interviewer's hints instead of using them.

Course recap: You learned to start from requirements and numbers (lessons 01 to 03), to grow a system step by step from one server (04), and the building blocks: networking and APIs (05, 06), load balancers (07), caches and CDNs (08, 09), choosing and modeling databases (10, 11), replicas, shards and IDs (12), queues (13), rate limiting (14), resilience (15), observability, deployment and security (16), and microservices (17). Then you applied them to a URL shortener, chat, news feed, notifications, autocomplete, video streaming and ride-hailing (18 to 24), and today a flash sale.

What next: Cloud Computing (deep-cse-7-3) shows how to run these designs on rented infrastructure with containers and managed services. Advanced Database Systems & Big Data (deep-cse-7-2) goes deep into storage engines and distributed query processing. Fault Tolerant Systems (deep-cse-7-10) studies reliability with real rigour. Data Engineering (deep-cse-7-11) builds the pipelines behind analytics and feeds, and Information Retrieval (deep-cse-7-9) explains search ranking. The best practice of all: pick an app you use daily and design it on paper, numbers first.
key_points: A flash sale sells a tiny fixed stock to a huge simultaneous crowd; 1,000 units for 2 million visitors means 99.95 percent won't buy.
Serve the read side cheaply: CDN for assets, pre-warmed cache for page data, client-side countdown.
Rate limiting, bot detection and a virtual waiting room with signed tokens turn a traffic wall into a steady stream.
Prevent overselling with an atomic conditional update or atomic decrement, never read-then-write.
Winners get a reservation with expiry; unpaid stock returns automatically.
Orders flow through a queue; payment uses idempotency keys, a saga with compensation and a circuit breaker.
Isolate the sale with bulkheads, load test it and watch golden signals during the event.
Interview: requirements, numbers, API, simple design, deep dive, failures, and explicit trade-offs in about 45 minutes.
lessons.tip: For every design you practise, finish by writing one sentence per component in the form 'I chose X because Y, and the cost is Z'. If you cannot write Y and Z, you do not need X yet.
lessons.task: With a friend, play the flash sale on paper: write stock = 3 and let five people try to 'buy' at once, first with read-then-write (both read the number, then write), then with one person allowed to change the number at a time. Count how many sales each way gives.

quiz.q: 1,000 phones and 2,000,000 visitors. What fraction of visitors can win?
quiz.explain: 1,000 / 2,000,000 = 0.0005, or 0.05 percent, so the design must turn away almost everyone cheaply.

quiz.q: Which statement safely prevents overselling in a relational database?
options: SELECT the count, then UPDATE count = new value in a separate step
UPDATE stock SET count = count - 1 WHERE product_id = 77 AND count > 0, then check the affected row count
Cache the count in the browser
Let the CDN decide who wins
quiz.explain: The conditional update is atomic: if zero rows change, the item is sold out, and no two buyers can take the last unit.

quiz.q: What is the job of the virtual waiting room?
options: To admit users to checkout at a rate the system can handle, using short-lived tokens
quiz.explain: It turns a wall of simultaneous users into a steady stream, like a token bucket for people.

quiz.q: Why do reservations have an expiry time?
options: So stock from users who never pay returns to sale automatically
To make the sale end earlier
quiz.explain: Without expiry, abandoned reservations would lock up stock forever.

quiz.q: In a 45-minute system design interview, what should you do before drawing boxes?
options: Draw the most complex architecture you know
Clarify requirements and estimate the numbers
quiz.explain: Requirements and estimation decide which building blocks you actually need.
